orgs.d: Propaganda Due (P2), Licio Gelli's secret Masonic lodge, enrolled people running the Italian and Argentine states and used them for the lodge. Its list of 962 names, found on 17 March 1981, included the heads of all three Italian intelligence services, the Chief of Defence Staff, the financial police commander, 195 officers, 44 MPs and two serving ministers. Parliament's Anselmi commission found in 1984 that it aimed to undermine democracy. Gelli and a member in military intelligence planted false evidence to steer the Bologna bombing inquiry. In Argentina, members including junta admiral Emilio Massera and foreign minister Alberto Vignes got Gelli a diplomatic post, passports and a state honour.
orgs.cite: Italian Parliamentary Commission of Inquiry into the P2 Lodge (Anselmi Commission), 1984; Law 17/1982; Wikipedia 'Propaganda Due'; Il Post, 'Quarant'anni fa la scoperta della P2', 17 March 2021
orgs.reach_src: Countries where P2 had lodges or members, per Wikipedia 'Propaganda Due' (drawing on the Anselmi Commission and later histories).

orgs.d: Members of the United Grand Lodge of England, the governing body of most English Freemasonry (a fraternal order with private rituals, organised in local lodges), have served as police officers, judges and magistrates. Because lodge loyalties among people who investigate and judge cases are not visible to the public, Home Secretary Jack Straw in the 1990s required police officers, judges and magistrates who were Freemasons to declare their membership. In 2009 Straw dropped the rule for judges and magistrates, reportedly over fear of losing at the European Court of Human Rights. In 2026 the High Court upheld the Metropolitan Police's own rule that its officers declare membership. The Grand Lodge has over 200,000 members in more than 6,800 lodges.
orgs.cite: UK Home Office disclosure rule (1998) and its withdrawal (2009); Wikipedia 'United Grand Lodge of England'
orgs.reach_src: UGLE says it runs 33 overseas District Grand Lodges, but the source used does not name them; only the home jurisdiction is listed as documented.

orgs.d: Freemasons of the Grand Orient de France, France's largest Masonic body, reached into the army's promotion system. From 1901 its lodges compiled files on officers' religious and political views, coordinated by its secretary-general Narcisse-Amédée Vadecard, and General Louis André's War Ministry secretly used them to block Catholic officers from promotion; historian Serge Berstein counted 18,818 files in 1901–1903. Deputy Jean Guyot de Villeneuve exposed the scheme in the Chamber of Deputies on 28 October 1904, in what became the Affaire des Fiches ('affair of the index cards'), and André was forced to resign on 15 November 1904.
orgs.cite: Affaire des Fiches, Chamber of Deputies debate 1904; Wikipedia 'Grand Orient de France'; Wikipedia 'Affair of the Cards' (Vadecard, Berstein count, Guyot de Villeneuve 28 Oct 1904, André resignation 15 Nov 1904)
orgs.reach_src: Lodges outside France named in Wikipedia 'Grand Orient de France'.

orgs.d: The Afrikaner Broederbond ('Afrikaner Brotherhood'), a secret society of Afrikaner Calvinist men, got its members into the offices that ran South Africa: every prime minister and state president from 1948 to 1994, the years of National Party and apartheid rule, was a member. After 1948 key public-service posts went to Broederbond members, and members included security chief Hendrik van den Bergh and foreign minister Pik Botha. As early as 1945 Prime Minister Jan Smuts ordered civil servants and state teachers to leave it or resign. Press reports exposed parts of its membership from the 1960s, and Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom's 1978 book 'The Super-Afrikaners' published a list of about 7,500 members. Its last chairman, Tom de Beer (1993–94), went on to chair its successor, the Afrikanerbond.
orgs.cite: Wilkins & Strydom, The Super-Afrikaners (1978); Wikipedia 'Afrikaner Broederbond'

orgs.d: During its 1920s revival, when it had an estimated 3–6 million members, the Ku Klux Klan, a white-supremacist secret order, got members and allies elected and then used them to fill public posts with Klansmen. In Indiana its Grand Dragon (state leader) D. C. Stephenson backed Edward Jackson's 1924 win for governor, and Jackson was later tried for offering a bribe on the Klan leader's behalf to fill state offices with Klansmen. In Colorado the Klan won the governorship and a House majority in 1924, and the governor took direction from its state leader. In Denver a Klansman mayor appointed a Klansman police chief under Klan pressure.
orgs.cite: Enforcement Acts 1870–71; Wikipedia 'Ku Klux Klan'; Encyclopedia of Indianapolis, 'D. C. Stephenson'; Wikipedia 'Ray Sprigle'; Pulitzer Prizes, Raymond Sprigle (1938)
orgs.reach_src: Wikipedia 'Ku Klux Klan' (Saskatchewan organisers 1926–28 and influence in the provincial Conservative party).

orgs.d: The Black Hand, a secret society of Serbian army officers, used its members' posts inside the army and military intelligence to overthrow rulers and organise killings abroad. Its leader, Colonel Dragutin Dimitrijević ('Apis'), had led the May 1903 coup in which officers killed King Alexander Obrenović and Queen Draga in Belgrade, and he went on to head Serbia's military intelligence. The society was formally constituted on 9 May 1911, with members in cells of three to five and hundreds by 1914. Apis allegedly used that position to have three young Bosnian Serbs recruited, trained and smuggled into Bosnia to kill Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo in 1914. Whether Apis was involved, and whether the society's executive committee approved it, is disputed.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Black Hand (Serbia)'

orgs.d: Opus Dei, a Catholic institution of mostly lay members, reaches into institutions through people and foundations tied to it. In Spain, people and foundations linked to Opus Dei held the core of Banco Popular's board and shares, and a 2024 book says the bank sent money to Opus Dei causes, which those involved deny. Pope Francis's decree Ad charisma tuendum (in force 4 August 2022) moved Opus Dei's oversight to the Vatican's Dicastery for the Clergy and barred its head from becoming a bishop.
orgs.cite: Opus Dei, 'Regional Circumscriptions of Opus Dei'; Ad charisma tuendum (2022); Wikipedia 'Opus Dei'; Wikipedia 'Alberto Ullastres'
orgs.reach_src: Opus Dei's own list of countries in its regional circumscriptions (opusdei.org). Hong Kong, Macau, Puerto Rico and Taiwan are also listed there but are not on the canonical country list; 'Congo' on that list is unspecified.

orgs.n: Institute for the Works of Religion (Vatican Bank, IOR)
orgs.d: The Institute for the Works of Religion (IOR), known as the Vatican Bank, was the main shareholder of Italy's Banco Ambrosiano and was tied to the offshore companies through which Ambrosiano's money was moved. When Ambrosiano collapsed in 1982, the missing money was traced to those companies; Ambrosiano's chairman, Roberto Calvi, belonged to the secret P2 Masonic lodge. The IOR denied legal liability, acknowledged 'moral involvement' and in 1984 paid US$224 million to Ambrosiano's creditors. In February 1987 Milan magistrates sought the arrest of IOR president Archbishop Paul Marcinkus and two IOR officials, but Italy's top court ruled that the 1929 Lateran Treaty between Italy and the Holy See shielded them, so they were never tried in Italy.
orgs.cite: 1984 IOR settlement with Ambrosiano creditors; Vatican tribunal 2021; Wikipedia 'Institute for the Works of Religion'

orgs.n: Unification Church / Family Federation for World Peace and Unification
orgs.d: The Unification Church, founded by Sun Myung Moon in Seoul in 1954, pays politicians for favours and has bought into banks through members. In South Korea a Seoul court on 31 August 2026 sentenced church leader Han Hak-ja to two years for arranging luxury gifts for first lady Kim Keon-hee and 100 million won for ruling-party lawmaker Kweon Seong-dong; both were convicted. A special counsel found thousands of followers joined the ruling party before its leadership vote. In 1978 it bought shares in members' names to gain hidden control of a Washington bank, and a Uruguayan bank it part-owned lent about a sixth of its loans to its firms.
orgs.cite: Tokyo District Court dissolution order 25 Mar 2025; Seoul special counsel indictment Oct 2025; Wikipedia 'Unification Church'; Korea Times, 'Unification Church leader sentenced to 2-year prison term in bribery case', 31 Aug 2026; Korea JoongAng Daily on Han's appeal; AP, 'Half of Japan governing lawmakers tied to Unification Church', 8 September 2022
orgs.reach_src: Countries with named activity in Wikipedia 'Unification Church'; the church says it is in about 100 countries.

orgs.d: The Church of Scientology placed its own members in government offices to copy files about the church. Under Operation Snow White (1973–77), run by its Guardian's Office, it put a member in a clerk's job at the Internal Revenue Service (the US tax authority), where he copied the agency's files; eleven senior officials, including Mary Sue Hubbard, were convicted in 1979. Its secret Project Normandy planned to penetrate and 'handle' Clearwater's city offices and local media. In Canada the church placed members as staff in Ontario police and prosecution offices and was convicted in 1992 of breach of public trust.
orgs.cite: United States v. Hubbard (D.D.C. 1979); R. v. Church of Scientology of Toronto (1992); Paris criminal court 2009; Wikipedia 'Operation Snow White'
orgs.reach_src: Countries with Scientology organisations, official inquiries or court cases named in Wikipedia 'Scientology' and 'Operation Snow White'.

orgs.d: Followers of the Islamic preacher Fethullah Gülen moved into Turkey's police, prosecution service, courts and army over decades and, Turkish authorities say, used those posts for the movement rather than the state. Prosecutors say leaked civil-service and judge exam questions went to followers to get them hired, and in 2010 followers won seats on the judicial board and placed about 107 of their people in the top appeals court. Police and prosecutors seen as Gülen-aligned opened the 2013 corruption probe against the government. Courts found officers tied to the movement carried out the 15 July 2016 coup attempt, and 2,745 judges were removed in one day. Gülen denied it.
orgs.cite: Turkish National Security Council designation 2016; Statutory decrees 2016; Maarif Foundation statement 2021 (Turkish Minute); Wikipedia 'Gülen movement'
orgs.reach_src: Countries with Gülen-linked schools named in Wikipedia 'Gülen movement'; Maarif takeover counts from Turkish Minute (2021). 'Congo' in the source is unspecified.

orgs.d: The Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist movement founded by Hassan al-Banna in Egypt in 1928, works to put its members into power through its own parties and offshoots. Its party won Egypt's presidency in 2012 with Mohamed Morsi. Its parties have held seats in Jordan's parliament and, in Kuwait, in parliament and at times the cabinet. In Sudan its leader Turabi was made attorney general in 1979, and its offshoot the National Islamic Front used army officers to seize power in 1989 and placed supporters as judges and prosecutors. In the UAE, the Islah group was accused of trying to infiltrate ministries and universities.
orgs.cite: Egyptian cabinet designation Dec 2013; US State/Treasury designations 13 Jan 2026 (Times of Israel); Wikipedia 'Muslim Brotherhood'
orgs.reach_src: National branches and affiliates named in Wikipedia 'Muslim Brotherhood' and the 2026 US designations. Hamas (Palestine) is not on the canonical country list.

orgs.d: Hizb ut-Tahrir, a pan-Islamist party that aims to restore a caliphate (a single Islamic state under one ruler), has allegedly tried to take power by recruiting army officers into coup plots rather than by elections. It was allegedly behind failed coup attempts in Jordan and Syria in 1968–69 and in Egypt in 1974, and a 2004 Nixon Center report cited credible reports of members in coup plots in Jordan, Syria, Egypt, Tunisia and Iraq. Later cases include a brigadier inside Pakistan's army and officers in a coup plot in Bangladesh. Founded in Jerusalem in 1953, it operates in more than 50 countries and is banned in many, including Russia, Pakistan, Germany, Turkey, the UK and Indonesia (2017).
orgs.cite: National bans; Nixon Center report 2004; Wikipedia 'Hizb ut-Tahrir'
orgs.reach_src: Countries where it operates or has been banned (a ban implies presence), per Wikipedia 'Hizb ut-Tahrir'.

orgs.d: The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), a Hindu nationalist organisation founded in 1925, trains full-time organisers (pracharaks) and places them in politics and public bodies, mainly through the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). It sends one of its own organisers to be the BJP's general secretary, the party's top organisational post, to make sure it follows the RSS chief's instructions. In Modi's second government 38 of 53 ministers had RSS roots. In 2014 the leader of an RSS history body was made head of India's history research council. The official Liberhan inquiry found RSS-family groups worked with the Uttar Pradesh government to let the Babri mosque be demolished in 1992.
orgs.cite: Government of India ban orders 1948, 1975, 1992; Wikipedia 'Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh', 'Hindu Swayamsevak Sangh'
orgs.reach_src: RSS in India; Hindu Swayamsevak Sangh branches named in Wikipedia 'Hindu Swayamsevak Sangh' (which claims 156 countries).

orgs.d: Nippon Kaigi ('Japan Conference'), a nationalist lobby that wants to revise Japan's pacifist constitution, gets its people into government through a league of members of parliament that it runs. After the 2014 reshuffle, 15 of the 19 members of Prime Minister Shinzo Abe's third cabinet belonged to that league, putting the group's agenda in the hands of the ministers running the government. The pattern continued in 2025, when 10 of the 19 ministers in Sanae Takaichi's first cabinet were in the league. Membership is public but little reported, and it drew attention through journalists' counts of cabinet members. Formed in 1997, it claims about 40,000 members.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Nippon Kaigi'

orgs.d: Soka Gakkai, a lay Buddhist movement, put its own party into Japan's government. Its leader Daisaku Ikeda founded Komeito in 1964, and from 1999 until 2025 Komeito sat in government as junior coalition partner of the Liberal Democratic Party. Komeito members ran the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism, which oversees roads, railways and public works, without a break from December 2012 to October 2025, starting with Akihiro Ota and ending with Hiromasa Nakano. The coalition ended in 2025. Soka Gakkai claims 8.27 million member households in Japan; scholar Levi McLaughlin estimated under 4 million individuals in 2018. A 1995 French parliamentary report listed it among 173 groups it called cults.
orgs.cite: French National Assembly report on cults 1995; Wikipedia 'Soka Gakkai'; Wikipedia 'Minister of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism', 'Akihiro Ota', 'Hiromasa Nakano', 'Kazuyoshi Akaba'
orgs.reach_src: Wikipedia 'Soka Gakkai'; Soka Gakkai International claims many more countries, not listed in the source.

orgs.d: Shincheonji Church of Jesus is a South Korean religious movement founded by Lee Man-hee in 1984, and investigators found it signed up tens of thousands of its members to the governing People Power Party (PPP). Party members vote in choosing candidates, so mass sign-ups give a group weight inside a party. A joint prosecutor-police team counted at least 56,472 Shincheonji members registered with the PPP between July 2021 and August 2023, including 6,482 in July 2021 alone. Lee was arrested on 24 June 2026 and, with seven other leaders, indicted on 13 July 2026 under the Political Parties Act, which bars forcing anyone to join a party.
orgs.cite: Suwon District Court 2021; Supreme Court of Korea 2022; Wikipedia 'Shincheonji Church of Jesus'
orgs.reach_src: Wikipedia 'Shincheonji Church of Jesus' (the church claims MOUs in 84 countries).

orgs.d: El Yunque ('The Anvil') is an alleged secret Catholic far-right society whose members, critics say, held posts in Mexico's National Action Party (PAN) and in President Vicente Fox's cabinet without declaring membership. Journalist Álvaro Delgado first described it in his 2003 book, saying it was founded in Puebla in the early 1950s. Named figures, including Governor Juan Manuel Oliva, denied it. In 2014 a Madrid judge said evidence possibly linked members of the Spanish group HazteOír to El Yunque but could not confirm the organisation exists. Nearly all claims come from critics and ex-members, so its reach is unproven.
orgs.cite: Delgado, El Yunque (2003); Madrid court ruling 2014; Wikipedia 'El Yunque (organization)'

orgs.n: Aum Shinrikyo (now Aleph / Hikari no Wa)
orgs.d: Aum Shinrikyo, a Japanese religious group founded by Shoko Asahara in Tokyo in 1987, recruited members inside the Japan Self-Defense Forces (Japan's armed forces) and the Tokyo Metropolitan Police. In May 1996 a former Tokyo police officer who was an Aum follower confessed to shooting Takaji Kunimatsu, head of the National Police Agency, on 30 March 1995, eight days after police raided the group over its sarin nerve-gas attack on the Tokyo subway. Police kept the confession secret; when that was exposed, Tokyo's police chief Yukihiko Inoue resigned. No one was ever charged and the time limit expired in 2010. The group's sarin attacks killed 8 people in Matsumoto in 1994 and 14 in Tokyo in 1995; Asahara and 12 others were executed in July 2018.
orgs.cite: Tokyo District Court verdicts; Wikipedia 'Aum Shinrikyo'; Japan Times, '1995 shooting of police chief goes unsolved', 30 March 2010

orgs.hq: NATO Clandestine Planning Committee (SHAPE) and Allied Clandestine Committee; national HQs e.g. Rome
orgs.d: NATO and Western intelligence services set up secret armed 'stay-behind' networks inside European countries after 1945, meant to resist a Soviet invasion, and placed them inside national armies and security services without most parliaments knowing. They were coordinated by NATO's Clandestine Planning Committee and, from 1958, the Allied Clandestine Committee, which per the Belgian inquiry covered ten countries. In Turkey a US-funded Counter-Guerrilla unit sat hidden inside the army, financed and guided from outside without the prime minister's knowledge. In Belgium, NATO secretly funded the network, which sat inside military intelligence and State Security. The European Parliament on 22 November 1990 called for all such networks to be investigated.
orgs.cite: Andreotti statement to the Chamber of Deputies 24 Oct 1990; European Parliament resolution 22 Nov 1990; Belgian and Swiss parliamentary reports 1990–91
orgs.reach_src: National stay-behind networks documented in Wikipedia 'Operation Gladio' (Italy Gladio; Denmark Absalon; Greece LOK/Sheepskin; Turkey Counter-Guerrilla; Switzerland P-26; Austria OeWSGV; France Plan Bleu etc.).

orgs.d: Ergenekon is the name prosecutors gave an alleged secret 'deep state' network in Turkey; the infiltration claim on this map is about who ran the case against it. Turkey's government says followers of the Gülen movement, a religious network led by the preacher Fethullah Gülen, had placed themselves in the police and courts and used those posts to prosecute 275 people from 2008. On 21 April 2016 Turkey's top appeals court overturned the convictions, finding no proof Ergenekon existed and that evidence came from illegal wiretaps and searches; 235 defendants were acquitted at a 2019 retrial. The Gülenist role is the government's claim, not a court finding.
orgs.cite: Istanbul 13th High Criminal Court 2013; Court of Cassation 2016; Wikipedia 'Ergenekon trials'

orgs.n: Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI)
orgs.d: The Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI), founded in 1972 by Agha Hasan Abedi, took secret control of banks through front owners and paid the officials meant to regulate it. In 1981 the US Federal Reserve approved its takeover of First American Bankshares, a Washington bank, on false assurances that BCCI was not involved; front shareholders included a former Saudi intelligence chief, chairman Clark Clifford was indicted and president Robert Altman was acquitted. It also secretly owned a Brazilian bank through associates of the president, and is accused of paying central bank officials in Argentina and Peru, where about three-tenths of the reserves were then deposited with it.
orgs.cite: Kerry–Brown report, 'The BCCI Affair', US Senate 1992; Luxembourg liquidation order 1991; Kerry–Brown report, 'The BCCI Affair', Executive Summary (irp.fas.org)
orgs.reach_src: Countries named in Wikipedia 'BCCI' (also Cayman Islands and Hong Kong, not on canonical list). The bank said it operated in 78 countries.

orgs.hq: Harold Pratt House, 58 East 68th Street, New York
orgs.d: The Council on Foreign Relations, a private New York membership body founded in 1921, reached inside US foreign policy by writing policy for the government in secret. During the Second World War its War and Peace Studies group, funded by the Rockefeller Foundation, wrote 682 confidential memoranda that the State Department classified and circulated as its own postwar planning. A memo on Greenland was taken up by President Roosevelt, and the US then declared Greenland part of North America. Allen Dulles, who led a Council study group on occupied Germany, carried its plans into the wartime OSS and later ran the CIA.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Council on Foreign Relations'
orgs.reach_src: Offices in New York and Washington only.

orgs.hq: Mont Pèlerin, Switzerland (founded); secretariat Lubbock, Texas
orgs.d: The Mont Pelerin Society, a private membership society of free-market economists founded by Friedrich Hayek on 10 April 1947, has had its members take the government and central-bank posts that set economic policy. Ludwig Erhard was West Germany's economics minister and later chancellor; Luigi Einaudi was Italy's central banker and then president; Václav Klaus was Czech finance minister, prime minister and president; Antonio Martino became an Italian minister after serving as the society's president. Other members in office included UK Chancellor Geoffrey Howe, finance ministers Carlos Cáceres (Chile) and Ruth Richardson (New Zealand), Sri Lankan prime minister Ranil Wickremesinghe, US Secretary of State George Shultz and Federal Reserve chairman Arthur Burns. The overlap is shown by the society's member lists.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Mont Pelerin Society'
orgs.reach_src: Member countries named in Wikipedia 'Mont Pelerin Society'.

orgs.d: Corporations write laws for US states through the American Legislative Exchange Council (ALEC), which pairs corporate members with state legislators to draft 'model bills' that the legislators then introduce at home as their own. By 2011 ALEC had about 2,000 legislator members, over a quarter of all US state legislators; about 1,000 bills based on its model language were introduced each year and roughly 20% became law. After Florida's 2005 'Stand Your Ground' law (allowing deadly force in self-defence without first retreating), ALEC adopted it as a model and similar laws spread to about 30 states. On 13 July 2011 the Center for Media and Democracy published over 800 of the model bills as 'ALEC Exposed'. Coca-Cola and Microsoft left after the 2012 killing of Trayvon Martin.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'American Legislative Exchange Council'; Center for Media and Democracy press release, 13 July 2011 (Common Dreams)

orgs.d: The United Front Work Department, a department of the Chinese Communist Party, works through overseas Chinese groups, donors and recruited insiders to gain influence inside foreign politics. In January 2022 MI5 warned that London solicitor Christine Lee covertly worked with it and had given more than £420,000 to Labour MP Barry Gardiner, whose office employed her son; neither was charged, and China denied it. In Australia a donor tied to it paid Senator Sam Dastyari's bills, and he then backed China's line. In Taiwan a retired admiral and a retired cabinet official were charged with recruiting officers and officials for China's united front system.
orgs.cite: MI5 interference alert Jan 2022; Federal Court of Canada 2022; US sanctions Jan 2021; Wikipedia 'United Front Work Department'; The Week, 'Christine Lee: the Chinese spy with links to a Labour MP', Jan 2022
orgs.reach_src: Countries with documented cases in Wikipedia 'United Front Work Department'.

orgs.d: The Grey Wolves (Ülkü Ocakları), the youth and paramilitary wing of Turkey's Nationalist Movement Party (MHP), worked from inside parts of the Turkish state. Former prosecutor Emin Değer documented its ties to the Counter-Guerrilla, Turkey's branch of NATO's secret stay-behind network, during the 1976–80 street violence, including the 1978 Maraş massacre of over 100 Alevis. The link came to light in the 1996 Susurluk car crash, which killed its second-in-command Abdullah Çatlı, a wanted fugitive, in a car that also carried a police chief and an MP; Interior Minister Mehmet Ağar had signed papers for Çatlı. A parliamentary inquiry followed in 1997. MHP founder Alparslan Türkeş served as deputy prime minister, and since 2018 the MHP has been allied with Erdoğan's AKP.
orgs.cite: Emin Değer; Susurluk parliamentary inquiry 1997; French decree of dissolution Nov 2020
orgs.reach_src: Wikipedia 'Grey Wolves (organization)' (presence and bans). Northern Cyprus is not on the canonical list.

orgs.d: Uniter e.V., an association set up by André Schmitt ('Hannibal'), a soldier from the German army's Special Forces Command (KSK), brought current and former soldiers and police into chat groups preparing for a 'Day X' collapse of public order. Investigators found the chat groups in 2017 while looking into soldiers preparing for Day X. Germany's domestic intelligence agency, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, classed Uniter internally as a review case by February 2020 and placed it under surveillance in early July 2020. Schmitt was fined under the explosives law after training grenades, smoke cartridges and fuses were found on him.
orgs.cite: t-online, 19 February 2020; Star Tribune (AP), 3 July 2020
orgs.reach_src: German authorities' classification and AP reporting.

orgs.d: The Congress for Cultural Freedom was an anti-communist organisation of writers and intellectuals, founded in West Berlin in 1950, that the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) secretly paid for and ran. It was run from Paris by Michael Josselson, a CIA officer, had offices in 35 countries and published more than 20 magazines, including Encounter and Preuves. The New York Times reported the CIA funding in April 1966, and in 1967 former CIA official Thomas Braden admitted the agency had funded it for more than ten years. It was then renamed the International Association for Cultural Freedom, funded by the Ford Foundation, and dissolved in 1979.
orgs.cite: CIA Center for the Study of Intelligence; Saturday Evening Post (Braden), May 1967
orgs.reach_src: Offices, magazines and conferences listed in CCF/IACF publication lists (Bombay 1951, Rangoon, Mexico City, Tokyo, Ibadan, Copenhagen office 1960, Quadrant in Australia, Transition in Uganda)

orgs.n: Asia Foundation (formerly Committee for a Free Asia)
orgs.d: The Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) created the Asia Foundation, a US body running education and governance programmes in Asia, and ran it as a 'proprietary', an organisation the CIA secretly owned while it appeared independent. A CIA memorandum of 22 June 1966 says it was set up in 1954, under the code name DTPILLAR, to do cultural and educational work for the US government 'in ways not open to official U.S. agencies'; it grew out of the Committee for a Free Asia (1951). Its Asian partners therefore could not see that the CIA stood behind it. After press disclosures of CIA funding of private groups in 1966–67, the US government kept the foundation and funded it openly.
orgs.cite: FRUS 1964-68 vol. X doc. 132
orgs.reach_src: CIA memorandum (programme countries not listed in the memo)

orgs.d: The CIA secretly paid for the international programme of the United States National Student Association, a confederation of US college student governments, from the early 1950s to 1967, and used it to help build anti-communist international student bodies. The association was founded at the University of Wisconsin in 1947. Ramparts magazine exposed the funding in February 1967, and the Church Committee (the US Senate inquiry into intelligence abuses) later documented it in 1976. The association cut its CIA ties in August 1967 and merged into the United States Student Association in 1978.
orgs.cite: Ramparts, Feb 1967; Church Committee Book I (1976)

orgs.d: The American Federation of Labor's Free Trade Union Committee passed money, including CIA funds, to anti-communist trade unions in Western Europe. Created at the AFL's 1944 convention with $1 million and run by Jay Lovestone, with Irving Brown as its man in Paris, it funded France's Force Ouvrière from 1948, Italy's CISL union federation, and anti-communist dockworker groups in French, Italian and Greek ports. Historian Anthony Carew found it carried CIA money for about 20 years, starting with the 1948 Italian election.
orgs.cite: Anthony Carew, Labor History (1998); Ted Morgan, A Covert Life (1999)

orgs.n: American Institute for Free Labor Development
orgs.d: The American Institute for Free Labor Development, set up by the US union federation AFL-CIO with business and government partners, trained Latin American union leaders, and its director said Brazilian trainees took part in the 1964 coup that overthrew Brazil's government. It was chartered in August 1962 under the Alliance for Progress (a US aid programme for Latin America) and funded by contracts with USAID, the US aid agency. It trained leaders in their own countries and in the United States. Director William Doherty Jr. said its Brazilian trainees were 'intimately involved' in the coup. In the mid-1990s it was merged into the American Center for International Labor Solidarity.
orgs.cite: Cliff Welch, Latin American Research Review

orgs.d: The Brazilian Institute of Democratic Action (IBAD), an anti-communist body linked to the CIA and financed by multinational companies, paid for the campaigns of many opposition candidates in Brazil's October 1962 elections, so that politicians it funded would sit in office. A parliamentary inquiry commission investigated it, and President João Goulart closed it in 1963. In 1977 former US ambassador Lincoln Gordon admitted that the US had funded the opposition in that election.
orgs.cite: Brazilian CPI on IBAD (1963); Lincoln Gordon (1977)

orgs.d: Radio Free Europe and Radio Liberty were US-run stations broadcasting from Munich into the Soviet bloc that presented themselves as private but were secretly created and funded by the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA). Radio Free Europe was launched in 1949 by the National Committee for a Free Europe, a CIA front organised by Allen Dulles, and Radio Liberty followed in 1951. The CIA and State Department set broad policy for both. After Senator Clifford Case moved in 1971 to take their funding out of the CIA budget, CIA money ended in 1971–72; from 1974 Congress funded them openly. They merged in 1976 and moved to Prague in 1995.
orgs.cite: US Congress (Case bill, 1971); Board for International Broadcasting Act 1973

orgs.n: CIA conduit foundations and front groups (International Organizations Division)
orgs.d: The CIA's International Organizations Division secretly passed money through US private foundations to labour, youth, student and cultural groups, so that the funds looked like ordinary charitable grants. Thomas Braden headed the division from 1950. The Church Committee (the US Senate inquiry into intelligence abuses, reporting in 1976) found CIA money in at least 108 of 700 large grants made by 164 US foundations in 1963–66, and in nearly half of their international grants. The Katzenbach Committee ended covert funding of US educational and private voluntary groups in 1967.
orgs.cite: Church Committee Final Report, Book I (1976), pp. 182-192

orgs.d: Tobacco companies placed their own consultants in posts at the World Health Organization (the UN health agency) and secretly paid 'independent' experts to undermine its tobacco-control work, an expert committee chaired by Swiss scientist Thomas Zeltner found in 2000. The committee said the placements raised 'serious questions about whether the integrity of WHO decision-making has been compromised'. It found the companies also used academic-style groups whose industry funding was hidden, and lobbied delegates from developing countries to resist anti-tobacco resolutions. In 2010 the Council of Europe's Parliamentary Assembly criticised WHO's H1N1 flu decisions for lack of transparency about industry ties.
orgs.cite: Zeltner Committee report (2000); PACE Res. 1749 (2010); CBS News, 'WHO slams Big Tobacco's global tactics', Aug 2000

orgs.d: Sports-marketing companies and World Cup bidders paid officials of FIFA, the world football federation, and its regional bodies for marketing rights and votes, the US Justice Department charged in 2015; seven FIFA officials were arrested at Zurich's Baur au Lac hotel on 27 May 2015. People seeking the 2018 World Cup for Russia allegedly paid members of FIFA's executive committee, the body that chose the hosts, to vote for Russia, and people seeking the 2022 World Cup for Qatar allegedly paid members in return for their votes for Qatar.
orgs.cite: US DOJ press releases, 27 May and 3 Dec 2015
orgs.reach_src: FIFA case defendants who held public office

orgs.d: Cities bidding to host the Olympic Games gave gifts and money to members of the International Olympic Committee, whose votes choose the host. In 1999 the IOC expelled ten members and sanctioned ten others over gifts from the Salt Lake City bid. In 2021 a Brazilian federal court in Rio convicted Carlos Nuzman, head of the Rio 2016 bid, of buying IOC votes, after Rio governor Sérgio Cabral admitted paying $2 million to IOC member Lamine Diack.
orgs.cite: IOC ad hoc commission (1999); 7th Federal Criminal Court, Rio (2021)

orgs.n: Rhodes's secret society and the Milner Group (per Carroll Quigley)
orgs.d: Historian Carroll Quigley wrote that Cecil Rhodes founded a secret society in London in 1891 to extend British rule, and that its circle, later called the Milner Group, placed its members in government. Quigley names Alfred Milner, Reginald Brett (Lord Esher) and W. T. Stead as its 'Junta of Three'. Milner, whom Quigley treats as the leader of Rhodes's society after him, ran British South Africa from 1897 to 1905, and Quigley holds that the group caused the Boer War. The society's existence and membership rest on Quigley.
orgs.cite: Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment (written c. 1949, published 1981), ch. 1 and 3; Tragedy and Hope (1966), pp. 950–952
orgs.reach_src: Countries where Quigley places its members in office; membership itself rests on Quigley

orgs.d: Alfred Milner, Britain's High Commissioner in South Africa, recruited young Oxford graduates from 1901 to staff the colonial government of the Transvaal and Orange River Colony after the Boer War; the group, known as Milner's Kindergarten, then used those posts to push for union of the four colonies, achieved in 1910. Members included Lionel Curtis, Philip Kerr, Robert Brand, Geoffrey Dawson and Patrick Duncan. On returning to England in 1909 the group renamed itself the Round Table and continued as a policy network.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Milner's Kindergarten'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, ch. 4

orgs.d: The Round Table was a network of British imperialists formed in 1909 by Alfred Milner's former staff to promote imperial unity, and historian Carroll Quigley argues its members were placed in government and the press. Philip Kerr, founding editor of the network's journal, joined Lloyd George's new Downing Street secretariat as private secretary in 1916, and a historian found Milner's influence on its staffing. Lionel Curtis's study group with India Office officials worked out 'dyarchy', the shared rule written into the Government of India Act 1919. Geoffrey Dawson edited The Times during the appeasement of Hitler and cut stories to spare German opinion. The membership claims are Quigley's.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Round Table movement'; Quigley, Tragedy and Hope, pp. 950–951

orgs.n: Royal Institute of International Affairs (Chatham House)
orgs.d: Chatham House, formally the Royal Institute of International Affairs, is a private London foreign-policy institute whose wartime research unit was taken into the Foreign Office. During the Second World War it ran a Foreign Research and Press Service under the historian Arnold Toynbee, and from 1943 to 1946 that service was moved into the Foreign Office, so the institute's staff worked inside the ministry. Chatham House grew from a meeting that Lionel Curtis, a member of Lord Milner's network of imperialists, called in Paris on 30 May 1919; it opened in 1920 and received a royal charter in 1926.
orgs.cite: Chatham House, 'The Hotel Majestic and the Origins of Chatham House' (2019); Wikipedia 'Chatham House'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, ch. 10

orgs.d: The US Senate Internal Security Subcommittee under Pat McCarran reported in 1952 that the Institute of Pacific Relations (IPR), a private research body on Asia founded in 1925 and funded mainly by the Rockefeller and Carnegie foundations, 'was a vehicle used by the Communists' to shape US Far East policy through its staff and writers. The subcommittee reviewed about 20,000 IPR documents; Owen Lattimore, editor of the IPR journal, was a central target. The IRS revoked the IPR's tax exemption in 1955, but courts rejected all the IRS allegations in 1959. Historian Carroll Quigley argued that Wall Street money and the Milner Group, not Communists, had the greater influence on it. The infiltration claim is the subcommittee's, and remains disputed.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Institute of Pacific Relations'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, ch. 10
orgs.reach_src: Senate Internal Security Subcommittee 1952 (State Department policy)

orgs.d: The Wagner Group, a Russian mercenary company financed by Yevgeny Prigozhin and used by the Russian state, placed fighters, bodyguards and advisers inside governments in Syria and Africa, paid partly in mining and timber concessions. In the Central African Republic a Russian, Valery Zakharov, served as security adviser to President Faustin-Archange Touadéra; Ukraine's SBU said he was himself a Wagner member, and a November 2021 EU report found most deployed Central African army units operated under Wagner command or supervision. Wagner's African firms included Meroe Gold (Sudan) and Lobaye Invest (CAR). After Prigozhin's death in 2023 most operations moved to Russia's defence ministry.
orgs.cite: US Treasury designations 2020–2023; UN Panel of Experts on Libya (2020); Wikipedia; Wikipedia 'Wagner Group activities in the Central African Republic' (Zakharov; EEAS report Nov 2021)
orgs.reach_src: UN Panel on Libya; US Treasury; Wikipedia country articles

orgs.n: Prigozhin political-technologist and disinformation network (incl. AFRIC)
orgs.d: This was a network of Russian political strategists, social-media operators and front groups paid through companies of Yevgeny Prigozhin, the businessman behind the Wagner Group, that worked to shape who held office in African states from 2018. In Madagascar's 2018 presidential race, Proekt and the BBC reported, 15–20 of these strategists dealt with as many as eight candidates; candidate André Mailhol said he was given €5,000 in cash and ex-prime minister Omer Beriziky said he was promised $2 million. The winner, Andry Rajoelina, denied being Russia's candidate. Facebook removed three of the network's operations targeting eight African states in October 2019.
orgs.cite: Facebook takedown 30 Oct 2019; Stanford Internet Observatory; Proekt/BBC (2019); EPDE (2020)
orgs.reach_src: Facebook Oct 2019 announcement; EPDE AFRIC report

orgs.d: Hezbollah, a Shia Islamist armed movement in Lebanon aligned with Iran's Revolutionary Guards, reaches into foreign governments through financiers and people tied to it who pay leaders for state favours. In the Gambia, Hezbollah-linked financiers got state monopolies and half the state telecom firms through President Jammeh, sending over $100 million towards Hezbollah. In Paraguay, the US Treasury says people tied to it paid bribes that representatives of former president Horacio Cartes and the sitting vice-president collected. At least 28 countries list its armed wing as terrorist, and since August 2025 Lebanon's cabinet has backed an army plan to disarm it.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia; US Treasury designations

orgs.n: IRGC Quds Force and allied militia network
orgs.d: Iran's Quds Force, the foreign-operations branch of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), arms, trains and directs allied militias, several of which sit inside other countries' official security forces, notably Iraq's Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), a state-paid umbrella of mostly Shia militias. The PMF's deputy head, Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis, also led the Iran-backed militia Kataib Hezbollah and was killed alongside Quds Force commander Qassem Soleimani in a US strike in Baghdad in January 2020. The US listed the IRGC, including the Quds Force, as a Foreign Terrorist Organization in April 2019, and courts in several countries have convicted people described as its operatives.
orgs.cite: US State Department FTO listing (2019); Wikipedia; AP/PBS NewsHour, 'Iraqi militant killed in U.S. strike worked with Iran for decades', 3 Jan 2020; Al Jazeera, 7 Jan 2020

orgs.d: The Gupta brothers, Ajay, Atul and Rajesh, businessmen whose network was built around Sahara Computers and Oakbay Investments, used their closeness to President Jacob Zuma to get ministers and heads of state-owned companies to act for their businesses, a practice South Africans call 'state capture'. In March 2016 deputy finance minister Mcebisi Jonas said Gupta family members had offered him the post of finance minister to replace Nhlanhla Nene, shortly before Zuma removed Nene; the family denied it. The Zondo Commission, a judicial inquiry that reported in 2022, found ministers and state-company heads acted corruptly on behalf of the Guptas and their associate Salim Essa. The US sanctioned the brothers in 2019 and the UK in 2021. They have lived in Dubai since 2016.
orgs.cite: Zondo Commission (2022); US Treasury SM789 (2019); Statement by Deputy Minister of Finance Mcebisi Jonas, 16 March 2016 (National Treasury)

orgs.d: McKinsey & Company, a US management consultancy, bribed officials at Eskom, South Africa's state power company, and Transnet, its state freight company, in 2012–2016 to win contracts, according to a 2024 US Justice Department settlement. It worked on those contracts alongside Trillian, a firm linked to the Gupta family's state-capture network. McKinsey repaid about R1 billion to Eskom and R870 million to Transnet, and in 2024 paid a $122 million US penalty under a deferred prosecution agreement (a deal in which charges are dropped if the company meets set conditions).
orgs.cite: US Department of Justice (2024); Zondo Commission

orgs.d: People working for Huawei, China's largest telecoms-equipment maker, allegedly reached inside the European Parliament and Polish state bodies. Belgian prosecutors allege that associates of a former Huawei lobbyist gave gifts and payments to members of the European Parliament (MEPs), including up to €15,000 for writing and €1,500 for co-signing a 2021 letter against limits on foreign 5G equipment; eight people have been charged, and in June 2026 Parliament lifted the immunity of MEP Fulvio Martusciello, who denies wrongdoing. In Poland a senior Huawei employee and a former counter-intelligence official were charged in 2019 with spying for China; both pleaded not guilty.
orgs.cite: Wall Street Journal (2019); Le Monde (2018)

orgs.d: The Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank in Washington, organised Project 2025, a 900-plus-page plan for a conservative administration written with dozens of partner groups, and several of its authors then took the posts that carry it out. They include Russ Vought, who became director of the Office of Management and Budget (the White House budget office), and Brendan Carr, who became chairman of the Federal Communications Commission (the broadcast and telecoms regulator), in the second Trump administration in 2025.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Project 2025'; Axios, 26 November 2024

orgs.n: Federalist Society for Law and Public Policy Studies
orgs.d: The Federalist Society, a network of about 70,000 conservative and libertarian lawyers, helped draw up Donald Trump's 2016 Supreme Court shortlist, and 43 of his first 51 appeals-court nominees were members. Appeals courts are the federal courts just below the Supreme Court, and their judges serve for life. The society formed in April 1982 at Yale, Harvard and Chicago law schools. The liberal American Constitution Society was founded in 2001 as its counterpart.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Federalist Society'; New York Times, 16 March 2020

orgs.d: The Frente Parlamentar Evangélica is a registered cross-party caucus (a voting bloc of legislators from different parties) inside Brazil's National Congress, through which evangelical churches organise their members in office to push church causes in law. Its vice-president said in February 2023 that 132 deputies and 14 senators had signed on. Agência Pública counted 93 deputies tied to evangelical churches, led by the Assemblies of God, the Baptists and the Universal Church, which shows which churches supply most of the bloc's members.
orgs.cite: Agência Pública, February 2023

orgs.n: Church of God Ministry of Jesus Christ International
orgs.d: The Church of God Ministry of Jesus Christ International, a Pentecostal church founded in Colombia, has its own political party, MIRA, which puts church members into Colombia's Senate, House of Representatives and local councils. MIRA (Independent Movement of Absolute Renovation) was founded in 2000 and lists the church as its religion. The church therefore reaches lawmaking bodies directly through elected members who answer to the same religious movement, rather than by lobbying from outside.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Independent Movement of Absolute Renovation'

orgs.d: China's government placed Confucius Institutes, Chinese-language and culture centres, inside foreign universities and schools, funded through its education ministry (formerly via the agency Hanban). A US Senate subcommittee reported in February 2019 that Hanban chose the teachers, who signed contracts promising not to harm China's national interests, and that China had given US universities over $158 million since 2006. The National Association of Scholars counted about 550 institutes worldwide in 2020. The US State Department designated their US centre a foreign mission of China on 13 August 2020, and 104 of 118 US institutes had closed by June 2022.
orgs.cite: RFA, 13 August 2020; The Diplomat, November 2023; US Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, 'China's Impact on the US Education System', February 2019, via RFA, 1 March 2019

orgs.d: Philippine offshore gaming operators (POGOs), online gambling firms mostly owned by Chinese nationals, got their people into Philippine local government and paid officials. In Bamban, Alice Guo, later ruled to be a Chinese citizen, won the mayoralty of the town where a POGO hub ran; in August 2024 the Ombudsman (who disciplines officials) dismissed her, ruling she had planned the hub and run for mayor to protect it. In the 'pastillas' scheme, brokers paid immigration officers at Manila's airport to wave Chinese workers through without checks. POGOs grew from 2016 under licences from the regulator PAGCOR, and Congress banned them by law in October 2025.
orgs.cite: Philippine Senate hearings 2024; Executive Order 74 (2024); Anti-POGO Act (2025); Office of the Ombudsman ruling on Alice Guo, via BenarNews, 14 August 2024

orgs.n: Ma Ba Tha (Association for the Protection of Race and Religion)
orgs.d: Ma Ba Tha, a Buddhist nationalist monks' organisation formed in Myanmar in January 2014, wrote laws from outside Parliament: its members proposed the texts of four Race and Religion Protection Laws, which restrict interfaith marriage and religious conversion, and Parliament passed them in 2015. The group is linked to the 969 movement and the monk Wirathu. The state clergy council, the government-backed body that oversees Buddhist monks, ordered it disbanded in May 2017, but it continued under new names, and its leading figures have received donations and honours from military leaders.
orgs.cite: Human Rights Watch 2014; State Sangha Maha Nayaka Committee order, May 2017

orgs.d: Bodu Bala Sena, a Sinhala Buddhist nationalist organisation of monks founded in Sri Lanka in 2012, got its leader into a state post: in 2021 President Gotabaya Rajapaksa appointed its general secretary, Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara, to chair a government task force on a 'One Country, One Law' legal policy. The tie went back to 2013, when Rajapaksa, then Defence Secretary, opened the group's training centre. Gnanasara has been jailed several times; in 2026 the Supreme Court voided the presidential pardon he received in 2019 and he was returned to prison.
orgs.cite: Daily FT, 27 October 2021; Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, 10 September 2026

orgs.d: Fight Impunity, a Brussels non-profit set up by former Italian Member of the European Parliament (MEP) Pier Antonio Panzeri, served, according to Belgian prosecutors, as the channel through which Qatar and Morocco paid cash to MEPs to influence the Parliament's work. The case, known as 'Qatargate', came to light when police raided its office on 9 December 2022 and found about €600,000 in cash at Panzeri's home. Parliament vice-president Eva Kaili was charged, and MEPs Marc Tarabella and Andrea Cozzolino, who led its Gulf and Maghreb delegations, were charged or arrested after their immunity was lifted. Panzeri agreed a plea deal in January 2023.
orgs.cite: Belgian Federal Prosecutor's Office; Qatargate case file reported by Der Spiegel and Financial Times
orgs.reach_src: Belgian investigation as reported (suspects' nationalities and paying states)

orgs.d: Azerbaijan's government used gifts, paid trips and cash to buy the votes of European politicians, especially members of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE), a human-rights body that monitors elections and political prisoners; the European Stability Initiative named this 'caviar diplomacy' in 2012. A PACE investigation body reported in April 2018 on breaches by members from several countries. An Italian court jailed former PACE group leader Luca Volontè in 2021, and the Bundestag lifted two members' immunity from prosecution in 2021. The 2017 Azerbaijani Laundromat leak showed $2.9 billion moved through Danske Bank Estonia in 2012–2014, part of it to politicians.
orgs.cite: European Stability Initiative reports 2012 and 2016; PACE Independent Investigation Body report, 2018; OCCRP 2017
orgs.reach_src: PACE investigation body report 2018 and OCCRP laundromat recipients

orgs.d: Viktor Medvedchuk, a pro-Kremlin Ukrainian politician exchanged to Russia in 2022, paid European politicians to carry Russian positions inside their parliaments. Czech intelligence exposed the Prague-based site Voice of Europe in March 2024 as run for him by Artem Marchevskyi and used to pay European politicians; the EU sanctioned it in May 2024. In the UK, former Member of the European Parliament Nathan Gill was jailed in 2025 for taking bribes in 2018–2019 from Ukrainian MP Oleg Voloshyn, who passed on Medvedchuk's requests for speeches and statements.
orgs.cite: Czech Security Information Service 2024; EU Council sanctions May 2024; Old Bailey sentencing remarks, 21 November 2025
orgs.reach_src: Voice of Europe exposure 2024 (Czech, Belgian and Polish investigations; German politicians investigated) and the Gill case

orgs.n: Ilan Shor network (Șor Party and successors)
orgs.d: Russian money went undeclared into Moldovan elected offices through the party built around businessman Ilan Shor: in August 2025 its governor of the autonomous region of Gagauzia, Evghenia Guțul, was sentenced to 7 years for using undeclared Russian money, and its vice-president Marina Tauber was sentenced to 7½ years in 2025 for illegal party financing. Moldova's Constitutional Court declared the Șor Party unconstitutional on 19 June 2023, and its members have continued under successor parties.
orgs.cite: Constitutional Court of Moldova 2023; Moldovan court sentences 2025

orgs.n: Big Four accounting firms (Deloitte, EY, KPMG, PwC)
orgs.d: The Big Four accounting firms (Deloitte, EY, KPMG and PwC) get their staff inside governments by selling advice to ministries and lending, or 'seconding', employees to them, and the firms' other clients have benefited. In the PwC Australia case of 2023, an Australian Senate inquiry found that a PwC partner who advised the Treasury on new tax laws shared the confidential plans inside PwC to win business from clients avoiding tax. The UK Public Accounts Committee criticised in 2013 the practice of staff seconded to the Treasury. In South Africa, KPMG withdrew a 2017 report it had written for the tax service SARS. The firms also audit most large companies.
orgs.cite: Australian Senate inquiry 2023; UK Public Accounts Committee 2013; Parliament of Australia, joint committee report, Chapter 2 'The PwC breach of confidentiality obligations', 2023

orgs.d: Bain & Company, a US management-consulting firm founded in Boston in 1973, worked from inside South Africa's tax service, the South African Revenue Service (SARS), with President Jacob Zuma and SARS head Tom Moyane to restructure and weaken it, according to the Zondo Commission, the judicial inquiry into the capture of state bodies, in its Part 1 report of January 2022. South Africa suspended Bain from state work, and the UK barred it from government contracts in 2022, lifting the bar in 2023.
orgs.cite: Zondo Commission Part 1, Jan 2022

orgs.d: Uber is a US ride-hailing company that, according to leaked internal files, got a serving minister to act for it while it operated in breach of local taxi laws. The Uber Files, 124,000 internal documents from 2013–2017 published in July 2022, show Emmanuel Macron, as France's economy minister in 2015, working behind the scenes for Uber; after his office was contacted, a Marseille police ban on an Uber service was lifted two days later. Macron said he was proud of supporting the company.
orgs.cite: The Guardian / ICIJ, Uber Files, July 2022

orgs.d: Lex Greensill got inside the UK government as an adviser in the Cabinet Office, the department that runs central government, before founding the supply-chain finance firm Greensill Capital, which lends against invoices. The firm then employed former Prime Minister David Cameron, who lobbied ministers for it in 2020. Greensill collapsed in March 2021, and inquiries in 2021 by the Treasury Committee and by Nigel Boardman for the government examined how its founder's role inside government and Cameron's lobbying gave the firm access.
orgs.cite: UK Treasury Committee 2021; Boardman review 2021

orgs.d: Odebrecht, a Brazilian construction and engineering group renamed Novonor in 2020, paid officials in 12 countries to win public works contracts, running the payments through an in-house bribery unit it called the 'Structured Operations Division'. In December 2016 it admitted to US, Brazilian and Swiss authorities that it had paid $788 million in bribes, and it paid a record fine. The case led to convictions of presidents and ministers in Peru, Ecuador and elsewhere in Latin America.
orgs.cite: US DOJ plea agreement, Dec 2016
orgs.reach_src: US DOJ statement of facts (Wikipedia summary)

orgs.d: Privinvest, an Emirati-Lebanese shipbuilding group owned by Iskandar Safa (died 2024), paid Mozambique's Finance Minister Manuel Chang $7 million, US prosecutors said, while supplying boats under $2 billion in state-guaranteed loans that were hidden from the country's parliament and the IMF (the 'hidden debt' deals). Chang was tried in New York in 2024. London's High Court let Mozambique recover over $825 million from Safa's estate and companies.
orgs.cite: US v. Chang (E.D.N.Y.) 2024; UK High Court 2024

orgs.d: Goldman Sachs, the US investment bank, reaches into governments in two ways. Its bankers paid officials at Malaysia's state fund 1MDB and at Abu Dhabi's state funds to win the fund's bond business, and money from those bonds was diverted to bribe officials; Goldman's Malaysian unit pleaded guilty in the US in October 2020. Its executives also move into the posts that regulate or rescue banks. As Treasury Secretary, former co-chairman Robert Rubin argued for repealing a banking law the industry wanted gone, and former chief Henry Paulson ran the AIG rescue that paid Goldman $12.9 billion. A former Goldman economist led the New York Fed, which supervises Goldman.
orgs.cite: Goldman–Malaysia settlement July 2020; EU ethics committee Oct 2016; OCCRP, 'Goldman Sachs Pleads Guilty to $1 Billion Bribery Scheme Charges', October 2020

orgs.d: Glencore, a Swiss-based commodity trader and miner founded as Marc Rich + Co, paid officials in several African and Latin American countries to obtain oil, mining rights and favourable treatment. In 2022 it pleaded guilty to bribery in the US and UK, and agreed to pay the Democratic Republic of Congo $180 million to settle claims there.
orgs.cite: US DOJ and UK SFO, 2022
orgs.reach_src: UK SFO statement of facts; DRC settlement

orgs.d: Gunvor, a Geneva-based oil trader, paid more than $97 million to intermediaries between 2012 and 2020, part of it to bribe officials of Ecuador's state oil company Petroecuador, including senior official Nilsen Arias, who was also bought a gold Patek Philippe watch. In return Gunvor won oil-backed loan deals, arranged through other state companies acting as fronts so that no competitive bidding was required, and received confidential Petroecuador information; it made more than $384 million in profit. The money moved through US banks via shell companies in Panama and the British Virgin Islands. Gunvor pleaded guilty in New York in March 2024 and paid about $661 million to US and Swiss authorities.
orgs.cite: Swiss OAG 2019 and 2024; US DOJ 2024; US Attorney E.D.N.Y., 'Gunvor S.A. pleads guilty to scheme to bribe Ecuadorian officials', 1 March 2024

orgs.d: Trafigura, a commodity trader founded in 1993, paid officials at state oil companies to win business. It pleaded guilty in the US in 2024 to bribing officials of Petrobras, Brazil's state-controlled oil company, and was convicted in Switzerland in 2025 over bribes to an Angolan official (the Swiss verdict is under appeal).
orgs.cite: US DOJ 2024; Swiss Federal Criminal Court 2025

orgs.d: SNC-Lavalin, a Canadian engineering company renamed AtkinsRéalis in 2023, paid officials to win work abroad. In Libya it paid about C$47.7 million in bribes to officials tied to the ruling Gaddafi family, linked to Saadi Gaddafi, and it pleaded guilty in the resulting court case in 2019. The bribery charges over this work led it to lobby Ottawa for a deferred-prosecution law, which lets a company pay penalties instead of going to trial.
orgs.cite: Conflict of Interest and Ethics Commissioner, Aug 2019

orgs.d: The Adani Group, an Indian conglomerate in ports, airports, power and mining founded by Gautam Adani, promised more than $250 million in bribes to Indian government officials between 2020 and 2024 to win government solar power supply contracts, US prosecutors charged in November 2024. The contracts were projected to earn over $2 billion in profit over 20 years. The charges, against Adani and associates, were filed in New York because the scheme was hidden from US investors who were asked to fund the projects. The Adani Group called the charges baseless. Kenya cancelled its airport and power deals with Adani the next day.
orgs.cite: US Attorney E.D.N.Y. indictment, Nov 2024; PV Tech, 'Gautam Adani charged in US with US$250 million solar contract bribery scheme', Nov 2024; Semafor, 21 Nov 2024

orgs.d: FirstEnergy, an Ohio electric utility, funnelled about $60 million to a group around Ohio House Speaker Larry Householder, the leader of the state's lower house, in return for passing HB 6, a law that bailed out its nuclear plants with charges on customers' bills. Federal prosecutors brought the case, and FirstEnergy paid a $230 million penalty in 2021 under an agreement admitting the scheme.
orgs.cite: US Attorney S.D. Ohio, 2021–23

orgs.d: Commonwealth Edison (ComEd), Chicago's electric utility owned by Exelon, gave jobs and contracts to associates of Illinois House Speaker Michael Madigan to win his support for laws it wanted. It admitted the scheme in a 2020 deferred prosecution agreement, a deal in which a company admits wrongdoing and pays a penalty to avoid trial. Madigan, the longest-serving speaker of a US state legislature, was convicted in February 2025.
orgs.cite: US Attorney N.D. Ill.; verdict Feb 2025

orgs.d: Pharmally Pharmaceutical Corp., a company founded in 2019 with ₱625,000 in capital, won ₱8.68 billion in Philippine pandemic supply contracts, and a Senate inquiry linked it to Michael Yang, a former economic adviser to President Duterte, raising the question of whether a presidential insider steered state purchasing to it. The Senate Blue Ribbon Committee, which investigates misconduct by officials, held the inquiry in 2021–22.
orgs.cite: Senate Blue Ribbon Committee 2021–22

orgs.n: Sun Kian Ip Group (Ng Lap Seng)
orgs.d: Ng Lap Seng, owner of the Macau property group Sun Kian Ip, bribed John Ashe while Ashe was President of the UN General Assembly, the body of all UN member states, to back a UN conference centre Ng wanted to build in Macau. A New York federal jury convicted Ng in 2017.
orgs.cite: US District Court S.D.N.Y. 2017

orgs.d: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) lends to countries in crisis on condition that they change their policies, and it has pressed for its own people to be placed inside the governments it lends to. In Côte d'Ivoire in 1990 it pressed for Ouattara, its own former department director, to be put in charge of economic policy, where he ran the country under its programme. In Liberia from 2005, foreign controllers designed and funded by the IMF, World Bank and US agencies sat inside the country's main state firms and co-signed their major transactions.
orgs.cite: IMF Articles of Agreement

orgs.d: Pentecostal, charismatic and evangelical Protestant churches get their members and pastors into legislatures and governments and organise them there as voting blocs; this generic key is used when no single named church is the vehicle. In Brazil they sit as the Evangelical Parliamentary Front, with 213 deputies and 26 senators in the current legislature, which votes as a bloc mostly with the conservatives. In 2022 two pastors with no government posts steered money from the education ministry's school fund, allegedly for bribes, with the minister linked to the scheme. Each case record names the specific church.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Evangelical Parliamentary Front'; case records

orgs.n: Universal Church of the Kingdom of God (IURD)
orgs.d: The Universal Church of the Kingdom of God (IURD), a neo-Pentecostal church founded in Rio de Janeiro in 1977 by Edir Macedo and run from the top, built its own political party to get its clergy into office. Its pastors founded the Republicanos party in 2005 as a base for its bishops to run for office. Church bishop Marcos Pereira leads the party and became a federal minister in 2016. Through the party the church holds seats in Brazil's Congress.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Universal Church of the Kingdom of God' and 'Republicanos'
orgs.reach_src: Wikipedia article (bans, investigations and press reports by country; Crivella's mission in South Africa)

orgs.hq: Redemption City of God, Mowe, Ogun State
orgs.d: The Redeemed Christian Church of God, a Nigerian holiness Pentecostal church founded in 1952 by Josiah Akindayomi, had one of its senior pastors in Nigeria's second-highest office: Yemi Osinbajo, senior pastor of its Lagos Province 48, was Vice President of Nigeria from 2015 to 2023. The church reports a presence in 197 countries and territories and over 5 million members in Nigeria.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Redeemed Christian Church of God' and 'Yemi Osinbajo'

orgs.d: Family Watch International (FWI), an Arizona-based Christian lobbying group founded in 1999 by Sharon Slater, uses its UN consultative status and contacts with African lawmakers to push laws against abortion, sex education and homosexuality. A Ugandan activist named Slater as having lobbied for Uganda's 2023 Anti-Homosexuality Act, which sets life imprisonment and, in some cases, death. FWI had earlier called its position on the 2009 version of the bill 'complicated'. The law took effect, and the World Bank halted new lending to Uganda in August 2023 over it.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Family Watch International'

orgs.n: Hereditary Sufi shrine lineages (pirs / makhdooms) of Pakistan
orgs.d: Families that hold hereditary custody of Sufi shrines in Pakistan (pirs or makhdooms, religious lineages whose devotees follow their guidance) turn devotees' loyalty into votes and send family members into national cabinets. Shah Mahmood Qureshi, custodian of the Bahauddin Zakariya shrine in Multan, was foreign minister twice. The shrines also give these families income from offerings, which supports their political careers. This is a generic key for such lineages.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Shah Mahmood Qureshi'

orgs.d: The Knights of Columbus, a Catholic men's fraternal order (a membership society with lodges, here called councils) and insurance provider founded in New Haven in 1882, counts holders of high office among its members, including President John F. Kennedy and Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito. Its policy positions became an issue in the 2018–19 Senate confirmation of judge Brian Buescher, when senators asked whether membership would shape his rulings. It has councils in the United States, the Philippines and other countries.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Knights of Columbus'

orgs.d: Jesus Is Lord Church Worldwide, a Philippine Pentecostal church begun in 1978 by Eddie Villanueva with a Bible-study group at the Polytechnic University of the Philippines, has put its founding family into Congress. Villanueva ran for president in 2004 and 2010 and was a Deputy Speaker of the House from 2019 to 2022, and his son Joel Villanueva is a senator. Villanueva also founded the Philippines for Jesus Movement, a group of more than forty bishops.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Eddie Villanueva' and 'Jesus Is Lord Church'

orgs.n: Operation Rubicon / Thesaurus (CIA–BND ownership of Crypto AG)
orgs.d: The US CIA and West Germany's BND intelligence services secretly owned the Swiss company Crypto AG, which sold encryption machines to governments, and used it to read the coded messages of its government customers in more than 120 countries. The BND was co-owner from 1970 until about 1993 and the CIA until about 2018; the operation was called Thesaurus, later Rubicon. The Washington Post, ZDF and SRF revealed it on 11 February 2020, and the Swiss parliament held an inquiry the same year.
orgs.cite: Washington Post/ZDF/SRF, 11 Feb 2020; Swiss parliamentary inquiry 2020

orgs.d: Saudi Arabia's government pays insiders in foreign companies and states. Officials around Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman recruited a Twitter employee, Ahmad Abouammo, and paid him to look up private data on critics of the kingdom who used the platform; the FBI investigated, and a US jury convicted him in 2022. In Yemen a Saudi government 'Special Committee' kept about 2,700 political, tribal and military leaders on monthly pay and directed named sheikhs and a serving brigade commander.
orgs.cite: US v. Abouammo (N.D. Cal. 2022); Saudi anti-corruption committee statement 2019

orgs.d: North Korea places programmers inside foreign companies by having them take remote jobs under stolen or fake identities, mostly working from China and Russia, and their wages fund the state's weapons programmes. Paid facilitators run 'laptop farms', houses full of company laptops that make the workers appear to be in the employer's country. US prosecutors have found workers at hundreds of US firms in cases from 2024 to 2026, and Google reported a move into Europe in 2025.
orgs.cite: US Department of Justice cases 2024–26; Google Threat Intelligence Group, Apr 2025

orgs.d: China's Ministry of State Security, its civilian intelligence ministry, and other Chinese intelligence officers recruit and pay people inside foreign governments, armed forces and companies. In the US it had translator Larry Wu-tai Chin inside the CIA for three decades, recruited the FBI's top China informant Katrina Leung, and gave State Department employee Candace Claiborne gifts for documents; officer Xu Yanjun was convicted in 2021 of trying to recruit GE Aviation engineers. In Taiwan, agents paid an aide in the Presidential Office, recruited army major general Lo Hsien-che and paid soldiers guarding the Presidential Office. Other cases reach South Korea, Greece and the Philippines.
orgs.cite: US v. Xu Yanjun (S.D. Ohio 2021); 13-country joint advisory Aug 2025

orgs.d: The US National Security Agency (NSA), the country's signals-intelligence agency, paid the security company RSA $10 million to make Dual_EC, a random-number generator the NSA had designed with a weakness, the default in RSA's software, Reuters reported in December 2013. Random numbers are used to create encryption keys, so a predictable generator can let someone read encrypted traffic, and RSA's customers used the weak default without knowing. The same weakness was used in the backdoor found in Juniper's ScreenOS network software in 2015.
orgs.cite: Juniper advisory Dec 2015; Checkoway et al.; Reuters, 20 December 2013, as reported by The Register, 21 December 2013

orgs.n: Russian intelligence services (FSB, GRU) acting through companies and insiders
orgs.d: Russia's security service (FSB), military intelligence (GRU) and foreign intelligence (SVR) recruit and pay people inside other countries' governments, armed forces, parliaments and companies. Ukrainian investigators say the GRU paid over $10 million to build a network of MPs in Ukraine's parliament. In Estonia, Herman Simm, the official in charge of protecting state and NATO secrets, passed them to the SVR for thirteen years. The GRU built false identities to try to place officers on the International Criminal Court's staff while it investigated Russia, and paid serving officers in Austria, Sweden, Canada and Italy. A Russian trade official paid a SoftBank employee in Japan for network files.
orgs.cite: Court records in Japan and the Netherlands; US Commerce Department 2024

orgs.d: Jan Marsalek, chief operating officer of the German payments company Wirecard until June 2020, is described by German investigators and the UK Crown Prosecution Service as working for Russian intelligence while he held that post. After fleeing to Russia he directed a Bulgarian spy cell in Britain, convicted in 2025, and received material from Austrian intelligence officer Egisto Ott, convicted in 2026, so the network reached both a large company and a national intelligence service.
orgs.cite: Old Bailey 2025; Vienna court 2026

orgs.n: Chinese state talent-recruitment plans (Thousand Talents and local equivalents)
orgs.d: China's state talent-recruitment plans, such as Thousand Talents and local equivalents, recruit scientists and engineers working in foreign companies, and US prosecutors have tied members to theft of their employers' secrets. GE engineer Xiaoqing Zheng, a Thousand Talents member, was convicted in 2022, and Google engineer Linwei Ding, who had applied to a Shanghai plan, was tried in 2026.
orgs.cite: US v. Zheng (N.D.N.Y. 2022); US v. Ding (N.D. Cal. 2026)

orgs.d: Rostec, Russia's state corporation for defence and industrial technology, worked through the former management of Ukrainian engine maker Motor Sich, Ukrainian prosecutors charge: the executives colluded with Rostec to supply engines for Russian military helicopters. The SBU (Ukraine's security service) and the Prosecutor General brought the charges in 2022–23, alleging that managers inside a Ukrainian company had kept supplying Russia's military.
orgs.cite: SBU / Prosecutor General of Ukraine, 2022–23

orgs.n: Chinese Communist Party organisations inside companies
orgs.d: The Chinese Communist Party places its own organisations inside companies: under China's Company Law, any firm with three or more party members must set one up. 73.1% of private firms had one in 2018, all top state firms wrote the party's role into their charters (founding rules) in 2017, and some foreign joint ventures were asked to do the same, giving the party a voice in decisions at companies with foreign owners. In 2023 a spokesman of the AIIB development bank quit, saying party members dominate its management and filter what reaches its president.
orgs.cite: PRC Company Law; CCP Organization Department; CSIS

orgs.d: Sinochem Holdings is a Chinese state-owned chemicals group that, through ChemChina (later merged into it), took control of the Italian tyre maker Pirelli in 2015, putting a foreign state company in charge of a major Italian firm. It still held about 37% of Pirelli in 2025. In 2023 the Italian government used its 'golden power' national-security powers, which let it block or limit foreign control of strategic companies, to limit Sinochem's say over Pirelli by a decree of 4 August 2023. In April 2025 Pirelli's board ruled, citing that decree, that Sinochem's control had ended.
orgs.cite: Italian DPCM 4 Aug 2023

orgs.d: Sinovel Wind Group, a Chinese wind-turbine maker, recruited an insider at the Austrian unit of its US supplier AMSC and used him to steal AMSC's turbine control software. AMSC, a US maker of wind-turbine electronics, was Sinovel's main supplier at the time. A federal jury in Wisconsin convicted Sinovel of the theft on 24 January 2018.
orgs.cite: US District Court W.D. Wisconsin, 24 Jan 2018

orgs.d: Chen Li-ming, a former TSMC engineer who joined the Taiwan unit of Japanese chip-equipment maker Tokyo Electron, repeatedly asked engineers still working at TSMC to give him secrets on the etching equipment used in its 2-nanometer chip process, so Tokyo Electron could improve its machines and win orders. A Taiwan court ruled on 27 April 2026, sentencing Chen to 10 years and the TSMC engineers to shorter terms, and fined Tokyo Electron Taiwan NT$150 million.
orgs.cite: Taiwan court judgment, 27 Apr 2026; Taipei Times, 28 April 2026

orgs.n: CHJS (Chengdu chip venture of Choi Jin-seok)
orgs.d: Choi Jin-seok, a former Samsung executive, set up the chip venture CHJS in Chengdu, China, with about US$340 million from the Chengdu city government, and recruited a large number of Korean chip experts from Samsung and others. Korean prosecutors say CHJS was built on Samsung plant plans and process data taken by those recruits, including its chief plant designer, a former Samsung senior researcher. Police valued the leaked technology at 4.3 trillion won (about $3.2 billion).
orgs.cite: Seoul prosecutors 2023–24; The Korea Times, 10 September 2024

orgs.d: The Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC), Brazil's largest criminal organisation, which began in São Paulo's prisons and now trades cocaine internationally, gets its money and control inside legitimate companies, including fuel, fintech and transport firms. In Operação Fim da Linha on 9 April 2024, São Paulo prosecutors accused directors of the city bus operators Transwolff and UpBus, which held public transport contracts, of laundering money for the PCC. The city placed both companies under its own management the same day and later moved to cancel their contracts.
orgs.cite: São Paulo Public Ministry, Operação Fim da Linha 2024; Diário do Transporte, 9 April 2024

orgs.d: Cosa Nostra, the Sicilian Mafia, made up of family clans, placed its firms inside the supply contracts of Lidl Italia, the Italian arm of the German supermarket chain: a Milan court found in 2017 that the Laudani clan of Catania had done so in Lombardy. Prosecutors said clan-linked cooperative consortia, which handled logistics, security and store fit-outs, won orders by paying bribes to former Lidl officials and branch managers. Four Lidl regional directorates were placed under court administration for six months in May 2017; Lidl itself was not under investigation.
orgs.cite: Milan court 2017; Il Post, 15 May 2017

orgs.d: The 'Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia, gets its people into local councils, firms, ports and public services and buys politicians' votes. In Emilia-Romagna its Grande Aracri clan took over construction and other firms, including in post-earthquake rebuilding, leading to the Aemilia trial after 160 arrests in January 2015. In Calabria the state dissolved Reggio Calabria's council in 2012 and other town councils for mafia infiltration; clans steered appointments at a public health authority and control hiring at Gioia Tauro port. The Rinascita-Scott trial convicted a former senator, police and officials working for it, and in Lombardy a regional minister bought 4,000 of its votes.
orgs.cite: Court of Cassation, Aemilia rulings 2018 and 2022; Il Post, 'Il processo Aemilia', 21 October 2018

orgs.d: The yakuza are Japan's organised-crime groups, such as the Yamaguchi-gumi and Sumiyoshi-kai, and they placed workers inside the subcontracting chains of Japan's taxpayer-funded radiation clean-up after the 2011 Fukushima nuclear disaster, taking part of the workers' pay. The clean-up, worth about $35 billion, runs through layers of subcontractors. Police arrested yakuza members at least three times in 2012 for illegally placing workers under the construction company Obayashi; in 2013 a Sumiyoshi-kai member was arrested for taking about a third of the pay of men he sent. Reuters found gang-linked recruiters supplying homeless men from Sendai station.
orgs.cite: National Police Agency 2025

orgs.d: South Africa's 'construction mafia' are extortion groups calling themselves 'business forums' that demand a cut, often 30%, of public building projects and try to capture ward councillors, the local elected officials, by bribery, threats or joining local party branches, the Institute for Security Studies (ISS) reported in October 2021. Forums shut down sites that refuse to pay; the contractors' body SAFCEC estimated at least R25.5 billion of projects had been disrupted or halted by March 2019. The ISS said three Tshwane councillors had been killed in under four years in killings linked to such groups. Prosecutors agreed to charge violent extortion under organised-crime law.
orgs.cite: ISS/ENACT 2024

orgs.n: Ransomware and data-extortion groups that recruit insiders
