orgs.d: Ransomware and data-extortion groups, criminal gangs often based in Russia, bribe or recruit company employees and contractors to plant malicious software or copy customer data, then demand ransom. In 2020 a Russian, Egor Kriuchkov, offered a Tesla employee money to install malware and was convicted in the US in 2021; in 2025 Coinbase disclosed that criminals had paid support contractors to copy customer data.
orgs.cite: US v. Kriuchkov (D. Nev. 2021); Coinbase disclosure 2025

orgs.d: Boeing, the US maker of airliners and military aircraft, has its own employees do much of the safety certification of its planes on behalf of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the US air-safety regulator, under a scheme called Organization Designation Authorization. That puts company staff in the regulator's seat when its own aircraft are checked. Congressional and Inspector General inquiries after the 737 MAX crashes of 2018–2019 found Boeing withheld information from the FAA, which therefore approved the plane without knowing what Boeing knew.
orgs.cite: US House Transportation Committee report, 2020
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Purdue Pharma, the Sackler-owned maker of the opioid painkiller OxyContin, paid Practice Fusion, a company whose electronic health-record software doctors use during consultations, from about April to December 2016, in exchange for Practice Fusion steering prescriptions of Purdue's long-acting opioids. Practice Fusion built on-screen alerts nudging doctors to prescribe them, without saying a drug maker had paid for them. Purdue pleaded guilty in 2020 to federal charges including two counts of conspiracy to break the anti-kickback law, after an earlier 2007 plea for misbranding OxyContin. It went through bankruptcy and is being restructured.
orgs.cite: US DOJ press release on Purdue global resolution, 21 October 2020; CNBC, 28 January 2020; Reuters via Insurance Journal, 29 January 2020
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.n: US drug distribution industry (McKesson, Cardinal Health, AmerisourceBergen/Cencora)
orgs.d: The three largest US wholesale drug distributors (McKesson, Cardinal Health and AmerisourceBergen/Cencora) and their trade association hired former staff of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), the agency that polices opioid supply, and one of them helped write the law that curbed it. Reporting in 2017 by the Washington Post and CBS 60 Minutes found that former DEA lawyer Linden Barber, who later joined Cardinal Health, 'wrote the Marino bill', which became a 2016 law making it harder for the DEA to freeze suspicious drug shipments. The industry spent over $102 million lobbying Congress on it and related bills in 2014–16.
orgs.cite: Washington Post, 'The drug industry's triumph over the DEA', 15 October 2017
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Monsanto, maker of the herbicide Roundup (glyphosate) and genetically modified (GM) seeds, paid a senior Indonesian environment ministry official $50,000 in 2002, through a consulting firm it had hired, to drop the requirement for an environmental impact study before GM cotton could be grown. Monsanto admitted it in a 2005 US settlement and paid $1 million to the Justice Department and $500,000 to the SEC. US court documents also show its contacts with an EPA manager, and Germany's glyphosate review reproduced industry text. Bayer bought Monsanto in 2018.
orgs.cite: US DOJ press release, 6 January 2005
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: The International Life Sciences Institute (ILSI), a nutrition and food-safety science body funded by food, drink and chemical companies and founded by a Coca-Cola executive, had its China branch operate from inside China's Center for Disease Control and Prevention, the government agency that advises on diet and obesity policy. Academic research by Susan Greenhalgh, published in the BMJ in 2019, found this gave member companies a voice in Chinese nutrition policy. Mars left ILSI in 2018 and Coca-Cola in 2021.
orgs.cite: Greenhalgh, BMJ 2019
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Randox Laboratories, a Northern Ireland diagnostics company, paid Owen Paterson, a sitting Conservative MP and former cabinet minister, as a consultant, and he then lobbied government regulators and ministers on its behalf. The Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards, who polices MPs' conduct, found in 2021 that this was paid advocacy, which is banned for MPs. After the government first tried to overturn the finding, Paterson resigned as an MP in November 2021.
orgs.cite: Al Jazeera, 4 November 2021
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: PPE Medpro, a company set up in May 2020 and linked to Conservative peer (House of Lords member) Michelle Mone and her husband Doug Barrowman, won £200 million of Covid protective-equipment contracts after Mone referred it to the government's 'VIP lane', a fast track for suppliers recommended by ministers, MPs and peers. Mone denied any link for years, then admitted in December 2023 that she stood to benefit. The High Court ordered PPE Medpro in 2025 to repay about £122 million for supplying gowns that did not meet the contract.
orgs.cite: ITV News, 17 December 2023
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Servier, the French drug company that sold Mediator (benfluorex), hired former officials of the drug regulator as paid advisers. A Paris court in 2021 convicted Jean-Michel Alexandre, former director of drug evaluation at the national medicines agency, of an illegal conflict of interest for advising Servier, and gave him an 18-month suspended sentence and a €30,000 fine. The same trial convicted Servier of deception and manslaughter over Mediator, which damaged heart valves, and fined the agency itself €303,000 for withdrawing the drug only in 2009.
orgs.cite: Prescrire International, June 2021; Que Choisir, 29 March 2021
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Novartis, the Swiss drug company, paid employees of Greek state-owned or state-controlled hospitals and clinics to prescribe its drugs, through paid trips to overseas medical congresses in 2012–2015 and a sham study in 2009–2010. In June 2020 Novartis paid about $347 million in the US to settle bribery charges under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, which covers this Greek conduct and other cases. Separate Greek claims that Novartis bribed politicians were dropped.
orgs.cite: Van Bael & Bellis, July 2020
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Shell, the Anglo-Dutch oil and gas company, had its own people working inside the Nigerian government. A 2009 US diplomatic cable records a Shell executive saying the company had seconded (loaned) its staff to all the relevant Nigerian ministries dealing with oil. That placement gave Shell knowledge of officials' moves and of what those ministries were doing.
orgs.cite: WikiLeaks cable 2009; Dutch government memos 2018; Milan Tribunal 2021
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: A group around Timur Mindich, a businessman and co-owner of the Kvartal 95 studio, is accused by Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) of running 'shadow managers' inside Energoatom, Ukraine's state nuclear power company. NABU says they made contractors pay kickbacks of 10–15% of contract values to avoid blocked payments, and laundered about $100 million. NABU announced the case, called Operation Midas, in November 2025; former energy minister Herman Halushchenko was named a suspect and suspended as justice minister.
orgs.cite: OCCRP, 12 November 2025
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Electrogas, the consortium that built and runs Malta's Delimara gas power station under a government contract, had as a director Yorgen Fenech, who owned a secret Dubai company, 17 Black. Leaked emails listed 17 Black as an expected source of income for secret Panama companies set up by energy minister Konrad Mizzi and the prime minister's chief of staff, Keith Schembri. Fenech faces corruption charges with a former minister and chief of staff in the Maltese courts in 2025–2026.
orgs.cite: MaltaToday, 'Unravelling the 17 Black mystery', November 2018
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Shaul Elovitch, who formerly controlled Bezeq, Israel's largest telecoms company, and owned the Walla! news site, is accused of having Walla! give Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu favourable coverage in exchange for regulatory decisions worth hundreds of millions of shekels. Netanyahu was also communications minister, the post that regulates Bezeq. The indictment says he removed a ministry director-general who opposed Elovitch's requests. Elovitch is co-defendant with Netanyahu in this bribery case, Case 4000, under a 2020 indictment; both deny wrongdoing.
orgs.cite: Israel Hayom, 1 March 2019
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Telia Company, the Swedish-Finnish telecoms group (TeliaSonera until 2016), paid bribes to companies belonging to the daughter of Uzbekistan's president, who had influence over the government body that issued telecoms licences, to enter and stay in the Uzbek mobile market. In 2017 Telia paid about $965 million to settle US Justice Department and Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) bribery cases.
orgs.cite: US DOJ/SEC, 2017
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Airbus, the European maker of airliners and military aircraft, paid bribes through outside agents and consultants to officials and executives of its customers, including state airlines, to win aircraft orders. The UK case covered Sri Lanka, Malaysia, Indonesia, Taiwan and Ghana in 2011–2015. In 2020 Airbus paid about €3.6 billion under deferred prosecution agreements (deals in which charges are suspended if the company pays and reforms) in France, the UK and the US.
orgs.cite: UK Serious Fraud Office, 31 January 2020
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: BAE Systems, Britain's largest arms maker and prime contractor on the Al-Yamamah arms sales to Saudi Arabia, admitted giving 'substantial benefits' to a Saudi public official who could influence its fighter-jet sales. It also admitted making more than $150 million in payments through an offshore British Virgin Islands company that were likely used to sway foreign governments' decisions. BAE pleaded guilty in the US in 2010 to conspiracy and paid $400 million.
orgs.cite: SEC Actions, 'BAE Systems pleads guilty to FCPA violations', March 2010
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Rolls-Royce Holdings, the British aero-engine maker, paid bribes to win orders in several countries, which it admitted in 2017 settlements with UK, US and Brazilian prosecutors. In Indonesia its money reached the chief executive of Garuda Indonesia, the state-owned airline, which bought its engines. The Jakarta Corruption Court jailed the Garuda chief in 2020.
orgs.cite: Jakarta Corruption Court, 2020
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Samsung Group, South Korea's largest business group, reached the presidency through money paid by its head, Lee Jae-yong, to Choi Soon-sil, the close friend and unofficial adviser of President Park Geun-hye, in return for government backing for his takeover of the group from his father. Seoul courts convicted Lee of bribery between 2017 and 2021; the scandal also led to Park's impeachment. Lee was pardoned in 2022.
orgs.cite: Seoul courts, 2017–2021
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Tokyo Electric Power Company (TEPCO), operator of the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant, used its close ties with its regulators to weaken safety rules before the 2011 tsunami and meltdowns. The Japanese parliament's (Diet's) independent commission found in July 2012 that the regulator had been captured: it described collusion between TEPCO, regulators and the government, said TEPCO 'manipulated its cozy relationship with regulators to take the teeth out of regulations', and called the disaster man-made. It recommended a new, independent regulator.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia, 'National Diet of Japan Fukushima Nuclear Accident Independent Investigation Commission'
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Leonardo, the Italian defence group (formerly Finmeccanica), is accused through its helicopter maker AgustaWestland of paying bribes, through middlemen, to Indian officials to win a contract for VVIP helicopters (aircraft for India's top leaders). In 2017 India's Central Bureau of Investigation charged former air force chief S.P. Tyagi in the case, which is still pending, and middleman Christian Michel has also been charged. In Italy, Leonardo's former chief Giuseppe Orsi was acquitted in 2019. In Belgium in 1995, Agusta and Dassault were linked to a bribe taken by the economy minister during talks on their defence contracts, which forced NATO chief Willy Claes to resign.
orgs.cite: Hindustan Times, 2 September 2017; The Quint, September 2020
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC), the UAE's state oil company, had its chief executive, Sultan Al Jaber, preside over COP28, the UN's annual climate conference, in 2023. That put an oil company head in charge of the talks meant to cut fossil-fuel use. Leaked briefing papers reported by the BBC and the Centre for Climate Reporting in 2023 showed his COP28 team planned to raise oil and gas deals in meetings with foreign governments; Al Jaber denied it.
orgs.cite: BBC via CBS News, 27 November 2023
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.n: State Oil Company of Azerbaijan Republic (SOCAR)
orgs.d: People from Azerbaijan's state oil and gas company, SOCAR, led COP29, the 2024 UN climate conference in Baku where countries negotiate cutting fossil-fuel use. Its president, ecology minister Mukhtar Babayev, was a former SOCAR vice-president who had worked there for more than 24 years, to 2018. The summit's chief executive, deputy energy minister Elnur Soltanov, sat on SOCAR's board, and Global Witness secretly filmed him discussing investment in SOCAR gas fields with a man posing as an investor; the BBC reported the recording on 8 November 2024. This put the host's oil industry at the head of talks meant to reduce its product.
orgs.cite: Global Witness, 2024; CNBC, 8 January 2024; BBC / Global Witness, 8 November 2024 (via MyJoyOnline)
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: British American Tobacco (BAT), the second-largest listed tobacco company, is shown by leaked records to have paid government officials in East and Central Africa, with the aim of weakening tobacco-control laws and gaining advantage over rivals. The records were reported by BBC Panorama in 2015 and researchers at the University of Bath in 2021. The UK Serious Fraud Office closed its investigation in 2021 without charges.
orgs.cite: BBC Panorama 2015; University of Bath 2021
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.n: International Chamber of Shipping (with BIMCO and World Shipping Council)
orgs.d: The International Chamber of Shipping, the main global shipowners' association, working with BIMCO and the World Shipping Council, has members inside the national delegations at the International Maritime Organization (IMO), the UN body that sets shipping rules. InfluenceMap found in 2017 that the Chamber led industry efforts to delay climate rules, that 31 of 100 member states at one environment committee meeting brought business representatives in their delegations, and that five delegations were led by commercial ship registries.
orgs.cite: DeSmog, 23 October 2017
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: ABB, the Swiss-Swedish engineering group, paid over $37 million in bribes to an official at Eskom, South Africa's state electricity company, to win contracts at the Kusile coal power station, a large coal-fired plant Eskom was building. The payments bought the official's help from inside the state company. ABB admitted it in December 2022 settlements with the US Justice Department and Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).
orgs.cite: US DOJ / SEC, December 2022
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: SAP SE, the German business-software maker, paid bribes to government officials in South Africa and Indonesia to win public contracts. In January 2024 it agreed a deferred prosecution agreement with the US Justice Department, a deal in which charges are suspended if the company pays and reforms, and paid over $220 million in total.
orgs.cite: US DOJ DPA, January 2024
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Bosasa (later African Global Operations), a South African facilities and services firm run by Gavin Watson, won prison contracts after paying officials and politicians. The Zondo commission, the state inquiry into corruption and 'state capture', found in 2022 that Bosasa had influenced officials to get its contracts. The company went into liquidation in 2019.
orgs.cite: Zondo Commission Report Part 3, 2022
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Thales Group (formerly Thomson-CSF), the French defence and electronics group, paid Jacob Zuma, then South Africa's deputy president, an annual R500,000 through his financial adviser Schabir Shaik, starting in 2000, to protect it from investigation into the 1999 arms deal and help it win future tenders. Shaik was convicted of corruption and fraud in 2005 and sentenced to 15 years. Thales is co-accused with Zuma before the Pietermaritzburg High Court; the trial began in 2020 and is unresolved.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia, 'Jacob Zuma corruption charges'
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Process & Industrial Developments Ltd (P&ID) paid Grace Taiga, legal director of Nigeria's Ministry of Petroleum Resources, while it negotiated a 2010 gas-processing contract with the ministry; one payment came 11 days before signing. When the deal collapsed, P&ID won an $11 billion arbitration award against Nigeria. The High Court of England and Wales set the award aside in October 2023, finding it had been obtained by fraud and bribery.
orgs.cite: BusinessDay (Nigeria), 2020
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Italian prosecutors charged that Eni, Italy's state-controlled oil company, and Shell used the price of a Nigerian oil block to pay bribes to Nigerian officials. In 2011 Eni and Shell paid $1.1 billion through a Nigerian government account for the offshore block OPL 245, and the money went on to Malabu Oil and Gas, a company controlled by former oil minister Dan Etete. Prosecutors charged both companies and executives, including Eni chief executive Claudio Descalzi, with international corruption. On 17 March 2021 a Milan court acquitted all defendants, and in 2022 prosecutors dropped their appeal, so the bribery claim is unproven.
orgs.cite: Milan Tribunal, 2021
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: BSG Resources, the mining arm of Beny Steinmetz's group, won rights to the Simandou iron-ore deposit in Guinea by bribing a wife of President Lansana Conté, who used her position to influence the decision. Simandou is one of the world's largest untapped iron-ore deposits. A Geneva Criminal Court found in 2021 that the rights were won through these bribes and convicted Steinmetz of corruption.
orgs.cite: Geneva Criminal Court, 2021
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Ericsson, the Swedish telecoms equipment maker, paid bribes to government officials and others to win contracts in Djibouti, China, Vietnam, Indonesia and Kuwait, often through middlemen and sham consultancy contracts. It admitted this in a 2019 settlement with the US Justice Department and Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) worth over $1 billion.
orgs.cite: US DOJ / SEC, December 2019
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: JBS, the world's largest meat company, and its parent J&F Investimentos, controlled by brothers Joesley and Wesley Batista, paid politicians and officials for favours. The owners are accused of paying President Michel Temer for government help with the company's tax problems and a loan; in 2017 the Batistas gave plea testimony and a secret recording of Temer to prosecutors, and the Prosecutor-General charged him with corruption. The same year meatpackers including JBS and BRF were accused of paying Brazil's farm ministry inspectors to approve unfit meat.
orgs.cite: Prosecutor-General of Brazil, 2017
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Construction, energy and transport companies in Argentina paid cash to officials of the Kirchner governments in return for public-works contracts, according to the Notebooks case (Cuadernos), named after a government driver's notebooks recording cash deliveries. Their executives are on trial with former president Cristina Fernández de Kirchner at the Federal Oral Court since 2025; several testified as 'repentants', meaning cooperating defendants.
orgs.cite: Federal Oral Court, 2025
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Vitol, the largest independent oil trader, paid bribes to officials of state oil companies in Brazil (Petrobras), Ecuador (Petroecuador) and Mexico (Pemex) to win contracts to buy and sell their oil and fuel. The payments bought insiders who steered state business to Vitol. Vitol paid $135 million to US authorities in 2020, and a former Vitol trader was convicted in 2024.
orgs.cite: US DOJ, 2020 and 2024
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Instituto Pensar Agro (IPA), a think tank funded by 48 agribusiness associations, drafts the legislative agenda of Brazil's Agricultural Parliamentary Front, the cross-party farm caucus in Congress. Member firms include Bayer, BASF, Syngenta, Cargill and JBS. This lets companies write the bills that sitting legislators then put forward. The arrangement was documented by De Olho nos Ruralistas in July 2022.
orgs.cite: De Olho nos Ruralistas, July 2022
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.d: Glenn Defense Marine Asia, the Singapore ship-husbanding contractor (a company that supplies fuel, food and port services to visiting ships) run by Leonard Francis, bribed US Navy officers with cash, gifts and prostitutes for years. In return officers passed it classified ship schedules and steered ships to ports where it overcharged. 22 people pleaded guilty and Francis was sentenced to 15 years in 2024 in the US District Court for southern California.
orgs.cite: US District Court, S.D. California
orgs.reach_src: Cases in corp_cases.json and the cited forums.

orgs.n: Italian mafia groups (Cosa Nostra, 'Ndrangheta, Camorra, Puglia clans)
orgs.d: Italian mafia-type groups, as defined by article 416-bis of the criminal code (Cosa Nostra, the 'Ndrangheta, the Camorra and Puglia clans), get their people and influence into local councils, steering contracts and permits. Italy's Law 164/1991 lets the government dissolve a council found to be conditioned by such a group and send in commissioners. Il Sole 24 Ore counted 402 dissolution decrees from 1991 to September 2025.
orgs.cite: Il Sole 24 Ore count of dissolution decrees, December 2025

orgs.d: The Camorra, the network of clans in Naples and Campania, reached into national government. The Casalesi clan of Caserta controlled construction and waste businesses, and former economy undersecretary Nicola Cosentino was finally convicted by the Court of Cassation on 27 April 2023 of external complicity with it, meaning he helped the clan without formally belonging. Campania has many councils dissolved for mafia infiltration.
orgs.cite: Court of Cassation, 27 April 2023

orgs.n: Bari and Puglia clans (Parisi, Strisciuglio, Montani)
orgs.d: Clans of Bari and wider Puglia (Parisi, Strisciuglio, Montani), sometimes grouped with the Sacra Corona Unita, have members inside public bodies. In 2024 Parisi clan members working at AMTAB, Bari's city transport company, were charged with extortion, and a councillor's husband is on trial for buying clan votes. Puglia accounts for 26 council dissolutions for mafia infiltration since 1991.
orgs.cite: Bari prosecutors; Il Post

orgs.d: Mafia Capitale ('Mondo di mezzo'), a network led by Massimo Carminati and Salvatore Buzzi, bribed Rome city officials and politicians to win city contracts, including for services to migrants, from about 1999 to 2014. Rome prosecutors brought the case in 2014. The Court of Cassation ruled it was not a mafia-type association, but corruption convictions stand.
orgs.cite: Rome prosecutors; Court of Cassation

orgs.n: Karen Border Guard Force / Karen National Army (Saw Chit Thu)
orgs.d: The Karen Border Guard Force, renamed the Karen National Army in 2024, is a Karen militia placed under the Myanmar army in 2010, and Chinese-run crime groups partnered with its leader, Colonel Saw Chit Thu, to build scam centres. In 2017 he partnered with She Zhijiang's Yatai group to build Shwe Kokko and dealt with Wan Kuok-koi's Dongmei Group over Saixigang; Wan, a former 14K triad leader, was sanctioned by the US in 2020. The junta gave Saw Chit Thu its Thiri Pyanchi honour in November 2022. The UK and then the US sanctioned him for links to forced labour in scam centres.
orgs.cite: UK and US sanctions designations

orgs.n: Chinese Unification Promotion Party and Bamboo Union
orgs.d: The Chinese Unification Promotion Party (CUPP), founded in 2005 by former Bamboo Union triad leader Chang An-lo, has members who recruited Taiwanese military officers for Chinese intelligence. In 2025 Taiwan's Kaohsiung High Court sentenced CUPP deputy secretary-general Wen Lung and two retired officers for trying to recruit serving personnel. Taiwan's Interior Ministry says the party works with China on espionage and election interference and links 98 organised-crime cases to its members since 2010. It said in July 2026 it would ask the Constitutional Court to dissolve the party.
orgs.cite: Taipei Times, 28 March 2025

orgs.d: Pemuda Pancasila (Pancasila Youth), an Indonesian paramilitary organisation founded in 1959, puts its members into Indonesia's parliament and party leadership. It took part in the 1965–66 killings, supported Suharto and was part of the Golkar party from 1982 to 2001. In 2024, 48 of its cadres were elected to the House of Representatives and 14 to the Regional Representative Council; its deputy chairman Bambang Soesatyo was speaker of the People's Consultative Assembly. Members are known for extortion and protection work. It was shown in the 2012 film The Act of Killing.
orgs.cite: Industry.co.id, 2024

orgs.d: In India, local strongmen and gang leaders get themselves elected to state and national legislatures, which gives them influence over police and local government. This is not one organisation. The official Vohra report of 1993 found crime syndicates protected by politicians and officials of all parties and placed in elected bodies, running a 'parallel government'. The Association for Democratic Reforms, an election watchdog, found 46% of MPs elected in 2024 declared pending criminal cases.
orgs.cite: Association for Democratic Reforms; Indian courts

orgs.d: The Peoples' Aman Committee, a gang from Lyari in Karachi led by Rehman Dakait and then Uzair Baloch, worked inside the ruling Pakistan Peoples Party's (PPP) local machinery. A Sindh government joint investigation team (JIT) report released in 2020 records Uzair Baloch saying that, with the then provincial home minister's help, he got his chosen police chiefs posted in Lyari and party tickets for his nominees in the 2013 election. The PPP denies this. The group was banned; a military court sentenced Uzair Baloch in 2020.
orgs.cite: Dawn, 7 July 2020

orgs.d: The brothers of Afghanistan's two top leaders were among the insiders who drained Kabul Bank, the country's largest private bank, which paid soldiers, police and civil servants. Its shareholders included Mahmood Karzai, brother of President Hamid Karzai, and Abdul Haseen Fahim, brother of First Vice-President Mohammad Qasim Fahim, and the bank gave millions to a presidential campaign against central bank advice. A 2012 anti-corruption committee report found close to $900 million taken, with most loans going to 19 people and companies. The founder and chief executive were jailed for five years; the two brothers were not charged. The state relaunched the bank as New Kabul Bank in 2011.
orgs.cite: Afghan special tribunal; anti-corruption monitoring committee
orgs.reach_src: cases in this file and Wikipedia

orgs.d: The Nour Zuhair network took about $2.5 billion from Iraq's General Commission for Taxes in 2021–22 through 247 cheques paid to front companies, which needed officials inside the commission and the government to approve them. A Baghdad court convicted 10 people in late 2024, including aides of former Prime Minister Mustafa al-Kadhimi, whose office was supposed to oversee such payments.
orgs.cite: Baghdad criminal court; The National

orgs.d: Haiti's armed gangs, which joined in the Viv Ansanm alliance in 2023, have people inside the state, according to the UN Security Council's panel of experts in a report released in October 2026. The panel says at least one member of a new Cité Soleil municipal commission is an active gang member and that some police officers supply gangs with weapons and information. It accuses former legislator Alfredo Junior Antoine of arming groups and sponsoring a 2025 attack that killed more than 100 people, and former senator Nenel Cassy of controlling a criminal group in Miragoâne; both deny it.
orgs.cite: UN Panel of Experts on Haiti; Global Affairs Canada

orgs.d: Rio de Janeiro's militias (milícias), armed groups made up largely of current and former police officers, control territory in west and north Rio, selling 'protection', gas, transport and land, and their members and allies have held elected office. Brazil's Supreme Federal Court convicted two politicians in 2026 of ordering the 2018 murder of city councillor Marielle Franco, who had investigated militias.
orgs.cite: Brazilian Supreme Federal Court (2026)

orgs.d: Los Dinámicos del Centro is a network that prosecutors say sold driving licences from inside the transport office of Peru's Junín regional government from 2012, and passed the money to the Perú Libre party. Selling licences this way meant regional officials issued them for payment rather than on test results. The Junín Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office has investigated the network since 2021.
orgs.cite: Junín Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office

orgs.d: The Rizzuto family, Montreal's Mafia, took a share of the city's public construction contracts through firms that also paid political parties, witnesses told a Quebec public inquiry. The Charbonneau Commission (2011–2015) investigated collusion and corruption in public construction contracts and organised-crime infiltration of the industry. During the inquiry Montreal mayor Gérald Tremblay resigned, and interim mayor Michael Applebaum and Laval mayor Gilles Vaillancourt were later convicted or pleaded guilty in related corruption cases. The commission reported on 24 November 2015.
orgs.cite: Charbonneau Commission final report (2015)

orgs.d: Italian-American crime families, including New York's Five Families, took control of waterfront hiring, union locals and construction rackets (organised extortion schemes), deciding who worked on the docks and taking a cut. The bi-state Waterfront Commission was created in 1953 to license dock workers and curb their hold on the port of New York and New Jersey; it was dissolved in 2023. Federal prosecutions have repeatedly charged families over this control.
orgs.cite: Waterfront Commission Compact; US federal prosecutions

orgs.n: Swedish criminal networks (Foxtrot, Rumba and others)
orgs.d: Sweden's criminal networks, such as Foxtrot and Rumba, which drive a high rate of shootings and bombings, get people and influence inside public bodies. Research for the think tank SNS in 2023 ('The Vulnerable State') found them infiltrating government agencies, welfare-sector companies and the social insurance system, through employees and bribes, with municipalities especially exposed.
orgs.cite: SNS, 'The Vulnerable State' (2023)

orgs.d: A group of businessmen, police officers and officials is accused of colluding with South Africa's Police Minister to protect its interests. KwaZulu-Natal police commissioner Nhlanhla Mkhwanazi alleged in July 2025 that Minister Senzo Mchunu had disbanded a task team investigating political killings to shield the syndicate; Mchunu denies it. The Madlanga Commission, a judicial inquiry, is examining the claims, and 13 officers had been charged by mid-2026.
orgs.cite: Daily Maverick, 6 July 2025; Mail & Guardian, 6 July 2025

orgs.n: Black Axe and the Neo Black Movement of Africa
orgs.d: Black Axe is a Nigerian confraternity, a secretive brotherhood founded at the University of Benin in 1977, that police in several countries treat as an organised-crime group, and the BBC linked it to a group given government jobs after election work. Leaked documents in a December 2021 BBC Africa Eye investigation suggested the Neo Black Movement of Africa (NBM) was paid 35 million naira to 'protect votes' in the 2012 Edo State governorship election and then given 80 government roles. Former members told the BBC that members hold posts in state assemblies and are hired by politicians for election violence. The NBM denies any link to Black Axe.
orgs.cite: BBC Africa Eye (December 2021)

orgs.d: Westwood Company Ltd, a Gambian firm that held the exclusive rosewood export licence, was co-founded by the country's own president, Yahya Jammeh, with Swiss national Nicolae Bogdan Buzaianu, according to TRIAL International. The president's office therefore awarded the licence to a company he part-owned. Gambia exported about $163 million of rosewood, mostly from Senegal's Casamance, to China in 2014–17.
orgs.cite: TRIAL International complaint (2019); EIA (2020)

orgs.d: Samherji, an Icelandic fishing company, paid people close to Namibia's government, including two ministers, to obtain fishing quotas, the state-issued rights to catch set amounts of fish, which those ministers' offices controlled. The payments were exposed in the 2019 Fishrot Files, leaked company documents. Namibia charged the two ministers under organised-crime law, and Iceland opened an investigation.
orgs.cite: Namibian prosecution; Fishrot Files (2019)

orgs.d: A cigarette and narcotics smuggling network led by Miloš Medenica was protected from inside Montenegro's judiciary by his mother, Vesna Medenica, former president of the Supreme Court, who used her position to shield it from investigation and prosecution. A Supreme Court president heads the country's highest court and has influence over the wider judiciary. The High Court in Podgorica sentenced both in January 2026.
orgs.cite: High Court in Podgorica (2026)

orgs.d: Albanian crime groups, active in drug trafficking in Albania, Italy, the UK and the Netherlands, have links to people elected to office. Albania's 2015 decriminalisation law, which bars people with criminal records from public office, removed seven MPs, three mayors and about 600 officials who had hidden their records, showing how far people with criminal pasts had reached into elected office.
orgs.cite: Albanian Central Election Commission; Exit News

orgs.d: A network around Martin Bozhanov, known as 'the Notary', is alleged to have gathered compromising material on Bulgarian judges and prosecutors, which could be used to pressure them over cases. This would give the network leverage inside Bulgaria's courts and prosecution service. The allegations are under investigation; Bulgarian National Radio and the state news agency BTA have reported them.
orgs.cite: Bulgarian National Radio; BTA

orgs.d: The Global (Russian) Laundromat moved $20–80 billion out of Russia in 2010–14 by using Moldovan judges inside the court system: they enforced fake debts, giving the transfers legal cover. The money then went through Moldindconbank and Latvian banks to companies worldwide. OCCRP, the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, and the Russian newspaper Novaya Gazeta exposed the scheme.
orgs.cite: OCCRP and Novaya Gazeta

orgs.d: The gang led by Sergei Tsapok in Kushchyovskaya, Krasnodar Krai, operated for years under the protection of local authorities, and Tsapok himself sat as a deputy on the district council. In November 2010 it murdered 12 people. The case showed how a gang could run a district while its leader held elected office there. Tsapok was convicted and died in prison in 2014.
orgs.cite: Caucasian Knot, 15 November 2010

orgs.d: Gangs in Chongqing, a large city in south-west China, were protected by senior police officers, who used their posts to shield the gangs from investigation. The city's 2009–11 crackdown arrested 4,781 suspects, including six district police chiefs, and the former deputy police head Wen Qiang was executed in 2010 for protecting gangs.
orgs.cite: Chongqing courts

orgs.n: Rothschild family banks (N M Rothschild & Sons; Rothschild & Co)
orgs.hq: New Court, St Swithin's Lane, London; Paris
orgs.d: The Rothschild banks are the family banking houses founded by Mayer Amschel Rothschild's sons, and bankers have moved from them into the French state. François Pérol advised Banque Populaire on a merger while at Rothschild, followed that merger from the president's office at the Élysée in 2009, and then took charge of the merged bank, BPCE. He was prosecuted for illegal taking of interest and acquitted. No court has found the bank directed his decisions.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Rothschild family', 'Rothschild & Co'; N. Ferguson, The House of Rothschild (1998)

orgs.hq: 23 Wall Street (historic); 270 Park Avenue, New York
orgs.d: J.P. Morgan & Co., the New York private bank, placed its men on company boards, and its successor has had people inside the bodies that oversee it. In 1913 the Pujo Committee, a congressional inquiry into banking power, found Morgan-linked men held 341 directorships in 112 corporations, giving the bank a say inside companies it lent to. JPMorgan Chase paid $264 million in 2016 for hiring about 100 relatives and friends of Chinese officials so that those officials would steer business to it. Its chief sat on the New York Fed's board while the Fed gave the bank emergency financing and a capital-rule exemption.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'J. P. Morgan', 'JPMorgan Chase', 'Pujo Committee'; Quigley, Tragedy and Hope pp. 52–53

orgs.d: Paul Warburg, a partner of the New York investment bank Kuhn, Loeb & Co., secretly helped write the plan for the US central bank. In 1910 Warburg joined Senator Nelson Aldrich, who chaired the national monetary commission, and other bankers at the Jekyll Island Club in Georgia, where they drafted the Aldrich Plan; it was published without naming its authors and laid the ground for the Federal Reserve. The secret drafting became public when fellow participant Frank Vanderlip described the meeting in the Saturday Evening Post in February 1935. Antisemitic writers later falsely claimed the firm financed the Bolsheviks. It merged with Lehman Brothers in 1977.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Jacob Schiff', 'Paul Warburg'; P. Roberts, American Jewish Archives Journal 49 (1997); Saturday Evening Post, 'Jekyll Island and the Secret Behind the Fed' (Vanderlip, 9 Feb 1935)

orgs.d: Historian Carroll Quigley describes the London partners of Lazard, an investment bank with houses in New York, Paris and London, as part of the Milner/Round Table group, a private British policy network that placed its people in state posts. Quigley writes that Lazard Brothers' chairman Robert Kindersley sat on the 1924 Dawes committee on German reparations, and that the Milner Group held half of Britain's delegation. The Dawes plan gave creditor states seven seats on the board of Germany's central bank. That account is Quigley's.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Lazard'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment; NAO (2014)

orgs.d: A member of the Barings banking family ran the finances of a country the bank lent to. Barings, a London merchant bank founded in 1762, held a significant stake in Egyptian debt when Evelyn Baring (later Lord Cromer) became Britain's financial controller of Egypt after the Khedive's 1876 bankruptcy, the post that oversaw repayment to European creditors; no conflict of interest was raised at the time. From 1883 to 1907 he was Britain's agent and consul-general, the real ruler of Egypt. Barings also financed the Louisiana Purchase (1803) with Hope & Co., was rescued in 1890 after Argentine losses, and collapsed in 1995 after Nick Leeson's £827 million trading losses; ING bought it for £1.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Barings Bank', 'Evelyn Baring, 1st Earl of Cromer'

orgs.n: Wallenberg family sphere (Stockholms Enskilda Bank, SEB, Investor AB)
orgs.d: The Wallenbergs are a Swedish banking and industrial family whose Stockholms Enskilda Bank held German-owned companies on paper during the Second World War so that the German firm Bosch kept control of them. In 1939–41 the bank bought Bosch subsidiaries, including the American Bosch Corporation, on condition that Bosch could buy them back after the war. The US treated this as 'cloaking', hiding the real owner behind a front, seized American Bosch in 1943 and blacklisted the bank from 1945 to 1947. At the same time the bank's heads led Sweden's trade talks: Jacob Wallenberg with Germany, Marcus Wallenberg Jr. with Britain.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Wallenberg family', 'Stockholms Enskilda Bank', 'Investor AB'

orgs.d: Credit Suisse, a Swiss bank taken over by UBS in 2023, arranged secret state-guaranteed loans to Mozambique in 2013–14 in a scheme in which bribes reached Mozambican officials and the bank's own staff. Three state companies borrowed $622 million from Credit Suisse and $535 million from Russia's VTB, backed by state guarantees never shown to parliament or the IMF, for projects with the shipbuilder Privinvest. The US Justice Department said at least $200 million went in bribes and kickbacks to bankers and officials. Credit Suisse pleaded guilty to wire fraud in the US in 2021, was fined almost $500 million and forgave $200 million of Mozambique's debt.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Credit Suisse', 'Tuna bonds'

orgs.d: Citigroup, the US bank formed in 1998, has written law for the government that regulates it, and its forerunner took control of a country's finances. In 2013 Citigroup's own drafting made up more than 70 of the 85 lines of a House committee bill weakening a derivatives rule the bank opposed. From 1915 National City Bank took Haiti's gold and came to own its national bank; with US control of Haiti's finances, a quarter of revenue went on debts held by that bank, for decades. Citigroup received a federal rescue in 2008.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Robert Rubin', 'Michael Froman'; The New Republic, 14 Oct 2016

orgs.n: Banco Espírito Santo / Grupo Espírito Santo
orgs.d: Banco Espírito Santo (BES) was the Portuguese bank of the Espírito Santo family, led by Ricardo Salgado, nicknamed 'Dono Disto Tudo' ('owner of all this'). In the Operation Marquês case, prosecutors link Espírito Santo group payments to former Prime Minister José Sócrates, saying the head of government received undue money, and charge Salgado with corruption. A judge threw out most charges in 2021, an appeal court reinstated them in 2024 and the trial began in July 2025; the defendants are presumed innocent. The bank collapsed in August 2014 and its good assets became Novo Banco.
orgs.cite: Portuguese Wikipedia 'Operação Marquês'; Wikipedia 'Ricardo Salgado'

orgs.d: In Lebanon, politicians and their families own most of the large commercial banks, which in turn lent heavily to the state those politicians ran. A 2016 study by economist Jad Chaaban found that 18 of the 20 largest banks had major shareholders linked to political elites, holding about 43% of the sector's assets, and that this affected the banks' lending and their exposure to public debt. The banks financed the state and the central bank, the Banque du Liban, under governor Riad Salameh, until the system collapsed in 2019 and froze depositors' savings.
orgs.cite: J. Chaaban, ERF Working Paper 1059 (2016)

orgs.d: The CIA, the US foreign intelligence agency, has paid and recruited heads of state, ministers, spy chiefs and politicians abroad and placed agents inside international bodies. It bribed members of Iran's parliament to remove the prime minister in 1953, paid more than half of Frei's 1964 campaign in Chile, secretly funded Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party, and paid Jordan's King Hussein millions a year for about twenty years. Panama's ruler Manuel Noriega and Peru's spy chief Vladimiro Montesinos were on its payroll. It recruited UN Under-Secretary-General Arkady Shevchenko and two future presidents of Mexico, and delivered bags of cash to Afghan President Karzai's office.
orgs.cite: Swiss parliamentary inquiry 2020; Trump statement Oct 2025

orgs.d: Crypto AG was a Swiss maker of cipher machines (devices that encrypt messages) that was secretly owned by the CIA and West Germany's BND intelligence service, so that the two agencies could read the messages of the governments that bought them. More than 120 governments were customers. The BND co-owned it from 1970 until about 1993 and the CIA until 2018, when the firm was liquidated. The machines were deliberately weakened. A Swiss parliamentary inquiry confirmed the secret ownership in 2020.
orgs.cite: Swiss parliamentary inquiry, 2020
reach_est: more than 120 customer states, not all named

orgs.d: India's foreign intelligence agency, the Research and Analysis Wing (RAW), cultivates foreign politicians and recruits insiders. Australia's security service ASIO said a foreign 'nest of spies' cultivated Australian politicians and a state police service and recruited an Australian with a security clearance and access to defence technology; in April 2024 Australian media and the Washington Post reported that the country was India and that two RAW officers were expelled in 2020. In the Maldives an Indian intelligence officer is reported to have explored paying 40 MPs, including the president's own, with Indian money to vote to impeach President Muizzu.
orgs.cite: ASIO 2021 speech; Washington Post/ABC April 2024
orgs.reach_src: cases in this file and existing records

orgs.d: Pakistan's main military intelligence agency, the Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), recruits and pays people inside India's armed forces and government, has worked to steer Pakistan's own politics and, the US says, uses a militant group as its arm inside Afghanistan's Taliban. In 1990 it passed money through Mehran Bank to chosen politicians to stop Benazir Bhutto winning. It recruited Indian diplomat Madhuri Gupta and paid Indian Navy sailors and a navy headquarters clerk. The top US military officer called the Haqqani network its arm; that network now runs the Taliban government's interior ministry and Kabul's security. Pakistan denies the ties.
orgs.cite: US v. Fai (2011); Mullen testimony 2011

orgs.d: Egypt's main intelligence service, the General Intelligence Service (GIS), had an agent working inside the German government's press office, which handles the chancellor's communications. German federal prosecutors charged the employee in November 2020 with working for the GIS since 2010, reporting on German media coverage and helping an attempt to recruit a further source, in return for favours for his family.
orgs.cite: German Federal Prosecutor, Nov 2020

orgs.d: Cuba's foreign intelligence service, the Intelligence Directorate (DI, formerly DGI), recruited people who rose inside the US government and helped run Venezuela's military counterintelligence. It recruited Ana Montes, who became the Defense Intelligence Agency's senior Cuba analyst and spied for Havana until her 2001 arrest; she was convicted in 2002. Former US ambassador Víctor Manuel Rocha also served Cuban intelligence. Under 2008 agreements seen by Reuters, Cuba's defence ministry oversaw the restructuring of Venezuela's military counterintelligence, which turned to watching Venezuela's own officers.
orgs.cite: US court records; Reuters 2019
orgs.reach_src: cases in this file and existing records

orgs.d: North Korea's main foreign intelligence and cyber body, the Reconnaissance General Bureau (RGB), places North Korean IT workers under false identities in jobs inside foreign companies to earn money for the state, according to US agencies. One US 'laptop farm' let such workers appear to be working from the US for more than 300 American companies, earning over $17 million; its American operator was jailed for eight years in 2025. US agencies also tie the RGB to the 2016 theft of $81 million from Bangladesh's central bank through fraudulent SWIFT payment orders sent from inside the bank's network.
orgs.cite: CISA 'BeagleBoyz' alert; US DOJ cases

orgs.d: Russia's domestic security service, the FSB, got inside the anti-doping testing at the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics to hide Russian athletes' drug use. The McLaren reports, commissioned by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) in 2016, found a 'state-directed' system in which FSB-linked staff, working with Russia's sports ministry and the WADA-accredited Moscow laboratory, opened supposedly tamper-proof sample bottles and swapped athletes' urine. The findings led to sanctions on Russian sport.
orgs.cite: McLaren reports 2016

orgs.d: The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) is the foundation, run jointly by the Olympic movement and governments, that sets drug-testing rules for world sport, and Russia's FSB security service and Ministry of Sport worked through a WADA-accredited laboratory to hide doped athletes. Richard McLaren's reports for WADA in 2016 found a 'state-directed failsafe system' involving the ministry, the FSB and the Moscow laboratory. FSB-linked staff opened supposedly tamper-proof sample bottles at the 2014 Sochi Olympics to swap urine. More than 1,000 Russian competitors benefited between 2011 and 2015, and at least 643 positive samples were hidden. Russian military intelligence hackers later attacked WADA.
orgs.cite: McLaren reports; Cottier reports 2024

orgs.d: World Athletics (formerly the IAAF), the governing body of track and field based in Monaco, had its president paid by Russian interests to hide Russian athletes' doping. Lamine Diack led it from 1999 to 2015. In September 2020 a Paris court convicted him of corruption for helping cover up Russian doping in return for money; about €3.2 million was extorted from suspected dopers so they could compete at London 2012.
orgs.cite: Paris Criminal Court, Sept 2020

orgs.d: The UN Secretariat in New York and UN offices are bodies where member states have sought influence over the officials inside them. Saddam Hussein's government in Iraq is alleged to have bribed the UN official in charge of the Oil-for-Food programme, the body meant to police Iraq's oil sales. An OHCHR staff member, Emma Reilly, also alleged that the UN human rights office in Geneva confirmed to China the names of Chinese activists attending UN meetings; OHCHR rejected her claims.
orgs.cite: see cases

orgs.d: Countries that sell citizenship or passports have let buyers pay their way into political circles and diplomatic posts. Al Jazeera reported in 2019 that an Iranian donor to Dominica's prime minister was given an ambassadorship and diplomatic passport, and that in Grenada businessmen were offered diplomatic posts; both governments deny wrongdoing. In the 2020 'Cyprus Papers', the Speaker of the House was filmed offering to help a convicted money launderer get a passport. In Comoros, ex-president Sambi was convicted in 2022 over the sale of passports to stateless Gulf residents (bidoon), and FinCEN warned in 2014 that sanctioned Iranians had bought St Kitts passports.
orgs.cite: FinCEN FIN-2014-A004; Al Jazeera Investigative Unit; OCCRP

orgs.d: Companies linked to UK businessman Zuneth Sattar won Malawi police and army contracts by paying officials, according to Malawi's Anti-Corruption Bureau. Its June 2022 report said five companies linked to him won 16 contracts worth over 150 million dollars from the police and the Malawi Defence Force in 2017–2021. The Bureau later arrested Vice President Saulos Chilima, accusing him of receiving about $280,000 and other items from Sattar in 2021 in return for helping two Sattar companies get government contracts. President Chakwera withdrew Chilima's delegated powers; Chilima denied wrongdoing and died in a plane crash in June 2024.
orgs.cite: Malawi ACB report, June 2022; TheCable / AFP, 'Malawi vice-president arrested over $280,000 bribery allegation', Nov 2022; VOA, 25 Nov 2022

orgs.d: Groups moving South American cocaine to Europe and the US, including Colombia's FARC rebels, buy or recruit officials along their routes: presidents, military and police chiefs, judges, customs officers and port staff. In Guinea-Bissau the navy, army and air force chiefs were charged in US cases, and former navy chief José Américo Bubo Na Tchuto pleaded guilty. Honduran president Hernández took traffickers' bribes to protect their shipments. In Suriname the president's son Dino Bouterse used his post as head of the counter-terrorism unit to traffic cocaine. In Ecuador traffickers paid judges, prosecutors and police, and at Antwerp, Rotterdam, Algeciras and Le Havre networks recruited port workers, police and customs staff.
orgs.cite: US SDNY indictments 2013–2015

orgs.d: Burmeister & Wain Scandinavian Contractor, a Danish power-plant builder, paid officials of the Mauritian administration through intermediaries during tenders for the Saint-Louis power station of the state Central Electricity Board, the African Development Bank found. In June 2020 the bank, which lends for such projects, debarred the company from its contracts for 21 months.
orgs.cite: AfDB sanctions decision, June 2020

orgs.n: VimpelCom, Telia and MTS (Uzbek telecom bribery)
orgs.d: Three telecom groups, VimpelCom, Telia and MTS, paid companies controlled by Gulnara Karimova, the Uzbek president's daughter, to get into Uzbekistan's mobile market. In US foreign-bribery settlements in 2016, 2017 and 2019 the firms admitted the payments, agreeing to pay 795, 965 and 850 million dollars respectively. Uzbek prosecutors put her kickbacks at 869.3 million dollars; she was convicted in Uzbekistan in 2017 and 2020.
orgs.cite: US DOJ/SEC FCPA resolutions

orgs.n: Cary Yan and Gina Zhou (Rongelap SAR scheme)
orgs.d: Cary Yan and Gina Zhou, China-born businesspeople, paid Marshall Islands legislators and other officials from 2016 to 2020 to pass a law creating a semi-autonomous 'Rongelap Atoll Special Administrative Region' that they would shape. Both pleaded guilty to bribery in New York and were sentenced in 2023, Yan to 42 months.
orgs.cite: US DOJ, 16 May 2023

orgs.d: Getax Australia, a Gold Coast phosphate trader, is charged by Australian federal prosecutors with conspiring to bribe Nauruan politicians between 2007 and 2012 to win phosphate deals; the case has been repeatedly delayed and the charges are unproven. In a related case, Sydney businessman Mozammil Bhojani pleaded guilty to paying over 120,000 dollars to a Nauruan MP and a minister and was jailed in 2018.
orgs.cite: Australian Federal Police

orgs.d: Firms paid by Australia's Home Affairs department to run asylum centres on Nauru and Manus Island passed money to Nauruan and Papua New Guinea political figures, a 2023 Sydney Morning Herald and Age investigation reported. It found millions in subcontracts going to firms tied to Nauru's leaders, including over 120,000 dollars in suspect payments to justice minister David Adeang, who denies wrongdoing; the reporters said they were not claiming the payments were bribes. A former Paladin director said a 1.5 million dollar invoice marked 'Visas' on the Manus contract was a bribe, which Paladin's former chief executive denies.
orgs.cite: SMH / The Age, July 2023

orgs.d: The Habilaj family ran an Albanian-Italian cannabis-trafficking group, and its link reached Albania's interior minister, Saimir Tahiri, who was in charge of the police and is a cousin of the family. Italian police arrested Moisi Habilaj in October 2017 in a probe into the group, which moved over 3.5 tonnes of cannabis, and wiretaps mentioned Tahiri. On 19 September 2019 Albania's Serious Crime Court convicted Tahiri of abuse of office and sentenced him to 3 years and 4 months, but dropped the drug-trafficking and organised-crime charges.
orgs.cite: Guardia di Finanza, Oct 2017

orgs.d: MOL, Hungary's state-influenced oil company, paid Croatia's prime minister to give it management control of Croatia's national oil company INA, according to Croatian courts. They found that Prime Minister Ivo Sanader took a 10 million euro bribe from MOL chief executive Zsolt Hernádi; the Supreme Court confirmed the conviction in 2021. Hungary has not handed Hernádi to Croatia, and MOL denies the bribe.
orgs.cite: Croatian Supreme Court, 2021

orgs.d: Yuri Borisov, a Russian businessman who ran the Lithuanian helicopter firm Avia Baltika, bought access to Lithuania's president with campaign money. He reportedly gave about 400,000 dollars to Rolandas Paksas's 2002 campaign and then received Lithuanian citizenship by Paksas's decree. In 2004 the Constitutional Court found Paksas had broken the constitution and his oath, and parliament removed him from office, the first European head of state impeached.
orgs.cite: Constitutional Court of Lithuania, 2004

orgs.d: 17 Black, a Dubai company owned by Maltese businessman Yorgen Fenech, was named in leaked papers as a planned source of payments to secret Panama companies of the Maltese prime minister's chief of staff Keith Schembri and energy minister Konrad Mizzi. Journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia exposed the companies and was murdered in 2017; Fenech is charged with commissioning the killing. Schembri and Mizzi resigned, and a 2021 public inquiry found the state had created an 'atmosphere of impunity'.
orgs.cite: Maltese public inquiry, 2021

orgs.d: Dmitry Rybolovlev, a Russian billionaire who owns AS Monaco football club, was suspected of courting Monaco officials, including the principality's former public prosecutor Jean-Pierre Dreno, to get favourable treatment in his legal disputes. The suspicion rested on messages found on the phone of his lawyer, Tetiana Bersheda. In November 2018 he was made a formal suspect in a corruption and influence-peddling probe, known as 'Monacogate'. The case was dismissed in 2023, and in February 2025 Monaco's courts closed it, ruling the phone data unlawfully obtained after a European Court of Human Rights finding.
orgs.cite: Monaco courts, Feb 2025

orgs.d: In San Marino, business owners paid politicians for building permits and banking licences, with the bribes run through a bank account in the name of 'Giuseppe Mazzini', a 19th-century Italian patriot. Twenty-one former political figures, including former state secretaries, went on trial in 2015; several were convicted in 2017 and the convictions were upheld in 2022.
orgs.cite: San Marino courts; Freedom House

orgs.d: Patria, a Finnish state-owned defence company, was accused of paying bribes, partly aimed at Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Janša, to win a 2006 deal for armoured vehicles. A Ljubljana court convicted Janša in 2013, but the Constitutional Court annulled the verdict and the case lapsed. An Austrian court convicted a middleman, and two Patria executives were convicted in Finland over separate Croatian deals.
orgs.cite: Slovenian and Finnish courts

orgs.n: Stanford Financial Group / Stanford International Bank
orgs.d: Allen Stanford's offshore bank, Stanford International Bank in Antigua, bribed the island's chief financial regulator to look away from a 7 billion dollar fraud. A 2009 US indictment charges Leroy King, head of Antigua's Financial Services Regulatory Commission, with taking more than 100,000 dollars from Stanford to ignore the bank's real assets and obstruct a US investigation; Antigua extradited him in 2019. Stanford was convicted in the US.
orgs.cite: US DOJ

orgs.d: Mohamed's Enterprise, a Guyanese gold trading firm of Nazar and Azruddin Mohamed, bribed customs and other officials, the US Treasury said when it sanctioned the family and firm in 2024. Treasury said they kept more than 10,000 kg of gold off customs declarations and evaded more than 50 million dollars in duty, paid officials for favourable treatment in court matters and bribed to win state contracts. It also sanctioned a home affairs ministry permanent secretary.
orgs.cite: US Treasury JY2401

orgs.hq: London — first grand lodge, 1717; each country has its own grand lodges
orgs.d: Freemasonry, a fraternal order with private rituals organised in lodges, has had members in police forces and local office use their posts for fellow Masons; this dot gathers grand lodges not mapped separately. In 1827 Freemasons in local office, including a county sheriff, abducted former Mason William Morgan, who was about to publish the rituals. That year the US envoy Poinsett used York Rite lodges to press Mexico's president into removing ministers. In Britain a 1984 book, 'The Brotherhood', described Masons spread through police forces, and a detective says Masonic officers took him off an Islington fraud case. In Sicily, prosecutors say a secret association steered Castelvetrano's town council.
orgs.cite: See the cases listed below.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: Shinto Seiji Renmei (Shinto Association of Spiritual Leadership), the political arm of Japan's Association of Shinto Shrines, runs a league of Diet (parliament) members who back its aims, such as constitutional revision and official honours for Yasukuni Shrine. In 2025, 12 ministers of Sanae Takaichi's first cabinet, including the foreign and finance ministers, belonged to its league, putting lawmakers who back the shrines' agenda in charge of key ministries. It works closely with Nippon Kaigi, a nationalist lobby.
orgs.cite: See the cases listed below.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: South Korea's intelligence agency, the KCIA, paid members of the US Congress in the 1970s through businessman Tongsun Park to keep US support for President Park Chung-hee's government. In 1978, under immunity, Park admitted giving money to 30 members. Former Representative Richard Hanna pleaded guilty and went to prison, and the House reprimanded three other members; former Representative Otto Passman was acquitted.
orgs.cite: See the cases listed below.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.n: PRC state proxies (United Front not named)
orgs.d: This dot gathers cases in which officials or intelligence officers of the People's Republic of China worked through people inside other countries' institutions, where the record does not name the United Front Work Department (the Communist Party body for overseas influence). In California a Beijing-directed campaign helped elect Eileen Wang to Arcadia's council; as mayor she pleaded guilty in 2026 as a Chinese agent. China's spy ministry had an MEP's aide, Jian Guo, inside the European Parliament. Chinese military intelligence recruited aides near Taiwan's president, and engineer Chi Mak passed US Navy technology from a defence contractor to China.
orgs.cite: See the cases listed below.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: This dot gathers cases where foreign governments, rather than a single named organisation, paid, recruited or placed people inside another country's institutions. Cases include US Senator Bob Menendez, convicted in 2024 as an agent of Egypt; a Twitter manager convicted in 2022 of spying for Saudi Arabia; Hungary's EU mission running a spy ring against the European Commission; and Canada's parliamentary intelligence committee (NSICOP) finding some parliamentarians 'witting' in foreign interference.
orgs.cite: See the cases listed below.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.n: Order of the Star Spangled Banner (Know Nothings)
orgs.d: The Order of the Star Spangled Banner, a secret anti-immigrant fraternal order, built the Know Nothing movement and its American Party and took over a state government. In the 1854 Massachusetts election it won the governorship, all 40 state Senate seats and all but three House seats. The 1855 legislature passed laws to deport poor or mentally ill Irish residents, to 'inspect' Catholic schools and convents and to require Protestant Bible reading in public schools.
orgs.cite: See the cases listed below.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: The Society of St. Tammany, a fraternal society with ritual offices called sachems, ran New York's Democratic Party machine and through it the city government. William M. 'Boss' Tweed became its Grand Sachem in 1863 and controlled the city while holding seats in Congress, the county board and the state Senate. A city committee in 1877 estimated he stole $25–45 million; he was convicted in 1873 on 204 of 220 counts.
orgs.cite: See the cases listed below.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: The Loyal Orange Institution (Orange Order), a Protestant fraternal lodge, had its members fill Canadian city halls and federal office. Twenty of Toronto's 23 mayors in the 19th century and every mayor in the first half of the 20th century were Orangemen, and in 1942 16 of 23 city council members were. Four prime ministers, including Mackenzie Bowell, a past Grand Master, were Orangemen.
orgs.cite: See the cases listed below.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: The Ordre de Jacques-Cartier, a secret French-Canadian Catholic society active from 1926 to 1965, worked by recruiting decision-makers and getting its members appointed to federal public-service jobs. Its members included Montreal mayor Jean Drapeau and politician Pierre Laporte, and it had about 11,300 members in 1955–56. It dissolved in 1965 after a former insider, Roger Cyr, exposed it in a 1964 book.
orgs.cite: See the cases listed below.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: The Knights of Saint Columbanus, a Catholic fraternal order founded in Ireland in 1915 and long described as secretive, had members inside Irish governments. In 1948 Justice Minister Seán MacEoin, a member, reportedly assured the order's Supreme Council that conflict between Church and State would be avoided, giving the order private undertakings on government conduct. These accounts rest mainly on biographies by John Cooney (1999) and Anthony Jordan (2007).
orgs.cite: See the cases listed below.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: The Service d'Action Civique (SAC), a Gaullist security association created in 1960 and run in practice by Jacques Foccart, de Gaulle's adviser on Africa, was a parallel network that recruited police officers. Its Marseille leader was himself a police inspector, Jacques Massié, whom an SAC commando murdered with his family in 1981. A National Assembly inquiry followed and the government dissolved the SAC in 1982 under the law on private militias.
orgs.cite: See the cases listed below.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: Westland New Post, a Belgian far-right paramilitary group founded by Paul Latinus, had members inside the gendarmerie (national police) and a NATO site. A former gendarme said he was recruited into 'Group G', a neo-Nazi cell inside the gendarmerie linked to the group, and NATO documents passed on by a member from the Evere transmission centre were found at another member's home. Latinus had been an informant for Belgium's State Security service. A parliamentary inquiry found no proof of a conspiracy behind the Brabant killings.
orgs.cite: See the cases listed below.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: The 'Patriotic Union' around Heinrich XIII Prinz Reuss, part of the Reichsbürger movement that rejects the modern German state, had a sitting judge, a former MP and special-forces soldiers among its members. Birgit Malsack-Winkemann, a Berlin judge and former AfD member of parliament, was to be its justice minister and led co-accused through the Reichstag twice in 2022. Federal prosecutors charged the group as a terrorist association planning to storm the parliament; trials began in 2024.
orgs.cite: See the cases listed below.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: Voice of Europe was a Prague-based pro-Russian news outlet that, Czech intelligence says, paid European politicians from Russian money supplied by Viktor Medvedchuk. The Czech government sanctioned it in March 2024. German prosecutors are investigating AfD politician Petr Bystroň over cash reportedly handed over in Prague, and both the Bundestag and, in May 2025, the European Parliament lifted his immunity; he denies the claims.
orgs.cite: See the cases listed below.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: The White Hand (Bela ruka), a secret Serbian officers' society founded in 1912 by Petar Živković, gained influence over the future King Alexander and put its leader in charge of government. Alexander suspended the constitution in 1929 with White Hand officers' support, and Živković was made prime minister, serving until 1932.
orgs.cite: See the cases listed below.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: P3 was a secret group, named by the press after the P2 lodge, that Italian prosecutors said sought undue influence on the state, including senior judges. In 2018 a Rome court convicted businessman Flavio Carboni and Arcangelo Martino under the 1982 Anselmi law, which bans secret associations, and gave a senior judge, Vincenzo Carbone, a suspended sentence for abuse of office.
orgs.cite: See the cases listed below.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: P4 is the press name for an information-trading network run by go-between Luigi Bisignani, which drew in officials who passed on confidential state information. In the 2011 inquiry, deputy and former prosecutor Alfonso Papa was accused of passing confidential information to Bisignani; he was convicted in 2016, but the charges lapsed on appeal. Bisignani took a plea of 1 year 7 months.
orgs.cite: See the cases listed below.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: In Italy, mafia groups such as the 'Ndrangheta have used 'covered' (secret) Masonic lodges to link up with officials, business and local government. In 2023 an 'Ndrangheta trial convicted civil servants, a police chief, a mayor and former senator Giancarlo Pittelli, whom a clan had drawn onto its side. Pittelli, described as a Freemason linking the clan to Masonic circles, was given 11 years for collusion.
orgs.cite: See the cases listed below.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: IDEA (Sacred Bond of Greek Officers), a secret society of army officers formed in 1945, placed its members at the head of the state through the 1967 coup. Several coup leaders, including Georgios Papadopoulos, were members, and IDEA members took key posts under the junta. In 1975 the junta leaders were convicted of high treason.
orgs.cite: See the cases listed below.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: Golden Dawn, a Greek neo-Nazi party that held up to 21 seats in parliament, had ties inside the police and was ruled a criminal organisation. In 2013 the Council of Europe's human rights commissioner said he had strong evidence of police links to the party, and after the 2012 election polling stations used by Attica police officers gave it just over 20% of the vote. In 2020 an Athens court convicted its leaders of running a criminal organisation, upheld on appeal in 2026.
orgs.cite: See the cases listed below.
orgs.reach_src: countries where this map holds a documented case

orgs.d: The Soviet Union's secret police and foreign intelligence (the NKVD, later the KGB) and its military intelligence (the GRU) recruited officials inside Western governments, spy services and weapons programmes, and paid politicians. Kim Philby ran MI6's anti-Soviet section while working for Moscow; Klaus Fuchs passed bomb designs from Los Alamos; Heinz Felfe led the BND's Soviet counter-intelligence for the KGB; Georges Pâques gave it NATO war plans. A New York congressman took NKVD money, and KGB notes describe cash taken to Indira Gandhi's house. Agents such as Ames and Hanssen kept working for its Russian successors after 1991.
orgs.cite: Venona decrypts (NSA); Andrew & Mitrokhin, The Mitrokhin Archive; Kellock–Taschereau Royal Commission, 1946; US DOJ; court records in the UK, Germany, Norway, Sweden, France and Israel

orgs.n: Russian state influence operations (agency not named)
orgs.d: This dot gathers cases where the Russian state, rather than a named agency or proxy, is said to have paid or steered people inside other countries' institutions. Moldova charged former president Igor Dodon with treason over Russian money that kept his party running and reached its MPs. Greece expelled Russian diplomats in 2018 for trying to bribe state officials. An inquiry found Russian officials paid the president of world biathlon's governing body, who then shielded Russian athletes and blocked efforts to root out Russian doping. The US says Serbia's intelligence chief Vulin used his posts to help Russia. Several of these claims remain allegations.
orgs.cite: Romanian CSAT documents, Dec 2024; Moldovan prosecutors and US Treasury; Greek Foreign Ministry, 2018; US Treasury on Vulin, 2023; IBU External Review Commission, 2021

orgs.n: North Korean party and state spy agencies (Workers' Party liaison bureaus, State Security)
orgs.d: North Korea's ruling Workers' Party, through its liaison and cultural-exchange departments, and its state security service run agents and cells inside South Korean parties, local politics and the army. The Ilsimhoe cell reached the leadership of the Democratic Labor Party, the Wangjaesan ring placed a member as secretary to a politician, and the Chungbuk cell tried to recruit regional politicians; South Korean courts convicted members in all three. An agent posing as a defector gave 52 lectures at army bases. A 1998 letter signed by a party secretary said $3 million went to Pakistan's army chief for nuclear help; Pakistan calls it fake.
orgs.cite: Seoul, Suwon and Cheongju district court rulings, 2007–2024; Washington Post, 8 Jul 2011; Daily NK; Korea JoongAng Daily

orgs.d: The HVA, the foreign intelligence arm of East Germany's Ministry of State Security (the Stasi), placed agents in West German government, parliament and intelligence, and in NATO. Günter Guillaume became Chancellor Willy Brandt's personal aide, and Brandt resigned two weeks after his arrest in 1974. Gabriele Gast rose to deputy head of the West German BND's Soviet section. Rainer Rupp, code name Topaz, copied about 10,000 pages inside NATO's Brussels headquarters, including its strategy document MC 161. SPD chief whip Karl Wienand was convicted in 1996 of spying for the Stasi.
orgs.cite: Bavarian High Court, 1991; Düsseldorf regional court, 1996; Reuters, 1994; Wikipedia 'Guillaume affair'

orgs.d: Mossad, Israel's foreign intelligence service, recruits or plants sources inside the ruling circles of hostile states. Ashraf Marwan, President Nasser's son-in-law, became a Mossad source in 1970, passed Egyptian war plans and warned of the 1973 war, and was later made Sadat's secretary for foreign relations. Mossad gave Eli Cohen the identity of a Syrian businessman; in Damascus he hosted ministers and officers and reported Syrian positions on the Golan Heights before he was caught and hanged in 1965.
orgs.cite: Uri Bar-Joseph, The Angel; London inquest, 2010; Wikipedia 'Eli Cohen'

orgs.d: Lekem was a small Israeli defence-ministry bureau that gathered scientific and technical intelligence, and it ran a paid agent inside US naval intelligence. Its head, Rafi Eitan, handled Jonathan Pollard, a US Navy analyst who passed classified material from 1984 until his arrest outside Israel's Washington embassy in November 1985. Israel paid him a salary that reached $2,500 a month. He was sentenced to life; Israel admitted in 1998 that he had been its agent, and the bureau was disbanded after the case.
orgs.cite: US District Court sentence, 1987; Wikipedia 'Jonathan Pollard'

orgs.d: Iran's intelligence services recruit and pay serving soldiers and officials of hostile states to pass them military material. In Israel, Iranian intelligence recruited soldiers in the Iron Dome unit and at air force headquarters to send images of military systems for payment. In Britain it paid Daniel Khalife, a serving soldier with high security clearance, for army material including details of special forces personnel. In Germany its intelligence ministry paid an interpreter in the armed forces for plans of military sites and defence ministry analyses.
orgs.cite: Shin Bet statement, Jun 2018; Jerusalem District Court, 2019

orgs.n: Czechoslovak intelligence services (StB and military intelligence)
orgs.d: Communist Czechoslovakia's state security (the StB) and its military intelligence paid British MPs for information and influence during the Cold War. Conservative MP Ray Mawby took £100 for each item under the code name 'Laval', handing over floor plans of the Prime Minister's Commons office and details of colleagues, according to Czech files the BBC revealed in 2012. Labour minister John Stonehouse was named as a Czechoslovak agent by a defector, a claim MI5's official history supported in 2009; he was never tried.
orgs.cite: BBC, 28 Jun 2012 (Czech security files); Christopher Andrew, The Defence of the Realm, 2009

orgs.d: China's military intelligence, run by the People's Liberation Army, recruits and pays scientists and officials abroad. In Estonia it recruited Tarmo Kõuts, a marine scientist on the defence ministry's scientific committee who had worked with NATO's undersea research centre, to pass it information from that work. He was paid about €17,000 and convicted in 2021, Estonia's first conviction for spying for China.
orgs.cite: Estonian Internal Security Service; ERR; NYT, 12 May 1999; Senate Governmental Affairs Committee report, 1998

orgs.d: Syria's military intelligence ran Lebanon's politics from inside during Syria's 1976–2005 military presence there.
