Its Lebanon chief from 1982, Ghazi Kanaan, vetoed anti-Syrian candidates, pushed pro-Syrian ones onto electoral lists, drew the boundaries of fourteen electoral districts after the 1989 Taif Agreement and shaped security and judicial appointments; the head of Lebanon's General Security agency reported to him. His deputy Rustum Ghazaleh took over in 2002. Syria withdrew its troops in 2005 after Rafik Hariri's assassination.
orgs.cite: UN Security Council Resolution 1559, 2004; Wikipedia 'Ghazi Kanaan'

orgs.n: Apartheid South Africa's security and propaganda services (Security Branch, Department of Information)
orgs.d: Apartheid South Africa's police Security Branch placed agents inside foreign bodies to fight its opponents. Security Branch officer Craig Williamson got himself made deputy director of a Geneva scholarship fund for African students. He used that post to reach the banned ANC, and he diverted the fund's donor money into South African covert operations. The Security Branch thus had its own officer running part of a foreign aid body that its opponents relied on.
orgs.cite: Erasmus Commission reports, 1978–79; Truth and Reconciliation Commission amnesty decisions; Wikipedia 'Information Scandal'

orgs.n: Foccart networks and French secret services in Africa (Françafrique)
orgs.d: France's secret services and Jacques Foccart's personal networks (réseaux) tied French officials and agents to the rulers of France's former African colonies, a system known as Françafrique, and placed French agents close to those governments. French mercenary Bob Denard, who worked with France's secret services, led the 1978 Comoros coup and then commanded the islands' presidential guard for about eleven years, using that post for his business interests. In 2025 Mali's junta said French intelligence worked through a French agent to win over two generals and other officers in its armed forces for a plot against the government.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Jacques Foccart', 'Françafrique', 'Bob Denard'

orgs.d: Britain's foreign intelligence service (MI6) and security service (MI5) run informers inside movements and states and have planned changes of ruler. Accounts based on British records say MI6, the Foreign Office and the Ministry of Defence planned the 1970 palace coup that put Qaboos in power in Oman, carried out by British-commanded troops. In Northern Ireland, Sinn Féin's Stormont administrator Denis Donaldson, accused in 2002 of running an IRA spy ring, was revealed in 2005 as an MI5 informer of twenty years. Iran hanged ex-deputy defence minister Alireza Akbari in 2023 as an alleged MI6 spy; he said he was tortured into confessing.
orgs.cite: The Guardian (Cobain), 2016; Mark Curtis, 2016; Public Prosecution Service NI, 2005; BBC, Jan 2023

orgs.d: Rwanda's army placed its own officers at the head of a neighbouring state's armed forces. Rwandan officer James Kabarebe planned the rebellion that brought Laurent-Désiré Kabila to power in Kinshasa in May 1997, and Kabila then made him chief of staff of the Congolese army, where units in the east recruited more Rwandan-linked troops. Kabila dismissed him in July 1998, fearing a coup; days later Kabarebe led an airborne assault with about 3,000 Rwandan and Ugandan soldiers, starting the Second Congo War's push on the capital.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'James Kabarebe'

orgs.n: United Arab Emirates state and intelligence networks
orgs.d: The UAE government and its security establishment buy access to foreign leaders and officials through companies, job offers and spy networks. A firm backed by national security adviser Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed secretly bought 49% of the Trump family's crypto venture for $500 million and put its executives on the board, the Wall Street Journal reported in 2026. The UAE negotiated a well-paid job with UN Libya envoy Bernardino León while he led peace talks, and he wrote that he was steering them in favour of the side it backed. Oman said in 2011 it broke up a UAE spy network in its government and army.
orgs.cite: US DOJ, 18 Jul 2023; Wall Street Journal, 31 Jan 2026; The Guardian, 5 Nov 2015; Oman News Agency, Jan 2011

orgs.d: The Sinaloa Cartel, one of Mexico's two largest drug-trafficking organisations, buys protection from ministers, governors, police, soldiers and prison staff in Mexico and in transit countries. A US court convicted Genaro García Luna, Mexico's public security minister from 2006 to 2012, of taking its bribes. Co-founder Ismael 'El Mayo' Zambada admitted in 2025 that it paid Mexican police and army commanders. Joaquín 'El Chapo' Guzmán bribed prison staff, including the director, to walk out of Puente Grande in 2001, and paid Honduran congressman Tony Hernández, the president's brother. US prosecutors say the Chapitos faction helped install Sinaloa's governor in 2021 and gained control of state and local police.
orgs.cite: US v. García Luna, E.D.N.Y., 2023; US v. Hernández Alvarado, S.D.N.Y., 2019; Zambada plea, Aug 2025; US v. Rocha Moya et al., S.D.N.Y., 2026; SDNY press release on Mario Estrada, 2020

orgs.d: The Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), a Mexican drug-trafficking organisation based in Jalisco, pays judges, governors and police chiefs and hides its money in ordinary businesses. The US Treasury found that Nayarit's governor Roberto Sandoval and federal judge Isidro Avelar took its payments. Tabasco's security secretary Hernán Bermúdez is accused of running a CJNG-linked gang, La Barredora, from his office. In 2026 the Treasury named more than fifty people and firms, including tequila distilleries and petrol stations, as CJNG fronts, and sanctioned a Puerto Vallarta resort that fed its timeshare fraud.
orgs.cite: OFAC designations, May 2019, Feb 2026 and Jul 2026; Fiscalía General del Estado de Tabasco, 2025

orgs.d: The Beltrán Leyva Organisation, a Mexican cartel that split from the Sinaloa Cartel in 2008, bought officials inside the agencies meant to pursue it. In 2008 the government admitted that at least 35 officials of SIEDO, the federal unit that prosecutes organised crime, had leaked raids and evidence to the cartel for up to four years for $150,000 to $450,000 a month each. In 2012 a former deputy defence secretary and three generals were charged with selling it military intelligence. Several of these cases collapsed in court.
orgs.cite: Los Angeles Times, 28 Oct 2008; Justice in Mexico, 9 Aug 2012

orgs.d: The Clan del Golfo, Colombia's largest armed cocaine-trafficking group, grew out of the gang of former paramilitary commander Daniel Rendón ('Don Mario') and places friendly people in prosecution offices and local government. Medellín's chief prosecutor Guillermo Valencia Cossio was convicted of shielding Don Mario's gang. In 2023 a serving prosecutor was charged with holding property for a Gulf Clan front man. The US Treasury said in 2020 that a trafficker working for the group funded mayoral candidates in several towns on a member's orders.
orgs.cite: Colombian Supreme Court ruling on Valencia Cossio; Fiscalía General de la Nación, Jul 2023; US Treasury sm1197, Dec 2020

orgs.d: The AUC, a federation of right-wing paramilitary armies that were also major cocaine exporters, bought or allied with Colombian legislators, intelligence chiefs and police. In the 'parapolítica' scandal about 30% of Congress was investigated, and 32 legislators and five governors were convicted by 2012. Jorge Noguera, head of the DAS intelligence agency, was convicted of putting it at the service of the AUC's Northern Bloc, including information used to kill trade unionists. President Uribe's security chief, General Santoyo, pleaded guilty in the US to aiding the AUC, and AUC-linked legislators bribed Supreme Court judges in the 'Cartel de la Toga'.
orgs.cite: Colombian Supreme Court rulings, 2006–2026; US v. Santoyo Velasco, E.D. Va., 2012; Human Rights Watch

orgs.d: 'Cartel de los Soles' is the name US prosecutors give to Venezuelan military officers and officials who, they say, used state forces to move cocaine with Colombia's FARC rebels; the name refers to the sun insignia on generals' uniforms. Hugo Carvajal, head of military intelligence, pleaded guilty in New York in 2025 after using his post to help traffickers and aid the FARC. A 2020 indictment charges President Nicolás Maduro, who US forces captured in January 2026, and names Diosdado Cabello as a leader. Apart from the guilty pleas, these charges have not been tested at trial.
orgs.cite: US v. Maduro Moros et al., S.D.N.Y., 2020; US v. Carvajal Barrios, 2025; US v. Alcalá Cordones, 2024; OFAC, May 2018

orgs.d: The Medellín Cartel, Pablo Escobar's cocaine organisation, bought heads of state, ministers and intelligence chiefs in Colombia and along its smuggling routes. Escobar won a seat in Colombia's Congress in 1982, gaining immunity. DAS intelligence chief Miguel Maza Márquez was convicted of a role in the cartel's 1989 killing of presidential candidate Luis Carlos Galán. Panama's ruler Manuel Noriega was convicted in the US of taking its money, Cuban officers were executed in 1989 for moving its cocaine, a Bahamian inquiry found drug money ran through Pindling's cabinet, and Antiguan minister Vere Bird Jr ordered Israeli weapons in the state's name for a cartel leader's forces.
orgs.cite: US v. Noriega, S.D. Fla., 1992; Cuban military tribunal Causa No. 1, 1989; Bahamas Royal Commission, 1984; Blom-Cooper inquiry, 1990; Colombian Supreme Court rulings

orgs.d: The Cali Cartel, a Colombian cocaine organisation that preferred bribery to violence, financed politicians and placed insiders in the bodies hunting it. The Proceso 8000 investigation found it had put money into Ernesto Samper's 1994 presidential campaign; the campaign treasurer, defence minister and comptroller were convicted, though Congress cleared Samper. A 1995 raid showed its counter-intelligence unit tapping calls, including the US Embassy's, with an insider at the phone company, and a senior officer of the police Search Bloc hid leader Miguel Rodríguez Orejuela in his car.
orgs.cite: Fiscalía General de la Nación, Proceso 8000; Chepesiuk, The Bullet or the Bribe

orgs.d: The Norte del Valle Cartel, a cocaine group from Colombia's Valle del Cauca that rose after the Cali Cartel fell, tried to buy protection against extradition to the United States. A 2004 US racketeering indictment said its leaders bribed Colombian police and legislators and ran their own wiretaps on rivals and on Colombian and US police. Its lawyer Gabriel Puerta Parra reportedly influenced the government on extradition, and a man accused of bribing high officials for leader Juan Carlos Ramírez Abadía was found poisoned in his cell on his extradition day.
orgs.cite: US DOJ indictment, 2004; Wikipedia 'Norte del Valle Cartel'

orgs.d: The Guadalajara Cartel, Mexico's first large trafficking organisation, worked with and paid the state's own police. Officers of the Federal Security Directorate (DFS), the political police, took part in the 1985 kidnapping and murder of US drug agent Enrique Camarena, and the DFS was dissolved that year. Federal police commander Armando Pavón Reyes, who was hunting leader Rafael Caro Quintero, reportedly took $300,000 to let him fly out of Guadalajara and was convicted of bribery in 1986.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Dirección Federal de Seguridad'; AP, 1986; Los Angeles Times

orgs.d: The Juárez Cartel, built by Amado Carrillo Fuentes in the 1990s, paid generals and governors to protect its cocaine flights. Mexico's anti-drug chief, General Jesús Gutiérrez Rebollo, was arrested in 1997 weeks after taking office and accused of protecting Carrillo for years. In 2002 a military court convicted Generals Arturo Acosta Chaparro and Francisco Quirós Hermosillo of drug smuggling for him; Acosta was later cleared. Quintana Roo governor Mario Villanueva let the cartel use the state's coast and airstrips and pleaded guilty in New York in 2010 to laundering its money.
orgs.cite: Transnational Institute, 1997; VOA, 2 Nov 2002; US v. Villanueva Madrid, S.D.N.Y., 2010

orgs.d: The Tijuana Cartel, run by the Arellano Félix brothers, tried to buy the officials charged with fighting it in Baja California. In March 1997 Mexico jailed Brigadier General Alfredo Navarro Lara, whom prosecutors accused of offering Tijuana's anti-drug official $1 million a month to protect a major trafficking group and threatening to kill him and his family if he refused; prosecutors linked the general to the Arellano Félix organisation. He was the second general jailed for drug corruption that month.
orgs.cite: AP, 18 Mar 1997

orgs.d: The Gulf Cartel, a drug-trafficking organisation based in Tamaulipas on the US border, paid federal prosecutors and, investigators suspected, state governors. Mario Ruiz Massieu, Mexico's deputy attorney general in charge of drug prosecutions in 1993–94, moved about $9 million into Houston bank accounts, and a Houston jury found in 1997 that traffickers, mainly the Gulf Cartel, had paid it for protection. In 2012 three former Tamaulipas governors were barred from leaving Mexico while investigated for cooperating with the cartel and Los Zetas; the US later indicted one of them, Eugenio Hernández, for laundering.
orgs.cite: US civil forfeiture, S.D. Tex., 1997; Excélsior, 30 Jan 2012; US indictment of Eugenio Hernández, 2015

orgs.d: Los Zetas, a cartel founded by army special-forces deserters as the Gulf Cartel's armed wing, took over local police forces and prisons in north-east Mexico and paid state officials. Mexico's National Human Rights Commission found Allende's municipal police took part in at least 38 abductions and killings for the Zetas in 2011. The Piedras Negras state prison was handed to the cartel as a base and a place to dispose of bodies. Former Zetas testified in Texas that the cartel paid Coahuila governor Humberto Moreira and the state attorney general for control of the state; the officials deny it and no court has ruled.
orgs.cite: CNDH, 2018; Colegio de México study, 2017; testimony in US v. Treviño Morales and other W.D. Tex. trials; El Financiero, 7 Nov 2017

orgs.d: La Familia Michoacana, a cartel based in Michoacán, was accused of working through mayors, state officials and a federal deputy. In May 2009 federal police arrested more than 30 officials, including ten mayors, in the 'Michoacanazo'; judges released every one of them within two years for lack of evidence. Julio César Godoy, half-brother of the state governor, was elected to Congress in 2009 while charged with ties to the cartel, slipped into the chamber to take his seat and immunity, and was stripped of it after recordings of him with leader Servando Gómez surfaced.
orgs.cite: PGR prosecutions, 2009; Mexican Law Review; El Universal and Proceso, 2010

orgs.d: The Knights Templar Cartel, which split from La Familia Michoacana in 2011, reached the top of Michoacán's state government. Jesús Reyna, the state's secretary of government and interim governor for six months in 2013, was detained in April 2014; the attorney general said the investigation confirmed he had met cartel leaders, and a state security document described three meetings with leader Servando 'La Tuta' Gómez. He was sent to the Altiplano prison on organised-crime charges. That August the governor's son was arrested after a video showed him meeting Gómez.
orgs.cite: Al Jazeera/AFP, 8 Apr 2014; InSight Crime, May 2014

orgs.d: The H-2 Cartel, a Nayarit-based offshoot of the Beltrán Leyva Organisation, bought the state's chief prosecutor and, US prosecutors alleged, Mexico's defence minister. Nayarit attorney general Edgar Veytia directed officers to wiretap and arrest the cartel's rivals and released its members from custody from 2013 to 2017; he pleaded guilty in Brooklyn and was sentenced to 20 years in 2019. Former defence secretary Salvador Cienfuegos was arrested in Los Angeles in 2020 on charges of shielding the cartel, but the US dropped the case weeks later at Mexico's request and the claims were never tested.
orgs.cite: US v. Veytia Cambero, E.D.N.Y., 2019; US v. Cienfuegos Zepeda, E.D.N.Y., 2019–2020

orgs.d: Guerreros Unidos, a heroin-trafficking gang in Guerrero state, had the mayor of Iguala and the town's municipal police acting for it. In September 2014 Iguala police took 43 students from the Ayotzinapa teacher-training college, who disappeared. Mayor José Luis Abarca was convicted of organised crime and kidnapping. Independent experts appointed by the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights documented that federal and state forces watched the events in real time. The case is a well-evidenced example of a town government working as an arm of a trafficking group.
orgs.cite: Mexican federal court judgments, 2019 and 2022; GIEI Ayotzinapa reports; Comisión para la Verdad, 2022

orgs.d: Los Cachiros, a Honduran drug-trafficking clan from the Colón department, laundered money through a powerful political family's businesses. In 2015 the US Treasury named members of the Rosenthal family, including a former vice-president and a congressman, as its launderers through their Grupo Continental, so the group's firms and bank handled the cartel's drug profits. The bank was liquidated and Yani Rosenthal pleaded guilty in New York.
orgs.cite: OFAC Kingpin designation, Oct 2015; US v. Yankel Rosenthal, S.D.N.Y., 2017; InSight Crime and El Faro, Sep 2024

orgs.d: A Ultranza Py is the name of Paraguay's largest cocaine and money-laundering investigation, opened in February 2022, and of the network it targets, which shipped cocaine down the Paraguay–Paraná river route to the Atlantic. Prosecutors charged police officers, prosecutors, court officials and a sitting member of the Chamber of Deputies alongside the traffickers, and seized hundreds of properties. One of the case's own prosecutors was later removed, and the man named as the network's central figure and several others fled before arrest.
orgs.cite: Ministerio Público del Paraguay, Operativo A Ultranza Py case file, 2022–2024

orgs.d: Comando Vermelho, Rio de Janeiro's oldest drug faction, which began in a prison in 1979, is accused of placing a representative in the state legislature and using police escorts. In 2025 police detained state deputy TH Joias, alleging he acted as the faction's arm in the Rio assembly, and his party moved to expel him. Investigations that year also showed police officers escorting its drug shipments. A police operation against the faction in the Penha and Alemão favelas in October 2025 left more than 120 dead.
orgs.cite: G1 and Folha de S.Paulo, 2025

orgs.d: Los Choneros, the Ecuadorian gang that has held sway in the country's prisons since 2011, runs its operations from inside them and is accused of buying the staff. Its leader José Adolfo Macías ('Fito') directed the gang from his cell, then vanished from La Roca prison in Guayaquil in January 2024; guards were suspected, a fence had been cut and a boat with guard uniforms was found nearby. About 30 officials were arrested in a linked operation and the government declared an 'internal armed conflict'. Fito was recaptured in 2025.
orgs.cite: Primicias, Reuters and AP, 2024–2025

orgs.d: The FARC, Colombia's largest guerrilla army, which financed itself through cocaine, had senior officials of neighbouring Venezuela working for it. In September 2008 the US Treasury sanctioned Hugo Carvajal, head of Venezuelan military intelligence, Henry Rangel Silva, director of the DISIP intelligence service, and former interior minister Ramón Rodríguez Chacín, accusing Carvajal of protecting FARC drug loads, supplying weapons and giving it official Venezuelan documents. Rangel Silva later became defence minister. The FARC disarmed under a 2016 peace deal; holdout factions continue.
orgs.cite: US Treasury press release, 12 Sep 2008

orgs.d: D-Company, the Mumbai-born crime syndicate of Dawood Ibrahim, now based in Karachi, bought customs and police officers in India and was tied to a Nepali minister. In February 1993 its smugglers paid customs officers and police to land about 3,000 kg of RDX explosive on the Raigad coast; it was used in the Bombay bombings that March. A special court convicted an assistant customs commissioner, customs superintendents, a police sub-inspector and four constables in 2006–07. In Nepal, MP and minister Mirza Dilshad Beg was reported to work with the syndicate before he was shot dead in 1998.
orgs.cite: TADA court verdicts, 2006–07; India Today, 1998

orgs.n: Jogo do bicho bosses (Rio's illegal lottery 'cúpula')
orgs.d: The bosses of the jogo do bicho, Rio de Janeiro's illegal numbers lottery, run a central commission that pays police, judges and politicians. Rio's attorney general called it 'a true Brazilian Mafia', and Judge Denise Frossard convicted its members in 1993. In 1994 police seized 200 account books at boss Castor de Andrade's base that named a former president, Rio's governor, three judges, 12 congressmen and 125 police; none was convicted. In 2007 federal police arrested bosses including the president of the samba-school league over payoffs to judges, police and prosecutors.
orgs.cite: Folha de S.Paulo, Veja and New York Times, 1994; O Globo, Apr 2007

orgs.d: The Tambov gang, a St Petersburg crime group, got control of businesses run by the city government. Vladimir Kumarin, named as its leader, was deputy president of the city-administered Petersburg Fuel Company in 1998–99, and in 2001 Russia's interior minister said the gang controlled up to 100 industrial enterprises, including that company. The city legislature's speaker was alleged to be close to Kumarin before he was killed in 1999. Kumarin was sentenced to 14 years in 2009; a Spanish case against the gang's branch there ended in acquittals.
orgs.cite: Vedomosti, 2009; Gryzlov statement, 2001

orgs.d: The Zemun clan, a Belgrade crime group with a share of the Balkan heroin trade, merged with the JSO, the special operations unit of Serbia's interior ministry. In March 2003 a serving JSO commander shot dead Prime Minister Zoran Đinđić. Belgrade's special court for organised crime convicted twelve people in May 2007, and the unit was disbanded.
orgs.cite: Special Court for Organised Crime, Belgrade, May 2007

orgs.d: The Kavač clan, a Montenegrin crime group trading cocaine across Europe and South America, had protection from senior officials, prosecutors say. Messages from Sky ECC, an encrypted phone service cracked by police and passed to Montenegro by Europol, led to charges against the former chief special prosecutor, a former assistant police director and his son, a state security officer. Separate indictments name a former Supreme Court president, two former police directors and the mayor of Budva.
orgs.cite: Special State Prosecutor's Office of Montenegro, indictments 2023–2024

orgs.d: The criminal organisation of Ridouan Taghi, once the Netherlands' most wanted cocaine trafficker, paid a police insider for searches. According to the Algemeen Dagblad in 2019, a senior Utrecht police officer was paid thousands of euros several times to look up people and photographs in police systems and pass them to the gang. The claim came from the crown witness Nabil B. The officer was dismissed and the Rijksrecherche, which investigates police misconduct, opened an inquiry. Taghi was sentenced to life in 2024 in the Marengo trial.
orgs.cite: Algemeen Dagblad / NL Times, 10 Jul 2019

orgs.d: Al-Shabaab, the al-Qaeda-linked Islamist insurgency in Somalia, places agents in government offices and trades with the forces sent to fight it. In 2019 a woman working in the Mogadishu mayor's office under a false name blew herself up at a security meeting, killing six officials and the mayor. The intelligence agency later named a government band singer as the group's accountant, and the government dissolved the Chamber of Commerce board after finding al-Shabaab representatives on it. A 2015 report said Kenyan army units in Somalia were part of a sugar and charcoal smuggling cartel with the group; Kenya denied it.
orgs.cite: Al Jazeera, 25 Jul 2019; Daily Nation, Jan 2020; Journalists for Justice report, Nov 2015

orgs.d: Boko Haram, the jihadist group fighting in north-east Nigeria since 2009, had sympathisers inside the Nigerian state, according to the country's own president. On 8 January 2012 President Goodluck Jonathan said the group had infiltrated the army, the police and the executive and legislative branches of government. He named no one, and no specific infiltrators were publicly identified at the time, so the claim stands as an admission from the head of state rather than a proven case.
orgs.cite: BBC News and Reuters, 8 Jan 2012

orgs.n: National Congress for the Defence of the People (CNDP)
orgs.d: The CNDP, a Rwanda-linked Tutsi rebel group in eastern Congo's North Kivu, was folded into the Congolese army in 2009, and its chief of staff Bosco Ntaganda served as a general despite an International Criminal Court arrest warrant. A UN expert group reported in 2011 that he profited from mines, including through a 'parallel' mine police at Rubaya. In 2012 he and about 300 loyal troops left the army, starting the M23 rebellion. The ICC convicted him of 18 counts, including murder, rape and child recruitment, and sentenced him to 30 years in 2019.
orgs.cite: UN Group of Experts, 2011; ICC judgment, 2019

orgs.d: ETA, the Basque armed separatist group, used the party Batasuna to hold elected seats and public money, Spanish courts found. Judge Baltasar Garzón suspended the party in 2002, and in 2003 Spain's Supreme Court declared it illegal as part of ETA; a court found it had financed ETA with public funds. Batasuna lost its elected representatives, and in 2009 neither it nor parties seen as its proxies could stand in the Basque election. The European Court of Human Rights upheld the ban that year. ETA announced its dissolution in 2018.
orgs.cite: Spanish Supreme Court, 2003; ECtHR, Herri Batasuna and Batasuna v. Spain, 30 Jun 2009

orgs.d: The Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF) and Ulster Defence Association (UDA), Protestant loyalist paramilitary groups in Northern Ireland, had members serving in the British Army's locally recruited Ulster Defence Regiment and in the police. A 1973 military intelligence report estimated 5–15% of UDR soldiers belonged to 'Protestant extremist groups' and called the regiment their 'best single source of weapons'. The Glenanne gang combined the UVF's Mid-Ulster Brigade with serving soldiers and RUC officers and killed about 120 people; a 2006 international panel found police or soldier involvement in 74 of 76 killings it examined.
orgs.cite: 'Subversion in the UDR', 1973; Stevens Inquiry, 1989; Cassel report, 2006; Barron reports, 2003

orgs.d: Egyptian Islamic Jihad, an armed Islamist group, built a cell inside Egypt's army and used it to kill the head of state. Led by Lieutenant Khalid al-Islambuli, the squad rode in an army truck in the 6 October 1981 military parade, stopped in front of the reviewing stand and killed President Anwar Sadat with grenades and gunfire; a round-up of 1,500 people weeks earlier had missed it. Five, including al-Islambuli, an army sergeant and plot leader Muhammad Abd al-Salam Faraj, were executed in 1982. The group later merged into al-Qaeda.
orgs.cite: Egyptian trial records, 1982; Wikipedia 'Assassination of Anwar Sadat'

orgs.d: The People's Mojahedin (MEK), an Iranian armed opposition movement now based in Albania, was accused by Iran of planting members inside the new Islamic Republic's offices in 1981. On 30 August that year a bomb in the prime minister's office killed President Rajai, Prime Minister Bahonar and the police chief; it was attributed to Masoud Keshmiri, secretary of the office and of the Supreme National Security Council, who fled abroad. Two months earlier a man who had got a job as a sound engineer at the ruling party's headquarters planted a bomb that killed about 70 officials. No group claimed either attack.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia '1981 Iranian Prime Minister's office bombing' and 'Hafte Tir bombing'

orgs.d: The Iron Guard, Romania's fascist Legionary Movement, was placed inside the state in September 1940 when General Ion Antonescu declared the 'National Legionary State'. Its leader Horia Sima became deputy prime minister, and the Guard took the interior, education, foreign and religious affairs ministries, the Bucharest police command and the prefect's office in all fifty counties. Guardists killed 64 former officials at Jilava prison, and in January 1941 the Guard attempted a coup with a pogrom that murdered about 200 Jews in Bucharest. Antonescu expelled it from government.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'National Legionary State', citing Romanian and Holocaust historians

orgs.d: The Arrow Cross, Hungary's fascist movement, was put in charge of the state by Nazi Germany in October 1944, after Germany detained Regent Horthy for trying to leave the war. Leader Ferenc Szálasi became 'Leader of the Nation' and prime minister the same day, heading a government dominated by his party until March 1945. Arrow Cross death squads killed up to 38,000 Hungarian Jews in under three months, and its officers helped Adolf Eichmann restart deportations from Budapest. Szálasi and three associates were hanged in 1946.
orgs.cite: Hungarian People's Tribunal records; Wikipedia 'Arrow Cross Party'

orgs.d: The Committee of Union and Progress, an oath-bound secret society begun by military medical students in Constantinople in 1889, organised in cells sworn to a Central Committee and placed officers in the army and party-chosen 'responsible secretaries' over provincial officials. In January 1913 CUP men forced the grand vizier to resign at gunpoint, and Talât, Enver and Cemal then ran the Ottoman Empire as a one-party regime. Its Special Organisation, answering to the Central Committee, was used in the genocide of Armenians, Pontic Greeks and Assyrians. Many members were court-martialled after 1918.
orgs.cite: Zürcher; Hanioğlu; Wikipedia 'Committee of Union and Progress'

orgs.d: Hanahoe was a secret club of South Korean army officers from the 11th Korea Military Academy class, topped up with a few hand-picked members from each later class, who placed one another in key commands. Led by Chun Doo-hwan and Roh Tae-woo, its members seized the army on 12 December 1979 and the government in 1980; Chun and then Roh served as president until 1993. President Kim Young-sam broke up the club in March 1993 by dismissing the army chief of staff and the security command chief. Chun and Roh were convicted in 1996 and pardoned in 1997.
orgs.cite: Encyclopedia of Korean Culture; Hankyoreh; Korea Times

orgs.n: Military Committee of the Ba'ath Party (Syria)
orgs.d: The Military Committee was a secret body of Syrian army officers, formed in 1958 by al-Jundi, Umran, Jadid and Hafez al-Assad, whose members swore to hide it even from their own Ba'ath Party leaders. It carried out the coup of 8 March 1963 that brought the Ba'ath to power and then held the real power inside the ruling council as a 'junta within a junta'. Jadid ousted the party's civilian leaders in 1966, with Assad as defence minister; Assad seized power in 1970, and he and his son Bashar ruled Syria until December 2024.
orgs.cite: Seale, Asad, 1990; Rabinovich, 1972

orgs.d: The Free Officers were a clandestine network of junior Egyptian army officers, led from 1950 by Gamal Abdel Nasser, who recruited inside the army and enlisted General Mohamed Naguib as their public face. On 23 July 1952 they seized power and forced King Farouk to abdicate. Their Revolutionary Command Council ran the state, the monarchy was abolished in 1953, and Nasser ruled until 1970. Its successor, the Supreme Council of the Armed Forces, still sits at the top of Egypt's state, and the model was copied by officers in Iraq and Libya.
orgs.cite: Al-Ahram Online; Wikipedia 'Free Officers movement (Egypt)'

orgs.d: The Iraqi Free Officers were a secret underground group of army officers modelled on Egypt's, led by Brigadier Abdul-Karim Qasim, who planned a revolt using units under their own command. On 14 July 1958 their forces took Baghdad, King Faisal II and the crown prince were killed at the palace, and the Hashemite monarchy ended. Qasim made himself prime minister and defence minister, and Colonel Abdul Salam Arif became deputy prime minister and interior minister. The coup began a long period in which officers' factions decided who governed Iraq.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia '14 July Revolution'

orgs.d: The Free Unionist Officers were about 70 young Libyan army officers whom Muammar Gaddafi organised inside the army, backed by enlisted men mostly from the Signal Corps. On 1 September 1969, while King Idris was abroad, they launched a bloodless coup from Benghazi, abolished the monarchy and declared a republic. A twelve-member Revolutionary Command Council of the plotters formed the government, with Gaddafi as chairman and de facto head of state. He ruled Libya for 42 years, until his death in 2011.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia '1969 Libyan revolution'

orgs.d: Khana Ratsadon, the People's Party, was founded in Paris in 1927 by seven Siamese students, including Pridi Banomyong and Plaek Phibunsongkhram, and grew to about 102 officers and civilians in secret branches. On 24 June 1932 its members used army units to stage a bloodless revolution that ended Siam's absolute monarchy. Members then held the prime ministership for about two decades, including Phahon (1933–1938) and Phibunsongkhram (1938–1944). The party split into civilian and military wings and dissolved in 1947, but the army's habit of taking power by coup dates from it.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Khana Ratsadon'

orgs.d: The Sakurakai was a secret society of Imperial Japanese Army officers inside the Army General Staff, founded in 1930 by Lieutenant Colonel Kingoro Hashimoto, chief of its Russian section, with the aim of overthrowing party government and installing military rule. It grew from about ten staff officers to more than 50 by early 1931 and possibly several hundred. With civilian ultranationalists it tried twice in 1931, in the March Incident and the Imperial Colours Incident. Its leaders were arrested and it was dissolved, but such plots helped push Japan towards military government.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Sakurakai'

orgs.d: The Reform the Armed Forces Movement was founded in 1982 by junior Philippine officers of the Military Academy class of 1971, led by Gregorio Honasan, security chief to Defence Minister Juan Ponce Enrile, who reportedly approved it. About 300 officers declared themselves in 1985. In February 1986 RAM planned to oust Ferdinand Marcos; when the plot was found, Enrile and Fidel Ramos took refuge in the military camps and the crowds that gathered became the People Power Revolution. RAM then attempted six coups against Corazon Aquino's government before an amnesty in 1996.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Reform the Armed Forces Movement'

orgs.d: The GOU was a secret nationalist lodge of Argentine army officers, mostly colonels and lieutenant colonels, formed in March 1943 with an oath of loyalty. Most historians credit it with a crucial role in the coup of 4 June 1943, though Robert Potash plays this down. Its members then took key posts: Juan Perón headed the Labour Department, then became war minister and vice-president, Emilio Ramírez ran the Buenos Aires police and Luis Perlinger the interior ministry. The GOU dissolved itself in 1944, and Perón used his labour post to build the union base that won him the presidency in 1946.
orgs.cite: Potash; Félix Luna; Wikipedia 'Revolution of 1943'

orgs.d: The Lautaro Lodge was a secret lodge set up in Buenos Aires in 1812 by José de San Martín, Carlos María de Alvear and José Matías Zapiola, officers back from Spain; historians are unsure whether it was truly Masonic. It organised the revolution of 8 October 1812, in which San Martín's and Alvear's troops removed the First Triumvirate. Co-founder Alvear later became Supreme Director, the head of government, and San Martín backed fellow member Juan Martín de Pueyrredón for the same post. San Martín set up a Chilean branch after his army crossed the Andes.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Lautaro Lodge' and 'José de San Martín'

orgs.d: MBR-200 was a secret movement that Hugo Chávez and fellow officers founded inside Venezuela's army in 1982 under the Samán de Güere tree near Maracay. Starting as a study circle, it recruited officers and planned a coup; on 4 February 1992 about 2,367 military personnel from 10 battalions took part in a failed attempt to seize power. The movement became Chávez's Fifth Republic Movement and he won the presidency in 1998. Co-founder Jesús Urdaneta was put in charge of the intelligence service, and fellow 1992 plotters became governors of Zulia and Caracas.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Revolutionary Bolivarian Movement-200' and 'Hugo Chávez'

orgs.d: RADEPA was a secret lodge of young Bolivian army officers founded in 1934 by prisoners of war held in Paraguay during the Chaco War, who wanted the army in politics and limits on foreign control of Bolivia's resources. In late 1943 it worked in secret with the Revolutionary Nationalist Movement (MNR), and on 20 December 1943 the two overthrew President Enrique Peñaranda. RADEPA member Gualberto Villarroel became head of state and MNR figures such as Víctor Paz Estenssoro took cabinet posts. Crowds stormed the palace and killed Villarroel in 1946.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Gualberto Villarroel'

orgs.d: The Unión Militar Española was a clandestine, pro-fascist society of officers inside the armed forces of the Spanish Republic, formed in 1933 and led by Captain Bartolomé Barba Hernández. By early 1936 it was estimated to include almost half of all serving officers, many also in the Falange. Member Valentín Galarza opened contact with General Franco in 1935, and in 1936 the UME put itself at the disposal of General Mola's conspiracy and joined the planning of the July coup that began the Civil War. It is also linked to killings that helped trigger the war.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Unión Militar Española'

orgs.d: The Golden Square was a cabal of four pro-Axis Iraqi colonels, Salah al-Din al-Sabbagh, Kamil Shabib, Fahmi Said and air force chief Mahmud Salman, encouraged by German and Italian envoys. Because Iraqi governments of the 1930s needed army backing to survive, these officers decided who governed. On 1 April 1941 they and Rashid Ali al-Gaylani overthrew the regent's government and set up a 'National Defence Government'. Britain invaded in the Anglo-Iraqi War that followed; all four were later returned to Iraq and executed.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Golden Square (Iraq)'

orgs.d: The Irish Republican Brotherhood, a secret oath-bound society founded in 1858 to win an Irish republic, worked by placing its members in senior posts inside armed bodies; Michael Collins presided over its Supreme Council. After the Civil War it re-formed as a faction holding posts inside the Free State's National Army behind defence minister Richard Mulcahy. The fight over its grip on those posts led to the 1924 Army Mutiny; IRB officers were dismissed and the society dissolved itself.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Irish Republican Brotherhood'

orgs.d: The Illuminati were a secret society founded on 1 May 1776 by Adam Weishaupt, a professor at the University of Ingolstadt in Bavaria. It recruited heavily among lawyers, academics, churchmen and officials, and its members came to hold seats in many civic and state bodies, where some court officials reportedly favoured fellow members. About 650 members can be verified at the end of 1784, perhaps 1,300 in all. Elector Charles Theodore banned it and other secret societies by edicts from 1784, and the government seized and published its papers in 1787.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Illuminati'

orgs.d: The Carbonari were a secret revolutionary society whose members in the Kingdom of Naples included nobles, priests, officials and army officers. On 1 July 1820 two officers, Michele Morelli and Joseph Silvati, led cavalry regiments towards Nola, General Guglielmo Pepe and many other officers and officials joined them, and King Ferdinand I agreed to grant a constitution and a parliament. An Austrian army sent by the Holy Alliance defeated the movement in 1821; Morelli and Silvati were sentenced to death and Pepe went into exile.
orgs.cite: Villari, 1911; Wikipedia 'Carbonari'

orgs.d: La Cagoule was a secret far-right society founded in 1936 by Eugène Deloncle, organised in military-style cells sworn to secrecy on pain of death and funded by industrialists including L'Oréal founder Eugène Schueller and Louis Renault. Through Georges Loustaunau-Lacau's Corvignolles network it infiltrated parts of the French army to get weapons. It carried out assassinations and bombed two employers' buildings in 1937 to blame communists, and planned to overthrow the Popular Front government that November. Police, who had infiltrated it, arrested about 70 men. Member Joseph Darnand later led the Vichy Milice.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'La Cagoule'

orgs.d: Ireland's Catholic bishops, through private letters and meetings with ministers, decided parts of government policy in the decades after independence. In 1951 Archbishop John Charles McQuaid of Dublin told Taoiseach John A. Costello that Health Minister Noël Browne's Mother and Child Scheme, free health care for mothers and children, was 'opposed to Catholic social teaching'. Costello said he would accept the Church's view even if it brought down the government, Browne was left alone in cabinet and resigned, and The Irish Times then published the correspondence between bishops and ministers.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Mother and Child Scheme'; The Irish Times, 12 Apr 1951

orgs.d: Jamaat-e-Islami, Pakistan's main Islamist movement, became the ideological and political arm of General Zia-ul-Haq's military government after 1977, with members at times holding cabinet posts including information and broadcasting. Journalist Owen Bennett-Jones writes that 'tens of thousands of Jamaat activists and sympathisers were given jobs in the judiciary', and that these appointments kept Zia's Islamisation programme alive after his death in 1988. Jamaat also backed Zia's support for the war against the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan.
orgs.cite: Owen Bennett-Jones, Pakistan: Eye of the Storm

orgs.d: Sudan's Free Officers were a clandestine group of army officers on the Egyptian model. On 25 May 1969 Colonel Gaafar Nimeiry, commanding the Khartoum garrison, joined other Free Officers in overthrowing the civilian government of Ismail al-Azhari in what they called the 'May Revolution'. Nimeiry made himself chairman of their Revolutionary Command Council and ruled Sudan until 1985, later bringing Islamists into government and imposing sharia law across the country in 1983.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Gaafar Nimeiry'

orgs.n: Project for the New American Century (PNAC)
orgs.d: The Project for the New American Century, a Washington think tank founded in 1997 by William Kristol and Robert Kagan, campaigned for the removal of Saddam Hussein and then supplied senior officials to the government that invaded Iraq. Ten of the 25 signatories of its 1997 statement of principles served under George W. Bush, among them Vice President Dick Cheney, Defence Secretary Donald Rumsfeld and his deputy Paul Wolfowitz; Scooter Libby became Cheney's chief of staff and John Bolton UN ambassador. Its members backed the 2003 invasion; some scholars argue its influence on the decision is exaggerated.
orgs.cite: Abelson; Parmar; Wikipedia 'Project for the New American Century'

orgs.d: Alliance Defending Freedom, a Christian conservative legal organisation, writes model laws for state legislatures and then defends them in court. It drafted the model for Mississippi's 15-week abortion ban, designed to provoke a challenge to Roe v. Wade; its lawyers joined the state's legal team, and in Dobbs v. Jackson (2022) the Supreme Court overturned Roe. ADF says it authored at least 130 bills in 34 states in 2022, more than 30 of which became law, including model 'bathroom bills'. Former ADF attorney Mike Johnson became Speaker of the House in 2023.
orgs.cite: Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization, 2022; ADF 'Who We Are'; NBC News, 2021; CBS News, 2023

orgs.d: The Fundación Mediterránea, a business-funded think tank in Córdoba, Argentina, trained the team of economists that Domingo Cavallo took into the economy ministry. Cavallo became economy minister in 1991, brought the foundation's economists with him and signed the Convertibility law fixing the peso at one US dollar, serving until 1996. Recalled in 2001, he froze bank deposits that November, the 'corralito', shortly before Argentina's economic collapse and record debt default.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Domingo Cavallo'

orgs.d: ICMI was formed in 1990 under minister B. J. Habibie, with President Suharto's permission as he courted Islamic support, and moved Muslim intellectuals into the state. In return for backing the regime its members gained posts in the civil service and central ministries, and it helped set up religious courts, Bank Muamalat and the newspaper Republika. It had about 80,000 members by 1994. Critics, including groups in Nahdlatul Ulama, called it a lobby for Suharto and a vehicle for Habibie, who became vice-president and then president in 1998.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Indonesian Association of Muslim Intellectuals'

orgs.d: The Israeli settler movement, which builds communities in the occupied West Bank, works through state ministries and now holds the office that governs land there. The 2005 Sasson report found the defence and housing ministries and others had funded unauthorised settler outposts against government rules, including 400 mobile homes, some on private Palestinian land; Gush Emunim and its building arm Amana drove the outposts. Under the 2022 coalition deal settler leader Bezalel Smotrich gained authority over West Bank civil affairs, aiming to expand settlements. The UK and others sanctioned him in 2025 for inciting settler violence.
orgs.cite: Sasson Report, 8 Mar 2005; Times of Israel; UK government, 10 Jun 2025

orgs.d: Militant, a Trotskyist group organised around its newspaper, worked secretly inside the Labour Party, a method called entryism, to take over its branches and seats. A Labour inquiry found in 1982 that it broke party rules, and five of its editorial board were expelled. In 1983 Militant-backed councillors took Liverpool City Council with Derek Hatton as deputy leader; the council set an illegal budget in 1985 and issued redundancy notices to about 30,000 workers, and 47 councillors were surcharged. Militant supporters Terry Fields, Dave Nellist and Pat Wall were elected Labour MPs.
orgs.cite: Labour NEC Hayward–Hughes report, 1982; House of Lords, 1987

orgs.d: The SS, Nazi Germany's party police and security force, took over the international police body that later became Interpol. After Germany annexed Austria in 1938 the Vienna-based International Criminal Police Commission came under German control and most member states stopped supporting it. From 1938 to 1945 its presidents were all SS generals: Otto Steinhäusl, Reinhard Heydrich, Arthur Nebe and Ernst Kaltenbrunner, who was executed after the Nuremberg trials. It moved its headquarters to Berlin in 1942. Interpol's own history acknowledges the period.
orgs.cite: Interpol history; Wikipedia 'Interpol'

orgs.d: The Sadrist movement of the cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, whose militia was the Mahdi Army, placed its members in Iraq's ministries after 2003. Hakim al-Zamili, deputy health minister from 2006 to 2007, was accused of running death squads that used ambulances and hospitals to kidnap and murder Sunni Arabs during the sectarian war, and of kidnapping a fellow deputy minister. US troops arrested him in 2007; he was cleared after key witnesses failed to appear, which was linked to intimidation. He became first deputy speaker of parliament in 2022.
orgs.cite: Washington Post, Mar 2008; Wikipedia 'Hakim al-Zamili'

orgs.d: The Mkhedrioni, a Georgian militia founded in 1989 by Jaba Ioseliani and accused of extortion and drug smuggling, was given a place inside the state after it helped overthrow President Zviad Gamsakhurdia in 1991–92. It served as interior forces and later as the semi-official 'Georgian Rescue Corps'. Ioseliani sat in parliament with armed members as 'bodyguards', and its men ran roadblocks where drivers were 'fined'. Eduard Shevardnadze ordered it disarmed in 1995; it was outlawed and Ioseliani jailed until an amnesty in 2000.
orgs.cite: Jamestown Foundation; Wikipedia 'Mkhedrioni'

orgs.d: Menzil, a branch of the Naqshbandi Sufi order, moved its followers into Turkish state posts emptied by the purge of Gülen followers, according to journalists and its own leader. The book Metastaz by Barış Terkoğlu and Barış Pehlivan says that from 2014 new police recruits came largely from Naqshbandi and other orders, with Menzil dominant, and T24 reported promotions made by reference to Menzil membership. The order's chief told Sözcü that two ministers were members and that it had 'men everywhere in the state'. The interior minister denied it, and a court ordered T24's article removed.
orgs.cite: Foreign Policy, 15 Jan 2020; Terkoğlu and Pehlivan, Metastaz

orgs.d: The Vishva Hindu Parishad, a Hindu nationalist body in the RSS family, has had its officials placed in state roles over cases and projects it campaigned on. Gujarat's government appointed VHP lawyers as public prosecutors in trials over the 2002 riots in which VHP members were accused, and a 2010 Special Investigation Team report said political affiliation appeared to have influenced the appointments. In 2020, nine of the 11 key trustees of the government-formed trust building the Ayodhya Ram temple, including its chairman and general secretary, came from the VHP or RSS.
orgs.cite: Supreme Court hearings, 2003 and 2021; SIT report, 17 May 2010; The Week, 19 Feb 2020

orgs.d: Harkat-ul-Jihad al-Islami, a Pakistani Deobandi militant group, worked with serving army officers in 1995 to seize power from inside the army. With HuJI chief Qari Saifullah Akhtar, officers planned to storm a corps commanders' meeting in Rawalpindi, kill Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto and the army chief, and declare a caliphate under Major General Zahirul Islam Abbasi. They were detained in September 1995 after Akhtar turned informer. A court martial gave Abbasi seven years and Brigadier Mustansir Billah 14.
orgs.cite: Dawn, Feb 2022; Wikipedia 'Zahirul Islam Abbasi'

orgs.d: The Madkhali Salafis follow Rabee al-Madkhali, a Saudi cleric in Medina whose ultra-conservative teaching demands obedience to rulers, and in Libya they have built positions inside both rival governments' security forces and religious offices. The International Crisis Group reported in 2019 that in Tripoli they are strong in the Special Deterrence Force (Rada), given a national remit by decree in 2018, while in the east they form units of Khalifa Haftar's army and dominate the endowments authority that runs mosques and issues fatwas. A former official estimated most Tripoli mosques were under their influence.
orgs.cite: International Crisis Group, Addressing the Rise of Libya's Madkhali-Salafis, 25 Apr 2019

orgs.n: Chongryon (General Association of Korean Residents in Japan)
orgs.d: Chongryon, the association of pro-North Korean residents in Japan that serves as Pyongyang's de facto embassy, controlled a network of Korean credit unions called Chogin and drew money out of them. Its former finance bureau chief, Kang Yong-gwan, took ¥837 million from the Chogin Tokyo credit union in 13 transactions between 1994 and 1998; the credit union collapsed in 1999. Police searched Chongryon's headquarters in 2001 and arrested other Chogin chairmen over illicit loans. Kang was sentenced to six years for embezzlement in 2004.
orgs.cite: Japan Times, 29 Nov 2001, 27 Mar 2004 and 7 Oct 2005

orgs.d: The Ottoman Public Debt Administration was a body of European bondholders placed inside the Ottoman state after it stopped paying its foreign debt. Created by the Decree of Muharrem in October 1881, it represented holders from Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Austria and the Netherlands alongside Ottoman bondholders, and was given the right to collect various taxes and customs duties directly to pay creditors. Part of the empire's tax system thus became an agency run for foreign lenders.
orgs.cite: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Decree of Muharrem'; Wikipedia 'Ottoman public debt'

orgs.d: The Caisse de la Dette Publique (Public Debt Fund) placed European creditors' commissioners over Egypt's finances after it fell behind on its loans. Set up by Khedive Isma'il's decree of May 1876, it represented Austria-Hungary, France and Italy, joined by Britain in 1877 and Russia and Germany in 1885, and oversaw debt payments, how taxes were raised and what Egypt could afford to pay. Alongside it France and Britain ran 'dual control' of Egypt's finances until Britain occupied the country in 1882. It lasted until 1940.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Caisse de la Dette Publique'

orgs.d: The International Financial Commission was a six-member body of Greece's creditor states, Britain, France, Austria-Hungary, Germany, Russia and Italy, placed inside the Greek state in 1898 after its 1893 bankruptcy and its defeat in the 1897 war. A Greek law gave it control of the salt, oil, match, playing-card and cigarette-paper monopolies, Naxos emery, the tobacco tax, stamp duties and Piraeus port duties, and let it assess state agencies' tax collection. It stayed in Athens until 1936 and in the 1920s handled League of Nations lending.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'International Financial Commission'

orgs.d: The Fugger banking house of Augsburg, led by Jakob Fugger, bought an imperial election and was repaid with state mines. In 1519 more than 850,000 guilders went to the seven prince-electors who chose the Holy Roman Emperor, and Fugger supplied about 550,000 of it; Charles of Habsburg was elected unanimously. By 1521 Charles owed him more than 600,000 guilders and repaid part with the silver and copper mines of Tyrol and, in 1523, a quicksilver concession at Almadén. Fugger reminded the emperor he could not have won the crown without him.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Jakob Fugger'

orgs.d: Banca Romana, one of Italy's note-issuing banks, lent money, often interest-free, to politicians for election campaigns and to newspapers in return for favours. Under governor Bernardo Tanlongo it had 135 million lire in notes circulating against a legal limit of 75 million, plus 40 million in duplicate-numbered notes. When it failed in 1893, documents implicated Prime Minister Giovanni Giolitti, who had tried to make Tanlongo a senator with immunity, and former premier Francesco Crispi. Giolitti resigned, and the scandal led to the founding of the Bank of Italy.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Banca Romana scandal'

orgs.n: Second Bank of the United States
orgs.d: The Second Bank of the United States, a privately run national bank headed by Nicholas Biddle, used loans and retainer fees to win support in Congress for renewing its charter. Senator Daniel Webster reportedly received an annual fee for defending it; Senator George Poindexter received a $10,000 loan after backing renewal and $8,000 more while the first was unpaid, in breach of the bank's charter; and it gave money to Henry Clay and pro-bank editors before the 1832 election. President Andrew Jackson vetoed the renewal and removed federal deposits from the bank.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Bank War'

orgs.n: Panama Canal Company (Compagnie universelle du canal interocéanique)
orgs.d: The French Panama Canal Company, through the financiers Jacques de Reinach and Cornelius Herz, paid members of parliament and a minister to approve its fundraising from the public. Ferdinand de Lesseps was accused of paying bribes in 1888 to permit a stock issue; Reinach handled right-wing deputies and Herz the radicals. When the company collapsed, about 800,000 investors lost around 1.8 billion gold francs. Inquiries found 104 legislators involved; former minister Charles Baïhaut was sentenced to five years and most others were acquitted.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Panama scandals'

orgs.d: OneWest Bank, founded by Steven Mnuchin's investor group from the failed IndyMac, supplied the regulator of US national banks while Mnuchin was Treasury Secretary. Its former chief executive Joseph Otting became Comptroller of the Currency in 2017. In 2020 his office rewrote the rules under the Community Reinvestment Act, which requires banks to lend in poorer neighbourhoods, broadening what counts as such lending; community groups said it would cut lending in low-income areas, and Congresswoman Maxine Waters linked it to the complaints OneWest had faced.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Joseph Otting'

orgs.d: Hypo Alpe-Adria-Bank, an Austrian regional bank that expanded across the Balkans before its 2009 collapse, was accused of paying a commission to a future Croatian prime minister. Ivo Sanader was charged with taking nearly $695,000 for arranging a Hypo loan in 1995, when he was deputy foreign minister. He was sentenced to ten years in 2012 in a verdict that also covered a MOL case, but the Constitutional Court quashed it in 2015, and on retrial he was acquitted in the Hypo case, upheld in 2025.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Ivo Sanader'; USKOK

orgs.d: Lockheed, the US aircraft maker, paid politicians, royals and fixers in allied countries to win aircraft orders; US Senate hearings in 1975–76 found its foreign bribes totalled $22 million. In Japan about ¥500 million went to Prime Minister Kakuei Tanaka's office for an airliner order, and he was convicted in 1983. In the Netherlands Prince Bernhard took $1.1 million over a fighter choice and gave up his public posts. In Italy former defence minister Mario Tanassi was convicted over Hercules transport planes, and President Leone resigned under the allegations.
orgs.cite: US Senate (Church) subcommittee hearings, 1975–76; Tokyo District Court, 1983; Italian Constitutional Court, 1979

orgs.d: Recruit, a Japanese recruitment-advertising and publishing company led by Hiromasa Ezoe, offered shares in its property arm Recruit Cosmos to senior politicians shortly before they went public in 1986; the price then rose sharply. Seventeen members of the Diet were involved and thirty more later found to have received favours, including Prime Minister Noboru Takeshita, former Prime Minister Yasuhiro Nakasone, Chief Cabinet Secretary Takao Fujinami and opposition leaders. The scandal broke in 1988 and forced Takeshita's cabinet to resign in 1989.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Recruit scandal'

orgs.d: The Flick industrial group gave about 25 million Deutsche Mark to all the main West German parties, which its manager Eberhard von Brauchitsch called 'cultivation of the political landscape', while seeking a tax exemption. Cash-book entries listed payments to CSU leader Franz Josef Strauss and CDU leader Helmut Kohl. Economics ministers Hans Friderichs and Otto Graf Lambsdorff approved Flick's tax exemption on a 1.9 billion DM sale of Daimler shares. Lambsdorff resigned in 1984, and in 1987 both were fined for tax evasion only.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Flick affair'; Der Spiegel

orgs.d: Siemens, the German engineering company, paid about $1.3 billion in bribes worldwide, and in Argentina more than $100 million went to officials, including two former presidents and cabinet ministers, to win and keep a $1 billion contract for national identity cards from about 1996 to 2007. In 2008 Siemens and its Argentine subsidiary pleaded guilty in the US to foreign-bribery offences as part of a $1.6 billion settlement with the US and Germany, and US authorities charged eight former executives over the Argentine payments in 2011.
orgs.cite: US SEC press release 2011-263; US DOJ, Dec 2008

orgs.d: KBR, the engineering firm then owned by Halliburton, led a joint venture that paid about $180 million in bribes to Nigerian officials from 1994 to 2004 to win contracts worth over $6 billion for the Bonny Island liquefied natural gas plant. One consultant received over $130 million to pay senior executive-branch officials and another over $50 million for lower officials, including at the state oil company NNPC. KBR pleaded guilty in the US in 2009, and with Halliburton paid $579 million in penalties; its former chief executive Albert Stanley had pleaded guilty in 2008.
orgs.cite: US v. Kellogg Brown & Root, 2009; SEC v. Halliburton and KBR

orgs.d: Unaoil, a Monaco-based firm that worked as a fixer for foreign oil-service companies, paid officials inside state oil bodies to steer contracts to its clients. In Iraq it paid more than $17 million to officials of the Ministry of Oil and the state South Oil Company for about $1.7 billion of pipeline and offshore mooring-buoy contracts after 2003. Britain's Serious Fraud Office prosecuted: in 2020 a jury convicted its Iraq manager Ziad Akle and Stephen Whiteley, and its Iraq partner Basil Al Jarah, who had pleaded guilty, was jailed.
orgs.cite: UK Serious Fraud Office, Jul and 8 Oct 2020; OCCRP, Jul 2020

orgs.d: Elf Aquitaine, the French state oil company and an unofficial arm of French policy in Africa, used secret company funds to buy political favour in France and Africa. Its Africa specialist André Tarallo was close to Gabon's President Omar Bongo, and former chairman Loïk Le Floch-Prigent admitted secretly funding parties, naming Jacques Chirac's RPR as the main beneficiary. Investigated by magistrate Eva Joly from 1994, the case ended in 2003 with a Paris court jailing Le Floch-Prigent and Alfred Sirven for five years and Tarallo for four in a $350 million embezzlement case. Elf merged into TotalFina in 2000.
orgs.cite: Paris court ruling, 12 Nov 2003; Transparency International

orgs.d: The Gürtel network was a group of businesses led by Francisco Correa that paid kickbacks to officials of Spain's People's Party (PP) for public contracts from PP-run local and regional governments, including Valencia and the Community of Madrid. In May 2018 Spain's National Court convicted 29 of 37 defendants, gave Correa 51 years and former PP treasurer Luis Bárcenas 33, and found that the party itself had taken part in the scheme since 1989. A week later Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy was removed by a vote of no confidence.
orgs.cite: Audiencia Nacional ruling, 24 May 2018

orgs.d: Bofors, the Swedish arms maker, paid kickbacks to win a 1986 contract to supply India's army with 410 field howitzers. Swedish Radio reported the payments in 1987 from a police investigator's leak, and The Hindu then obtained over 350 documents; payments to Indian politicians and defence officials were put at about ₹640 million. India's Central Bureau of Investigation named middleman Ottavio Quattrocchi, arms agent Win Chadha and the late Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi in 1999. The charges against Gandhi were quashed in 2004 and no one was finally convicted.
orgs.cite: Swedish Radio, 16 Apr 1987; CBI charge sheet, 1999; Delhi High Court, 2004

orgs.d: Alcatel, the French telecoms company, was accused in Costa Rica of paying a president for a state contract. Prosecutors alleged it paid more than US$800,000 to Miguel Ángel Rodríguez while he was president, for help winning a contract to supply 400,000 mobile phone lines. Rodríguez resigned as Secretary General of the Organization of American States in 2004, a month into the job, after a former associate accused him. A court sentenced him to five years in 2011, but an appeals court acquitted him in 2012, citing an unreliable main witness. Alcatel merged into Alcatel-Lucent in 2006, later bought by Nokia.
orgs.cite: Costa Rican court rulings, 2011 and 2012

orgs.d: Corpesca, a Chilean fishing company, paid a senator for his votes on the law that shared out the national fishing quota. Prosecutors said it paid Jaime Orpis of the UDI party 230 million pesos for favourable votes on the 2012 fisheries law, which allocated a large share of the quota to companies controlled by a few families indefinitely. A citizens' group filed a bribery complaint in 2015, Orpis lost his immunity in 2016, and in 2021 a court sentenced him to prison for bribery and fraud against the Treasury, upheld in 2022.
orgs.cite: Radio Universidad de Chile, 16 Apr 2021; Radio Cooperativa, 6 Jan 2022

orgs.d: Grupo Penta, a Chilean holding company, used fake invoices, with help from employees of the tax service, to pass money to political campaigns, mainly of the right-wing UDI party. Its directors Carlos Alberto Délano and Carlos Eugenio Lavín were charged in 2015, fined and ordered to attend ethics classes. Former UDI president Jovino Novoa received a suspended sentence for tax crimes, and two tax-service employees were given prison terms and fines. Several Penta employees and relatives were convicted of tax evasion, bribery and money laundering.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Penta case'

orgs.d: Penta, one of Slovakia's two biggest investment groups, appears in the 'Gorila' file, a leaked record said to come from a 2005–2006 intelligence-service wiretap of a Bratislava flat, in which its partner Jaroslav Haščák reportedly discussed kickbacks for privatisation and procurement contracts with Deputy Prime Minister Jirko Malchárek; Robert Fico and others are also named. The file appeared online in 2011. Penta called it fiction and no convictions followed, but a court confirmed in 2012 that it had authorised the wiretaps, and 'Protest Gorila' rallies shaped that year's election.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Gorilla scandal'

orgs.d: Countrywide Financial, then the largest US mortgage lender, gave hundreds of discounted 'VIP' home loans to members of Congress, their staff and other officials, including staff of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, the state-backed firms that bought its loans. A three-year House Oversight Committee investigation reported in 2012 that the programme was used to buy influence in Washington and protect Countrywide's special fee arrangement with Fannie Mae. Recipients named included Senators Christopher Dodd and Kent Conrad and four House members. Bank of America bought Countrywide in 2008.
orgs.cite: House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform report, 5 Jul 2012

orgs.d: Raytheon, the US weapons maker, has paid foreign officials who buy its products. In a 2024 case the US Justice Department found that it paid a Qatari air-force procurement chief through sham contracts and in return won contracts that he oversaw. At home the Defense Department is the main customer for Raytheon's missiles and other military systems.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Mark Esper'; US Senate votes, 2017 and 2019

orgs.d: Verizon, the US telecoms company, supplied the chairman of the regulator that oversees it. Ajit Pai, a Verizon associate general counsel from 2001 to 2003, chaired the Federal Communications Commission from 2017 to 2021. In December 2017 the FCC under him ended the 'net neutrality' rules that barred internet providers such as Verizon from blocking or slowing traffic or selling priority, rules broadband companies had fought since they were adopted in 2015.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Ajit Pai'; FCC order, 14 Dec 2017

orgs.d: Murray Energy, once the largest privately owned US coal producer, saw its lobbyist placed at the head of the agency that regulates coal pollution. Andrew Wheeler lobbied for Murray from 2009 to 2017 against Obama-era climate rules for power plants and in 2017 arranged a meeting at which Robert Murray pressed Energy Secretary Rick Perry for rollbacks. Wheeler became deputy head of the Environmental Protection Agency in 2018 and its administrator in 2019; in 2020 the EPA weakened mercury regulation. Murray Energy went bankrupt in 2019–2020.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Andrew R. Wheeler'

orgs.d: Microsoft got its partners onto national standards committees to vote its Office Open XML document format through ISO, the Geneva-based world standards body. In Sweden it admitted an employee had asked two partner companies to join the national committee and vote yes in return for 'marketing contributions', and the vote was annulled in 2007. In Norway the committee grew from about seven members to 30, and 13 members resigned after its vote was changed to approval. Similar complaints came from Switzerland, Poland and Portugal. The format was approved in 2008.
orgs.cite: Computer Sweden; Swedish Standards Institute statement, 2007

orgs.d: Gazprom, Russia's state gas company, used its subsidiary Nord Stream 2 AG to fund a German state body set up to finish its pipeline. The government of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern under Manuela Schwesig created a public 'Climate and Environmental Protection Foundation' whose charter stated the goal of completing Nord Stream 2, with the money coming from Nord Stream 2 AG; Reuters reported it was meant to help the project get around US sanctions. In 2024 media reported that Schwesig's office cut passages from a supposedly independent report saying closing the foundation was feasible.
orgs.cite: Reuters, 11 Feb 2022; Business Insider Deutschland, 7 Mar 2024

orgs.d: CEFC China Energy, a Shanghai oil conglomerate that promoted Xi Jinping's Belt and Road Initiative, funded a Hong Kong charity with UN consultative status that its envoy used to bribe African leaders. Patrick Ho, a former Hong Kong minister who ran it, had $500,000 wired to Uganda's foreign minister Sam Kutesa, just out of his term as UN General Assembly president, and offered Chad's President Idriss Déby $2 million hidden in gift boxes for oil rights. A New York jury convicted Ho of bribery and money laundering in 2018. CEFC's chairman denied authorising him.
orgs.cite: US DOJ, SDNY, 5 Dec 2018; OCCRP, Dec 2018

orgs.d: PowerChina, a Chinese state-owned construction group, built Ecuador's Coca Codo Sinclair hydroelectric plant through its arm Sinohydro from 2009 to 2018 with a $1.7 billion Chinese Export-Import Bank loan. In 2023 an Ecuadorian judge approved bribery charges against former president Lenín Moreno, vice-president during the build, and others over the contract; in the separate 'INA Papers' case prosecutors allege $76 million in kickbacks passed through a Belize company founded by Moreno's brother. Moreno denies it. The plant later showed 7,648 cracks, and PowerChina agreed $400 million compensation in 2026.
orgs.cite: Reuters, 23 Feb and 6 Mar 2023, 10 Apr 2026; New York Times, 24 Dec 2018

orgs.d: ZTE, a Chinese telecoms company controlled through state-owned shareholders, won a $329 million contract in 2007 to build the Philippine government's broadband network amid kickback claims. In Senate hearings economic planning secretary Romulo Neri testified that election commission chairman Benjamin Abalos offered him 200 million pesos to approve it; a witness said ZTE advanced $1 million to Abalos, and another linked President Gloria Arroyo's husband to the kickbacks. Arroyo cancelled the deal. The Ombudsman indicted Arroyo, her husband and Abalos in 2011; the case against Arroyo was dismissed in 2016.
orgs.cite: GMA News, 18 Sep 2007; Rappler, 7 Mar 2012; CNN Philippines, 16 Sep 2016

orgs.d: Group DF, the holding company of Ukrainian businessman Dmytro Firtash, co-owner of the gas trader RosUkrEnergo and a reported funder of Viktor Yanukovych's 2010 campaign, was accused in the US of bribing Indian officials. A Chicago grand jury indicted Firtash and five others in 2014 over an alleged $18.5 million bribe to obtain titanium mining licences in India. Arrested in Vienna, he fought extradition for years, and an Austrian court ruled it not permissible in 2024. He denies the charges; Ukraine's security council sanctioned him in 2021.
orgs.cite: US indictment, N.D. Ill., 2014; Vienna court, Nov 2024

orgs.d: Hanbo, a South Korean steelmaker that began building a huge plant in 1992, bribed politicians and bankers, who pressed banks to lend to it. It went into receivership in January 1997 with losses estimated at $6 billion, and a court found it had received illegal preferential treatment from President Kim Young-sam's government. Founder Chung Tae-soo got 15 years; those convicted included former home minister Kim Woo-suk, presidential aides, lawmakers and two former presidents of Korea First Bank, and the president's son was jailed in a related case.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Hanbo scandal'

orgs.d: Sagawa Kyubin, a Japanese parcel delivery company, made payments to senior politicians of the governing Liberal Democratic Party, alongside construction companies seeking political influence. LDP vice-president Shin Kanemaru, a former deputy prime minister and a leader of Noboru Takeshita's faction, was indicted in the 1992 scandal, resigned and was arrested in 1993 for evading tax on the payments. Investigators reported finding at least $51 million in bearer bonds and hundreds of pounds of gold at his home.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Shin Kanemaru'

orgs.d: S. Alam Group, a Bangladeshi conglomerate, took control of Islamic banks under the Awami League government. In 2017 it took over Islami Bank Bangladesh, installing a new chairman and remaking its board and management, and came to control First Security Islami, Union and Global Islami banks, buying half of Social Islami Bank through 19 subsidiaries beyond the 5 percent legal limit. Media reported it took Tk 300 billion in loans from Islami Bank, which needed emergency central bank money in 2023. Investigations opened after the government fell in 2024; the group denies wrongdoing.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'S. Alam Group'

orgs.n: Van Thinh Phat Group (Truong My Lan)
orgs.d: Van Thinh Phat, the Vietnamese property group of Truong My Lan, secretly controlled Saigon Commercial Bank through more than two dozen nominee shareholders and paid the bank supervisor to look away. Lan owned over 90 percent of the bank, and prosecutors said she used 916 fake loan applications to take $12.5 billion from it between 2018 and 2022. Do Thi Nhan, head of the State Bank of Vietnam's inspection department, took $5.2 million and kept the bank off the special-monitoring list. In 2024 a court sentenced Lan to death and Nhan to life.
orgs.cite: Ho Chi Minh City People's Court, 11 Apr 2024; RFA, 11 Apr 2024

orgs.d: Viet A Technology, a Vietnamese company, admitted paying officials more than $35 million to buy its Covid-19 test kits, which it imported from China at about $0.96 each, marketed as Vietnamese-made and sold to local authorities for about $20.75. Dozens of officials were charged by mid-2022, including Health Minister Nguyen Thanh Long and Hanoi's mayor Chu Ngoc Anh, both expelled from the Communist Party. In January 2023 two deputy prime ministers were removed and President Nguyen Xuan Phuc resigned.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Viet A scandal'

orgs.d: Tomorrow Holdings, the conglomerate of Chinese-Canadian billionaire Xiao Jianhua that owned banks, insurers and brokerages, gave Chinese officials shares, property and cash worth more than 680 million yuan from 2001 to 2021 to 'evade financial supervision', a Shanghai court said in 2022. Xiao was sentenced to 13 years for bribery and misuse of funds, and the group was fined a record 55.03 billion yuan. He had not been seen since being taken from a Hong Kong hotel in 2017, and regulators seized nine of the group's financial firms in 2020.
orgs.cite: Shanghai First Intermediate People's Court, 19 Aug 2022; Reuters

orgs.d: Yuanhua Group, Lai Changxing's company in Xiamen, ran a smuggling operation that corrupted hundreds of Chinese officials, up to a vice-minister of public security. It was believed to have smuggled about $10 billion of goods, including luxury cars and oil, avoiding $3.6 billion in taxes; officials were won with bribes, banquets, jobs for relatives and blackmail. About 300 officials were tried and 14 people executed. Lai fled to Canada in 1999, was deported in 2011 and sentenced to life in 2012.
orgs.cite: Xinhua; Canadian court records; Wikipedia 'Lai Changxing'

orgs.n: Delyan Peevski's media and political network
orgs.d: Delyan Peevski, a Bulgarian MP whose family's media group owned six of the 12 largest newspapers and controlled nearly 80% of print distribution by 2013, built a network the US says he used to control state institutions. In June 2013 parliament elected him head of DANS, the national security agency; mass protests followed and he stepped down the next day. In 2021 the US Treasury sanctioned him under the Global Magnitsky Act for 'regularly' using influence peddling and bribes to shield himself and exert control over key institutions and sectors. The UK sanctioned him in 2023.
orgs.cite: US Treasury designation, Jun 2021; UK FCDO, Feb 2023

orgs.n: Djoko Tjandra and Era Giat Prima
orgs.d: Indonesian tycoon Djoko Tjandra twice bought his way through state agencies. In 1999 his debt-collecting firm Era Giat Prima, run by Golkar deputy treasurer Setya Novanto, had officials of the bank rescue agency IBRA approve a Rp546 billion (about $80 million) fee from Bank Bali, part of which went to President Habibie's campaign. After fleeing a two-year sentence in 2009, Tjandra in 2020 paid two police generals to lift his Interpol Red Notice and a prosecutor $500,000 to seek a Supreme Court ruling clearing him. All four were jailed in 2021.
orgs.cite: Jakarta court verdicts, 2020–21; Wikipedia 'Bank Bali scandal'

orgs.d: The group of Nafiz Modack, whom South African police describe as a Cape Town underworld boss, paid police officers for their commands and their information. Brigadier Kolindhren Govender took R146,000 from Modack in 2011–13 and had officers under his command recover Modack's cars, putting police resources at Modack's service. Govender pleaded guilty in 2019, and Modack was convicted and sentenced to 10 years in 2025.
orgs.cite: Daily Maverick, 18 Jun 2020 and 21 Sep 2025; IPID reports

orgs.d: The A.Q. Khan network was the procurement and smuggling system built around Pakistan's uranium-enrichment programme by metallurgist Abdul Qadeer Khan, and it began with an insider in Europe. From 1972 Khan worked at a subcontractor to the Dutch partner of Urenco, the European enrichment consortium, visited its Almelo plant without clearance and in 1974 had 16 days of unsupervised access to centrifuge designs he was asked to translate. He left for Pakistan in 1975 with copied blueprints and contacts for nearly 100 suppliers. A Dutch court convicted him in absentia in 1983; the designs later reached Iran, Libya and North Korea.
orgs.cite: Carnegie Endowment, A.Q. Khan Nuclear Chronology, Sep 2005; Dutch court ruling, 1983 (overturned 1985)

orgs.d: Turkey's National Intelligence Organisation, MİT, is the country's main spy agency, and abroad it gathers information through staff at Turkish consulates and the people they recruit inside host-country institutions. In Germany, Federal Court of Justice rulings in 2025 describe a Cologne policewoman who, between March 2024 and February 2025, sent internal police information and assessments to an administrative employee of the Turkish Consulate General. The material covered the PKK, a Kurdish militant group, and incidents seen as hostile to Turkey. Prosecutors suspect the consular employee reported, at least indirectly, to MİT.
orgs.cite: German Federal Court of Justice rulings StB 37/25 and StB 42/25, via Middle East Forum, 2025

orgs.n: Algerian intelligence services and consular networks
