orgs.d: Algeria's intelligence services watch Algerian exiles and opponents in France partly through Algerian consulates, which obtain information from people working inside French state offices. French prosecutors said in March 2025 that a contact at Algeria's consulate in Créteil, near Paris, received information on Algerian asylum seekers and known government opponents from an employee of France's finance ministry, who was placed under formal investigation for spying for Algeria. A social worker at the French Office for Immigration and Integration was also accused of sharing asylum seekers' confidential files. The case deepened a crisis in relations between the two countries.
orgs.cite: Arab News / AFP, 13 March 2025

orgs.n: Belarusian military intelligence (Main Intelligence Directorate of the General Staff)
orgs.d: The Main Intelligence Directorate of the General Staff of Belarus's armed forces, its military intelligence service, recruits citizens of neighbouring NATO states and places them inside defence bodies. Two Lithuanians recruited after a trip to Minsk in May 2022 gathered information on Lithuania's armed forces, allied NATO equipment and the Belarusian opposition, and one joined the Lithuanian Riflemen's Union, a volunteer defence organisation linked to the army, in order to spy. They were paid at least €8,500, arrested in November 2023 and sentenced by the Klaipėda Regional Court in April 2026 to seven and six and a half years.
orgs.cite: LRT, 15 April 2026

orgs.d: Barrio 18, a street gang that began in Los Angeles and is now one of the largest gangs in Guatemala, El Salvador and Honduras, gets prison staff to work for it so that its leaders can keep running operations and escape. Between 8 and 11 October 2025 twenty of its high-risk leaders walked out of the Fraijanes II prison near Guatemala City. Authorities arrested 23 guards from the unit watching the prison's 256 Barrio 18 inmates for cooperating in the escape. Guatemala's interior minister resigned with his prisons and counter-narcotics deputies. The US designated the gang a terrorist organisation in September 2025.
orgs.cite: La Prensa (Honduras)/EFE, 25 October 2025; AP, October 2025; Tico Times/AFP, 15 October 2025

orgs.d: Tren de Aragua, a Venezuelan gang that has spread into Colombia, Peru and Chile, runs itself from inside prisons by controlling or buying the people who staff them. In Venezuela it held Tocorón prison as its headquarters, with its leader Héctor Guerrero Flores ('Niño Guerrero') left in charge as inmates' boss and inmates paying a fee called 'la causa' worth millions of dollars a year, until 11,000 troops retook it in September 2023. In Chile, 'Operation Apocalypse' in December 2025 charged 77 people, at least 42 of them Santiago 1 prison guards accused of smuggling phones and drugs for its jailed leaders.
orgs.cite: InSight Crime, 25 September 2023; El Ciudadano, 16 December 2025

orgs.d: Los Ardillos, a crime group in Mexico's Guerrero state led by the Ortega family, gets close to local government through meetings with mayors and relatives in town halls. In July 2023 a leaked video showed Norma Otilia Hernández, mayor of the state capital Chilpancingo, meeting Celso Ortega, the group's presumed leader; she admitted the meeting but denied any pact, and her party, Morena, expelled her in 2024. In May 2026 La Silla Rota reported that the mayor of nearby Chilapa is Ortega's sister-in-law and that his son is the town hall's private secretary. A former state congress president from the family denies criminal links.
orgs.cite: El Financiero, 2 August 2023; Expansión Política, 8 September 2024; La Silla Rota, 26 May 2026

orgs.d: Mahadev Online Book, an illegal online betting operation run from Dubai by promoters from Bhilai in India, is accused of paying police, officials and politicians in Chhattisgarh state to avoid action. Indian investigators say it took in about Rs 450 crore a month. A state anti-corruption chargesheet in June 2024 alleged the promoters paid protection money through hawala dealers, informal money-transfer brokers, with police staff passing cash on to other officers. The Enforcement Directorate alleges former chief minister Bhupesh Baghel received about Rs 508 crore; the federal CBI named him in its case. Baghel denies the allegations.
orgs.cite: ThePrint, 27 March 2025

orgs.d: Radaa, a Tripoli militia led by Abdel Rauf Kara, works as part of Libya's state security forces while holding key state sites for itself. From 2011 it controlled Mitiga, the only airport in the capital with commercial flights, as well as prisons and detention centres. In July 2025 Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah called the militias 'a state within the state' and demanded that Radaa hand over the airport, seaport and prisons and give up wanted men; the Attorney General had issued about 125 arrest warrants around Mitiga. A Turkish-brokered deal in September 2025 provided for a neutral force to run the airport.
orgs.cite: Libya Herald, July 2025; Arab News / AFP, 13 September 2025

orgs.d: The Stability Support Apparatus was the armed group of Abdel Ghani al-Kikli, built in Tripoli's Abu Salim district from 2011 and turned into a state body under Libya's Presidential Council in 2021. Through it, analysts said, his associates controlled the internal security agency, public companies, ministries and cash transfers from the central bank, earning him the name 'de facto king of Tripoli'. Amnesty International documented disappearances, deaths in custody and torture of migrants by its members, and a UN panel said in December 2024 he played a key role in militia financing through corrupt practices. He was killed on 12 May 2025.
orgs.cite: The National, 14 May 2025; Atlantic Council, May 2025

orgs.n: National Congress Party (NCP) and Sudanese Islamic Movement
orgs.d: The National Congress Party, the Islamist ruling party of Omar al-Bashir, banned after his fall in 2019, put its members back into Sudan's state after General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan's coup of October 2021. A special court reinstated scores of officials whom a civilian taskforce had dismissed from the central bank, judiciary, public prosecution, prime minister's office, foreign ministry and state media. Returning diplomats were sent to head missions abroad, and NCP leader Ibrahim Ghandour was acquitted and freed while the taskforce's leaders were jailed. Reuters reported in 2022 that NCP figures were rebuilding under military protection.
orgs.cite: Reuters analysis, April 2022

orgs.n: Haredi rabbinical councils (Councils of Torah Sages)
orgs.d: Israel's ultra-Orthodox (Haredi) parties take their decisions from councils of senior rabbis rather than from members or voters, and the rabbis use the parties' places in government to protect exemptions from military service for yeshiva (religious seminary) students. After the Supreme Court ordered the army in 2024 to start drafting them, United Torah Judaism's seven members of the Knesset left Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition on 15 July 2025; Degel HaTorah said it acted on the directive of its spiritual leader, Rabbi Dov Lando. Shas, guided by its own Council of Torah Sages, then gave up its government posts.
orgs.cite: Al Jazeera, 15 July 2025; Times of Israel, July 2025

orgs.n: Tufton Street think tanks (IEA, TaxPayers' Alliance, Centre for Policy Studies, Legatum)
orgs.d: A cluster of free-market think tanks and campaign groups based in and around Tufton Street in Westminster, close to Parliament, supplies staff and ideas to Conservative governments. When Liz Truss became prime minister in September 2022, people from these groups became her government's advisers: Adam Memon of the Centre for Policy Studies went to the Chancellor, James Price of the TaxPayers' Alliance became Cabinet Office chief of staff, and the Institute of Economic Affairs' Victoria Hewson and Radomir Tylecote advised the Foreign Office and Business Department. The groups applauded the September 'mini-budget' of unfunded tax cuts, which caused a market crisis.
orgs.cite: Byline Times, 4 October 2022; Left Foot Forward, September 2022

orgs.d: America First Legal, a legal group set up in 2021 after Donald Trump's first term to sue over diversity, immigration and election policies, moved its leaders into his second White House. Co-founder Stephen Miller became deputy chief of staff for policy and its president Gene Hamilton became deputy counsel to the president; before leaving, Miller received $175,000 and Hamilton $275,000 in bonus and 'adjustment' payments. AFL had filed more than 100 cases against diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programmes, and in January 2025 Trump ordered such programmes ended across the federal government. It raised $31.5 million in 2024.
orgs.cite: NOTUS, 10 December 2025

orgs.d: The America First Policy Institute, a think tank set up in 2021 by former Trump officials, works as a holding pen for a future administration's leaders, paying them and drafting their policies in advance. In Trump's second term its president Brooke Rollins became Agriculture Secretary and its board chair Linda McMahon Education Secretary; Pam Bondi, Kash Patel, John Ratcliffe, Lee Zeldin, Scott Turner, Doug Collins and Matthew Whitaker had also worked for it. Disclosures showed it had paid incoming officials nearly $2.6 million. Rollins said in April 2024 it had 298 executive orders drafted for a new president's first day.
orgs.cite: ABC News, 18 January 2025

orgs.n: WallBuilders and Project Blitz (Christian nationalist model-bill campaign)
orgs.d: WallBuilders, the Texas organisation of the activist David Barton, works with Christian nationalist groups to put ready-made 'model bills' into the hands of state lawmakers. Project Blitz, a playbook exposed in 2018, offered such bills off the shelf, and the Congressional Prayer Caucus Foundation's texts were used word for word in some states. Reporting by The 74 traced Barton to 28 bills in 18 states in a single year. In 2025 Texas passed Senate Bill 10, which he promoted, requiring a Ten Commandments poster in every public-school classroom; similar laws passed in Louisiana and Arkansas and all three were challenged in court.
orgs.cite: Baptist News Global, 20 October 2025; KLTV, 4 December 2025

orgs.d: The American Chemistry Council, the lobby group for US chemical makers, has had a former senior executive twice put in charge of the federal rules on its members' products. Nancy Beck ran chemical-safety rules at the Environmental Protection Agency in Donald Trump's first term, when career staff objected to her rewrites of toxic-chemical rules, and returned in January 2025 with decision-making power in the chemicals office and later oversight of pesticides. The New York Times, Washington Post and ProPublica reported moves to make PFAS 'forever chemicals' harder to track, scale back proposed bans on asbestos and other solvents, and loosen formaldehyde limits.
orgs.cite: Politico, 22 June 2017; New York Times, 22 January 2025; Washington Post, 23 January 2025; ProPublica, 8 December 2025

orgs.d: Liberty Energy, a Denver fracking-services company, had its founder and chief executive Chris Wright move straight into the post of US Secretary of Energy, which sets federal energy policy and funds energy research, after Senate confirmation on 3 February 2025. As secretary he ordered several coal power plants to stay open, his department published reports questioning mainstream climate science, and in October 2025 it cancelled 321 clean-energy grants worth $7.56 billion in states that had voted for Kamala Harris. Wright told Congress the cuts were not political; officials said in a July 2026 court filing that they rested on the states' political identity.
orgs.cite: American Nuclear Society Newswire, 4 February 2025; Senate record and court filings via Wikipedia

orgs.d: E.ON, one of Germany's largest energy companies, saw Katherina Reiche, chief executive since 2020 of its largest subsidiary, Westenergie, become Germany's economy and energy minister on 6 May 2025. As minister she planned 8 gigawatts of new gas power stations, against about 5 under her predecessor, and drafted an end to fixed payments for small rooftop solar from 2027. A 2025 monitoring report on the energy transition came from an institute whose founding funders include E.ON and RWE; Greenpeace documented 28 changes between draft and final versions. A Green MP said her grid package served E.ON, citing nine meetings with its representatives.
orgs.cite: Frankfurter Rundschau/leinetal24, 26 February 2026; LobbyControl

orgs.d: Banco Master, a Brazilian bank owned by Daniel Vorcaro, is alleged by Federal Police to have paid politicians, officials and relatives of Supreme Court justices while seeking a rescue by BRB, the state bank of the Federal District. Reported payments include R$300,000 a month to Senator Ciro Nogueira, who police say pushed to raise deposit-insurance cover, and a contract worth about R$130 million with the law firm of Justice Alexandre de Moraes's wife. The central bank rejected the BRB purchase and liquidated Banco Master on 18 November 2025, the day after Vorcaro was arrested trying to fly to Malta. Those named deny wrongdoing.
orgs.cite: Bloomberg, 18 November 2025; Federal Police, Folha and Estadão via Wikipedia

orgs.d: Smartmatic, a voting-technology company, is charged by US prosecutors with bribing the head of the Philippines' election commission to win and keep a contract to run national elections. A Florida grand jury indictment of August 2024 says its executives paid more than $1 million between 2015 and 2018 to Andres Bautista, then chairman of the Commission on Elections, for a $199 million contract for 94,000 vote-counting machines for the 2016 election and timely payment, moving money through shell companies and false invoices. A superseding indictment in October 2025 charged the company itself. Bautista, co-founder Roger Piñate and Smartmatic deny the charges.
orgs.cite: Philippine Daily Inquirer, October 2025; Daily Tribune, 8 August 2024; Philstar, 9 August 2024

orgs.d: Freepoint Commodities, a trading house in Stamford, Connecticut, paid bribes from about 2012 to 2018 to officials at Petrobras, Brazil's state-controlled oil company, for confidential information on competitors' prices and bids, which helped it win business and earn over $30 million in profit. On 14 December 2023 it agreed with the US Justice Department to pay more than $98 million, including a $68 million criminal penalty, under a three-year deferred-prosecution agreement, an arrangement in which charges are dropped if the company meets set conditions. Trafigura, Vitol and Glencore have also admitted bribing Petrobras staff.
orgs.cite: US Department of Justice, 14 December 2023; Compliance Week, December 2023

orgs.d: Telefónica, the Spanish telecoms group, operated in Venezuela through its subsidiary Telefónica Venezolana, which paid bribes to Venezuelan government officials so that it could take part in a state-run auction exchanging bolivars for US dollars, at a time when the government tightly rationed access to foreign currency, the US Justice Department found. In November 2024 the subsidiary agreed to pay more than $85 million to resolve the US investigation under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, the US law against bribing foreign officials.
orgs.cite: AP via WTOP, 8 November 2024; Dow Jones, November 2024

orgs.n: Indonesian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (Kadin)
orgs.d: Kadin, Indonesia's national chamber of commerce and industry, was given the lead in consultation on a law that rewrote dozens of the country's rules on labour, land and environmental permits. In December 2019 Coordinating Minister for Economic Affairs Airlangga Hartarto appointed Kadin chairman Rosan Roeslani to chair the task force on the Omnibus Law on Job Creation; its members included 14 Kadin members and heads of hotel and exporters' associations. Labour unions were still demanding a role in June 2020. The law passed in October 2020 amid mass protests, and environmental groups alleged conflicts of interest with coal and energy businesses.
orgs.cite: Jakarta Globe, 16 December 2019 (via APSN); Hukumonline, December 2019; Jakarta Post, 12 June 2020

orgs.d: China's intelligence bodies, not named in these records, recruit retired Taiwanese officers and businesspeople, who then pay serving soldiers for secrets. Retired colonel Liu Sheng-shu ran such a ring for eight years on NT$16.7 million and got 20 years. Prosecutors said retired general Kao An-kuo was recruited in 2019; he was convicted over an armed group and denied all charges. Recruiters reached soldiers short of money through pawn shops and a loan shark, and some recruits signed pledges of surrender. Less proven claims concern South Korea, Kazakhstan and Australia.
orgs.cite: Taipei Times, 2024-2026; Central News Agency, 2023-2026; Taiwan News, 2024-2026; RFE/RL, 2019-2024; AFP and Korea Times, 2015; Coroners Court of Victoria, 2020
orgs.reach_src: Taipei Times, 2024-2026; Central News Agency, 2023-2026; Taiwan News, 2024-2026; RFE/RL, 2019-2024; AFP and Korea Times, 2015; Coroners Court of Victoria, 2020

orgs.d: Israel's intelligence services, which include Mossad and military intelligence, are accused by Lebanon of recruiting insiders in its telecoms firms, security forces and politics; the records do not name the agency. A sweep begun in April 2009 brought more than 100 arrests by September 2011, and at least five of those convicted were sentenced to death. A military court gave Charbel Qazzi of state mobile firm Alfa seven years' hard labour. Retired general Fayez Karam got two years for contacting Israeli intelligence, but was not found guilty of spying. Colonel Shahid Tournieh told a tribunal his first confession was untrue.
orgs.cite: Ynet News, 2010-2011; Ynet News/AFP, 3 Sep 2011; Arutz Sheva, 2010-2012; VOA, 2010
orgs.reach_src: Ynet News, 2010-2011; Ynet News/AFP, 3 Sep 2011; Arutz Sheva, 2010-2012; VOA, 2010

orgs.n: Moroccan foreign intelligence and diplomatic networks
orgs.d: Morocco's foreign intelligence service and diplomats are accused of cultivating people inside French and UN institutions. French investigators say its secret service paid the captain running the border police information unit at Orly airport, who allegedly passed 100 to 200 files between 2014 and 2017 through a security-firm boss. His lawyer said he acted in France's interest, and no verdict was found. Leaked emails attributed to Morocco's UN ambassador in Geneva boasted of people in his pocket, including UN human rights official Anders Kompass. Kompass denied it; investigators said they found no evidence, closed the case, then reopened it.
orgs.cite: The Local France/AFP, 2020; Le Parisien and Libération via Bladi.net and Middle East Monitor; Foreign Policy, 2015; Inner City Press, 2014
orgs.reach_src: The Local France/AFP, 2020; Le Parisien and Libération via Bladi.net and Middle East Monitor; Foreign Policy, 2015; Inner City Press, 2014

orgs.d: Embraer, the Brazilian aircraft maker, used shell companies and go-betweens to pay officials who could decide state aircraft purchases. It admitted promising $3.52 million to a Dominican official to help win Senate approval for financing eight Super Tucano aircraft; the two men later accused denied any bribe, and a fresh trial was ordered in 2024. In Mozambique it paid $800,000, booked as 'sales commissions', for a jet sale to state airline LAM. Former transport minister Paulo Zucula and go-between Mateus Zimba each got ten years in 2021. Embraer settled with US and Brazilian authorities for $205 million in 2016.
orgs.cite: Tufts Compendium of Arms Trade Corruption; Diario Libre, 2022 and 2024; MarketScreener/AIM, Sept 2021; ch-aviation, Sept 2021
orgs.reach_src: Tufts Compendium of Arms Trade Corruption; Diario Libre, 2022 and 2024; MarketScreener/AIM, Sept 2021; ch-aviation, Sept 2021

orgs.d: Systra, the French rail engineering firm, won public contracts abroad by paying people inside the state bodies awarding them. In Uzbekistan, investigators found it paid nearly $576,000 to a Latvian account of a UK subcontractor whose beneficial owner was an official at the national railway company, in a rigged tender. In Baku, a subsidiary paid so-called commissions of about 30% of invoices, through intermediaries, to an agent of the metro company close to the minister in charge. Systra agreed a €7,496,000 French settlement covering both cases in July 2021.
orgs.cite: Parquet National Financier, 13 July 2021; Willkie Compliance Concourse, July 2021
orgs.reach_src: Parquet National Financier, 13 July 2021; Willkie Compliance Concourse, July 2021

orgs.d: Fresenius Medical Care, the German dialysis company, paid doctors and officials in state health systems so that public money bought its products, US regulators found. In Saudi Arabia its distributor made more than $4.9 million in improper payments, including to officials of a body approving dialysis products for tenders. In Morocco it bribed the chief kidney specialist at two military hospitals. In Turkey publicly employed doctors received free shares in joint ventures and sent it business from their employers. It agreed a $231 million US settlement in 2019 covering these and other countries.
orgs.cite: SEC, In the Matter of Fresenius Medical Care AG, 29 Mar 2019; CFO.com, Apr 2019; Constantine Cannon, 2019
orgs.reach_src: SEC, In the Matter of Fresenius Medical Care AG, 29 Mar 2019; CFO.com, Apr 2019; Constantine Cannon, 2019

orgs.d: The Provisional IRA, the republican paramilitary group that fought British rule in Northern Ireland, gained help from officers inside the Irish police, the Garda. The Smithwick Tribunal of 2013 found that someone in Dundalk Garda station helped the IRA when two senior Northern Ireland officers were killed in 1989, with no direct evidence against a named officer. It found Detective Sergeant Owen Corrigan had inappropriate dealings with the IRA, which he rejected. It also found Sergeant Leo Colton helped the IRA obtain false passport applications in 1995 and 1996; Colton denies any IRA involvement.
orgs.cite: Irish Times, 4 Dec 2013; RTÉ, 3 Dec 2013

orgs.d: National Action, a British neo-Nazi group banned as a terrorist organisation, tried to build membership inside the armed forces. Other members tried and failed to enlist, and a serving corporal in the Royal Anglian Regiment, Mikko Vehviläinen, acted as a recruiter. Prosecutors described him as a key part of the group's strategy to grow in the army. He was arrested in September 2017, convicted in March 2018 of belonging to the group and sentenced to eight years. He was cleared of possessing a document useful to a terrorist and of stirring up racial hatred.
orgs.cite: ITV News, 12 Nov 2018

orgs.d: The Naumann Circle, a group of former Nazi officials in West Germany, was accused of setting out to place trusted men in veterans' groups, local administrations and political parties, above all the liberal Free Democratic Party. It was led by Werner Naumann, last state secretary in the Nazi Propaganda Ministry, and included seven former Gauleiter, the regional party chiefs. British forces had tapped the group and arrested Naumann and six others in January 1953. In December 1954 a court dismissed the charges for lack of evidence, saying the group had no political effectiveness.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia, Naumann Circle (citing Frei 2002; Baldow 2012; The Times)
orgs.reach_src: Wikipedia, Naumann Circle (citing Frei 2002; Baldow 2012; The Times)

orgs.d: Nordkreuz, a German far-right Telegram group of about 30 people preparing for social collapse, drew on members of a police commando unit. Its founder, Marko G., was a former officer of the unit, known as the SEK. Prosecutors alleged three serving commandos stole police ammunition for it. Cartridges at his home were traced to about a dozen police and military depots, and another member's binder of political opponents held data from a police computer. An inquiry linked eight of the unit's 12 members to the network. Marko G. got a 21-month suspended sentence, final in February 2021.
orgs.cite: VICE, 27 Nov 2019; Nordkurier, Feb 2021; dpa via t-online, 31 Mar 2021; taz, 17 Mar 2022
orgs.reach_src: VICE, 27 Nov 2019; Nordkurier, Feb 2021; dpa via t-online, 31 Mar 2021; taz, 17 Mar 2022

orgs.d: This alleged cigarette-smuggling group, which prosecutors say Aleksandar Mrkić organised from the free customs zone at the Port of Bar, is accused of having senior police among its members. The indictment says former police chief Veselin Veljović passed it secret information over Sky ECC, an encrypted phone service, and that Mrkić told him in 2020 he could become police director; Veljović has denied such accusations in the past. Former Bar criminal police head Ilija Vasović was indicted in 2024 and pleaded not guilty. Their cases were merged, and no verdict had been reported by February 2026.
orgs.cite: AP via WTOP, 24 Jul 2023; Kurir, 30 Jan 2024; Vreme, 7 Jun 2024; Primorski, 2024-2025; ETV, 6 Feb 2026
orgs.reach_src: AP via WTOP, 24 Jul 2023; Kurir, 30 Jan 2024; Vreme, 7 Jun 2024; Primorski, 2024-2025; ETV, 6 Feb 2026

orgs.d: This crime group, which the US Treasury says is run by Kosovo Serb businessman Zvonko Veselinović, allegedly bribes security officials and backs politicians to protect its trade in northern Kosovo. Treasury said in 2021 that it paid Kosovar and Serbian officials to smuggle goods, money, drugs and weapons, and that politicians gave it business control and protection in return for campaign support. It sanctioned Veselinović, his brother, Srpska Lista vice-president Milan Radojičić and former police chief Željko Bojić. A 2019 indictment alleged Radojičić and Veselinović led a group behind the killing of Oliver Ivanović; they denied it.
orgs.cite: Prishtina Insight, 9 Dec 2021 and 28 Jun 2024, on US Treasury action
orgs.reach_src: Prishtina Insight, 9 Dec 2021 and 28 Jun 2024, on US Treasury action

orgs.d: The Belivuk gang, a Belgrade criminal group arrested in February 2021, had an official inside Serbia's organised-crime police acting for an associate. Veljko Belivuk is accused of leading it, under an indictment covering seven murders. A court convicted Goran Papić, former deputy head of the police service SBPOK, after he demanded against regulations that a seized car be returned to a close associate of Belivuk. He got one year and four months in August 2022, raised to two years on appeal that December. An N1 reporter said the gang's indictment contains nothing about ties to the state.
orgs.cite: N1 Serbia, 2022-2023; Kurir, 24 Aug 2022

orgs.d: This is not a formal body but the circle in two Slovak cases around lawyer Zoroslav Kollár, accused of paying judges and intelligence officials. In Operation Gale in 2020, police charged him and senior judges over bribes to judges; an outcome was not confirmed. Prosecutors also said he paid €40,000 to stop intelligence-service wiretaps, and Kollár admitted the bribe in a plea deal. Deputy director Boris Beňa and Ľudovít Makó, who allegedly carried the money, confessed. Former director Vladimír Pčolinský denied it and was acquitted in June 2025 for lack of clear evidence; prosecutors appealed.
orgs.cite: Slovak Spectator, 2021-2022; China-CEE, Nov 2020; SITA and Noviny, 16 Jun 2025
orgs.reach_src: Slovak Spectator, 2021-2022; China-CEE, Nov 2020; SITA and Noviny, 16 Jun 2025

orgs.n: Mofid, Senlian and Chinese timber traders in Mozambique
orgs.d: Chinese timber traders in Mozambique, chiefly Mofid and Senlian, allegedly pay ministers, customs and forest agents to move wood to port. The Environmental Investigation Agency, a campaign group, reported in 2013 that traders claimed help from two agriculture ministers, who denied it; the anti-corruption office found no evidence that Mozambicans held shares in either firm. A 2017 report alleged Mofid paid customs and forest agents around Pemba, and Mofid did not answer questions. In 2024 the agency quoted an anonymous former official describing sharing in bribes and said the ruling Frelimo party gains campaign funds from Chinese investment.
orgs.cite: EIA, 2013-2014; Wood Floor Business, 2013; Oxpeckers, 10 Jan 2017; VOA, 17 May 2024
orgs.reach_src: EIA, 2013-2014; Wood Floor Business, 2013; Oxpeckers, 10 Jan 2017; VOA, 17 May 2024

orgs.n: Queensway Syndicate (Sam Pa; China International Fund)
orgs.d: The Queensway Syndicate, a Hong Kong-based business network, is reported to have gained access to African resources by paying senior officials and a spy agency. Its China International Fund, headed by Sam Pa, and China Sonangol paid Guinea's mines minister, Mahmoud Thiam, $8.5 million for mining rights; a New York jury convicted Thiam of money laundering in 2017. In Zimbabwe, sources in the Central Intelligence Organisation told Global Witness that Pa gave the spy agency money and pick-up trucks in return for access to diamonds, cotton and property. The US sanctioned Pa in 2014. Global Witness's summary records no reply from him.
orgs.cite: US Justice Department, 25 Aug 2017; US Court of Appeals, 2019; Global Witness, 11 June 2012 and April 2014 update
orgs.reach_src: US Justice Department, 25 Aug 2017; US Court of Appeals, 2019; Global Witness, 11 June 2012 and April 2014 update

orgs.n: Malaysian-linked logging companies in Papua New Guinea and Solomon Islands
orgs.d: These foreign logging companies, many linked to Malaysian nationals, get forest access by paying or partnering with politicians and officials in the Pacific. They are not one firm. PNG's Barnett inquiry found corruption at every level of the industry; minister Ted Diro reportedly held a secret 35% or so of the Angus group's local company. A 2013 inquiry found farm leases over more than five million hectares 'hijacked', with nearly all operations foreign-run, Global Witness says. In Solomon Islands an Earth Movers businessman was convicted over a customs bribe, and an unverified 2008 report alleged firms paid MPs to join a party.
orgs.cite: PNGi Central, 2019; Green Left, 1991; Global Witness, Nov 2014; Solomon Times, 28 Oct 2008; Radio New Zealand, 2004-2005
orgs.reach_src: PNGi Central, 2019; Green Left, 1991; Global Witness, Nov 2014; Solomon Times, 28 Oct 2008; Radio New Zealand, 2004-2005

orgs.d: People connected with Mongolia's Oyu Tolgoi copper and gold mine, who are not one firm, allegedly paid ministers while its terms were being settled. Swiss prosecutors allege businessman Borkhuu Delgersaikhan paid €8.2 million into an account of finance minister Sangajav Bayartsogt, who signed the 2009 agreement and was reportedly convicted in 2020; he denied all charges. Mongolian state filings in New York alleged prime minister Sukhbaatar Batbold took kickbacks in 2010 from people associated with Ivanhoe, the mine's then owner. His adviser said he received none and called the case politically motivated.
orgs.cite: Swissinfo, June 2020; Reuters via Mining.com, 2019; OCCRP, 2022; Global Anticorruption Blog, 2020-2024
orgs.reach_src: Swissinfo, June 2020; Reuters via Mining.com, 2019; OCCRP, 2022; Global Anticorruption Blog, 2020-2024

orgs.d: Peru's illegal and informal gold-mining networks, which are not one organisation, allegedly get police to leak operations and protect their mines. Ojo Público reviewed police disciplinary cases from 2019 to 2024 and counted at least 37 implicating 96 officers, 36 of them in La Libertad, home of the Pataz mining area. Officers were accused of leaking operations, stealing gold and altering custody of seized ore; only six cases ended with sanctions fully upheld. Unnamed witnesses also alleged that Víctor Zanabria, later national police chief, sold protection to Arequipa miners. He said the case was archived.
orgs.cite: Ojo Público via Actualidad Ambiental, 28 May 2025; La República, 15 Sep 2026; RPP, 12 May 2025
orgs.reach_src: Ojo Público via Actualidad Ambiental, 28 May 2025; La República, 15 Sep 2026; RPP, 12 May 2025

orgs.d: La Oficina de Envigado, Medellín's main crime group, reaches into city government through officials who pass it information. Prosecutors said Gustavo Villegas, security secretary under Mayor Federico Gutiérrez and arrested on 4 July 2017, gave privileged information to jailed bosses, especially Edison Rojas, known as Pichi. Villegas reached a plea deal admitting abuse of office for meeting Oficina leaders, and in May 2018 Medellín's High Court upheld 33 months in prison and an 81-month ban from office. The Attorney General's Office objected that the deal did not reveal the truth. Gutiérrez said his administration fought the group.
orgs.cite: El Espectador, May 2018; Infobae, 9 Mar 2022

orgs.d: The Clan Rotela, a Paraguayan crime group led by Armando Rotela, allegedly took over the running of Tacumbú, the country's main prison, by bribing and threatening its staff. Former justice minister Ángel Barchini testified that guards protected the clan under threats and bribery, and a guard said staff lost control in 2021 and clan members decided shift changes. About 2,500 police and soldiers retook the jail on 18 December 2023. Prosecutors indicted Rotela and eight others in December 2024, and in May 2025 a judge sent the case to trial.
orgs.cite: ABC Color, 22 Dec 2024; Última Hora, 27 Jun 2025
orgs.reach_src: ABC Color, 22 Dec 2024; Última Hora, 27 Jun 2025

orgs.d: The Montoneros, an Argentine Peronist guerrilla movement of the 1970s, had one of its own inside an army regiment before attacking it. According to Infobae's account, drawing on Ceferino Reato's book, Luis Roberto Mayol was a Montonero who had served as a conscript at Regiment 29 in Formosa. On 5 October 1975 about 50 Montoneros tried to seize 200 weapons there, planning to bring in attackers on a hijacked airliner, but conscripts fought back. Infobae counts 32 dead and El Litoral 28. The sources do not set out exactly what Mayol passed on.
orgs.cite: Infobae, 27 Nov 2018; El Litoral; Wikipedia, Operation Primicia
orgs.reach_src: Infobae, 27 Nov 2018; El Litoral; Wikipedia, Operation Primicia

orgs.d: The Tupamaros, Uruguay's urban guerrilla movement and later a legal political force, recruited a sailor inside the navy to open a training centre to its raiders. According to the Cuban journal Pensamiento Crítico, second-class sailor Fernando Gorin, on guard at the navy's training centre in Montevideo in late May 1970, gave the signal, disarmed the roof sentry and helped subdue the duty petty officer. Militants identifying themselves as police were let in and left with over 300 long arms. Uruguayan police files list about 300 rifles, 170 revolvers and 30 pistols taken. Gorin went underground.
orgs.cite: Pensamiento Crítico no. 43, Aug 1970; Sitios de Memoria Uruguay
orgs.reach_src: Pensamiento Crítico no. 43, Aug 1970; Sitios de Memoria Uruguay

orgs.n: Communist Party of Venezuela (PCV) and Revolutionary Left Movement (MIR)
orgs.d: Venezuela's Communist Party and the Revolutionary Left Movement, opposition parties of the early 1960s, had links with serving officers who rose against President Rómulo Betancourt. On 4 May 1962 Captain Jesús Molina Villegas, Major Pedro Vegas Castejón and Lieutenant Héctor Fleming Mendoza led a marine battalion and a National Guard detachment in a rising at Carúpano. Accounts name party figures involved, including Congressman Eloy Torres and Douglas Bravo. Loyal forces retook the town within a day; one count gives 56 dead. Betancourt suspended both parties' activities by decree, and a second rising followed at Puerto Cabello.
orgs.cite: El Ciudadano, on the Carupanazo; Wikipedia, El Carupanazo
orgs.reach_src: El Ciudadano, on the Carupanazo; Wikipedia, El Carupanazo

orgs.d: M23 is a rebel movement fighting Congo's army in the east, which UN experts say Rwanda backs, and it has been accused of working with insiders in Congolese politics and mining. A military court found that sitting MP Édouard Mwangachuchu, who owned a company mining coltan at Rubaya, took part in M23. It sentenced him to death for treason on 6 October 2023 and said his minerals went to Rwanda. His lawyers said no link to Rwanda was proved. His appeal was pending in March 2024, and no result was found.
orgs.cite: Africanews, 7 Oct 2023; Actualite.cd, 14 Mar 2024; Wikipedia, Édouard Mwangachuchu
orgs.reach_src: Africanews, 7 Oct 2023; Actualite.cd, 14 Mar 2024; Wikipedia, Édouard Mwangachuchu

orgs.d: Hizbul Mujahideen, an armed group fighting Indian rule in Kashmir, allegedly has helpers on the state payroll. A National Investigation Agency charge sheet alleges police officer Davinder Singh, stopped in January 2020 with two Hizbul militants in his car, sheltered a commander and moved militants in his own vehicle; the reports give no verdict. Authorities also say about 80 Jammu and Kashmir employees, including two sons of Hizbul's leader, were dismissed as alleged collaborators with armed groups over five years. These dismissals need no inquiry, so the allegations are untested, and critics call them arbitrary.
orgs.cite: The Quint, 2020-2021; The Wire, 6 Jul 2020; Scroll, Jul 2021; Kashmir Life, 2023; ETV Bharat, 30 Oct 2025
orgs.reach_src: The Quint, 2020-2021; The Wire, 6 Jul 2020; Scroll, Jul 2021; Kashmir Life, 2023; ETV Bharat, 30 Oct 2025

orgs.d: Al-Qaeda's South Asian branch claimed an attack that relied on serving Pakistan Navy officers. On 6 September 2014 attackers came aboard the frigate PNS Zulfiqar at Karachi Naval Dockyard in uniform, showing service cards. The branch said it meant to turn the ship's missiles on American and Indian naval vessels, though the Pakistani Taliban also claimed the attack. A closed navy tribunal sentenced five officers to death in 2016 for terrorist links, mutiny and conspiracy, and one officer's father said the charge named Islamic State links. The navy has refused to release its inquiry report.
orgs.cite: Nukta, Dec 2024; Asia Times, Jun 2016; The Express Tribune, May 2016
orgs.reach_src: Nukta, Dec 2024; Asia Times, Jun 2016; The Express Tribune, May 2016

orgs.d: The Arab Movement of Azawad is an armed group in northern Mali whose pro-government wing had a member in parliament. Mohamed Ould Mataly sat in the National Assembly for President Keita's party while, according to UN listing summaries, being an influential member of the wing. The summaries say he and its military chief of staff coordinated an armed blockade of regional consultations in Gao in November 2018, stopping discussion of key parts of the 2015 peace deal. The UN listed him in July 2019 and froze his assets that December.
orgs.cite: UN Security Council Mali sanctions list via Hong Kong SFC; Kharon Brief, Dec 2019; Arab News/AFP, 10 July 2019
orgs.reach_src: UN Security Council Mali sanctions list via Hong Kong SFC; Kharon Brief, Dec 2019; Arab News/AFP, 10 July 2019

orgs.n: High Council for the Unity of Azawad (HCUA)
orgs.d: The High Council for the Unity of Azawad was an armed group in northern Mali, part of the CMA rebel coalition, which placed a member beside the region's state administration. According to the UN sanctions list, Ahmed Ag Albachar became special adviser to the Governor of Kidal in early 2018 and chaired the humanitarian commission of the regional administration. Sanctions findings summarised by Kharon, a research firm, say he used this to control aid projects and to intimidate and extort aid organisations. The UN listed him in July 2019 and froze his assets that December.
orgs.cite: UN Security Council Mali sanctions list via Hong Kong SFC and Government of Jersey; Kharon Brief, Dec 2019
orgs.reach_src: UN Security Council Mali sanctions list via Hong Kong SFC and Government of Jersey; Kharon Brief, Dec 2019

orgs.d: TIGO Guatemala, a mobile phone company owned by Millicom, bought support inside Guatemala's Congress with monthly cash bribes from 2012 to 2018, and the members backed laws that helped it. US prosecutors say a then-Guatemalan shareholder and senior staff ran the scheme. A law-firm account says cash reached the offices by helicopter and in duffel bags, and that some came from a banker laundering a drug trafficker's money. In November 2025 TIGO paid over $118 million under a deferred prosecution agreement, which holds off charges if it meets its terms for two years. No bribed official has been named.
orgs.cite: US Justice Department, 12 Dec 2025; Cleary Gottlieb client memo, 2025
orgs.reach_src: US Justice Department, 12 Dec 2025; Cleary Gottlieb client memo, 2025

orgs.d: Tenaris, the Luxembourg-based steel pipe supplier, made improper payments to staff of O'ztashqineftgaz, a state-controlled Uzbek oil and gas producer, to win contracts. For four public bids it hired an agent to obtain competitors' bid information, then secretly submitted better revised bids. It agreed to pay the agent 3.5% of the contracts' value, while aware or substantially certain that all or part would go to the firm's employees. In May 2011 it agreed a $3.5 million penalty with the US Justice Department and paid regulators $5,428,338. It had reported the conduct itself.
orgs.cite: US Justice Department press release 11-629, 17 May 2011; Eurasianet, 2011
orgs.reach_src: US Justice Department press release 11-629, 17 May 2011; Eurasianet, 2011

orgs.n: Alliance One International (formerly Dimon; now Pyxus)
orgs.d: Dimon, a global tobacco trader that became part of Alliance One International, paid Kyrgyz government officials so that its local subsidiary could buy tobacco. According to the US Securities and Exchange Commission, it paid more than $3 million in bribes, most of it delivered in bags of $100 bills to a high-ranking official, with tax officials also paid. The conduct began as early as 1996. In 2010 Alliance One paid $10 million in disgorgement, meaning surrender of profits, and accepted a monitor for three years. Its subsidiaries paid a $9.45 million criminal fine.
orgs.cite: US Securities and Exchange Commission press release 2010-144, 6 Aug 2010
orgs.reach_src: US Securities and Exchange Commission press release 2010-144, 6 Aug 2010

orgs.d: Och-Ziff, a New York hedge fund, lent money to a business partner in Congo, and a significant part paid high-ranking officials for access to state-controlled mines, US regulators said. More than $100 million was alleged over ten years, and one reported $11 million went to the official Augustin Katumba Mwanke. The fund settled for $413 million in September 2016 under the US foreign bribery law, and a subsidiary pleaded guilty. A person familiar with the matter identified the partner as Dan Gertler, who denied the allegations and had not been charged.
orgs.cite: Global Witness, 29 Sep 2016; Bloomberg via Mining Weekly, 30 Sep 2016; Quartz, 30 Sep 2016
orgs.reach_src: Global Witness, 29 Sep 2016; Bloomberg via Mining Weekly, 30 Sep 2016; Quartz, 30 Sep 2016

orgs.d: Areva, the French nuclear group, got money to two senior Mongolian officials through a chain of consultants while building its uranium business there. According to the Paris court president, it signed a €4 million contract with Eurotradia International, which signed a consultancy deal with a Mongolian businessman who received €1.275 million. He invested in a property project controlled by one official and paid a second; both had helped Areva set up in Mongolia. In December 2024 Areva agreed a €4.8 million fine under a French settlement that avoids trial. Orano Mining says it does not admit responsibility.
orgs.cite: Reuters via Easybourse, 9 Dec 2024; Pinsent Masons Out-Law, 17 Dec 2024
orgs.reach_src: Reuters via Easybourse, 9 Dec 2024; Pinsent Masons Out-Law, 17 Dec 2024

orgs.d: ADP Ingénierie, the engineering arm of the Paris airports group, allegedly gave a representative of the Emirate of Fujairah a personal share of its work there. Under an agreement with him, he and his company received commissions of 5% and 21.5% on payments to ADPI for Fujairah work. In 2011 ADPI also gave an excessively priced housing estate contract, with no deliverables found, to a subcontractor he majority-owned. The French settlement approved on 4 December 2023 set a €14.6 million fine. It also covered a Libyan airport tender where ADPI had confidential information.
orgs.cite: International Bar Association, 'France: CJIPs and Sediver'
orgs.reach_src: International Bar Association, 'France: CJIPs and Sediver'

orgs.d: Société Générale, the French bank, won investments from Libya's state financial institutions by paying senior officials through a Libyan intermediary. From 2004 to 2009 it paid him more than $90 million in commissions of 1.5% to 3% on fourteen transactions, and part of that money was diverted to officials. The transactions earned the bank $523 million in profit. In 2018 it settled with US prosecutors and France's financial prosecutor, whose settlement set a fine of €250,150,755. It was the first such French settlement negotiated in cooperation with the US Justice Department.
orgs.cite: Paul Weiss client memo, 7 June 2018; JD Supra; Les Petites Affiches, 2018
orgs.reach_src: Paul Weiss client memo, 7 June 2018; JD Supra; Les Petites Affiches, 2018

orgs.d: Total, the French oil company, paid about $30 million, disguised as a consulting contract with a firm called Baston, to help secure a deal on Iran's South Pars gas field. Prosecutors said much of the money was meant for Mehdi Rafsanjani, son of former president Hashemi Rafsanjani, who then ran subsidiaries of the National Iranian Oil Company. On 21 December 2018 a Paris court convicted Total of corrupting foreign officials over payments from 2000 to 2004 and fined it €500,000. It had paid US authorities $398 million in 2013.
orgs.cite: AFP via Tradingsat, 21 Dec 2018; RFE/RL, 21 Dec 2018
orgs.reach_src: AFP via Tradingsat, 21 Dec 2018; RFE/RL, 21 Dec 2018

orgs.d: Technip, the engineering group, reached Petrobras, Brazil's state oil company, through its Brazilian units. Technip Brasil and Flexibrás admitted unlawful acts, including improper advantages to public agents, in a leniency deal, an agreement to cooperate in exchange for lighter penalties. It was announced on 25 June 2019 as the first global deal of Operation Car Wash. They agreed to pay about R$1.13 billion, including R$191 million as restitution of bribes and damages to Petrobras. They gave evidence on more than 40 people and companies. The reports do not name the bribed officials.
orgs.cite: CGU/AGU leniency agreement, 2019; Legismap, 26 June 2019; Suno Notícias, 25 June 2019; Felsberg Advogados, 12 July 2019
orgs.reach_src: CGU/AGU leniency agreement, 2019; Legismap, 26 June 2019; Suno Notícias, 25 June 2019; Felsberg Advogados, 12 July 2019

orgs.n: MullenLowe Brasil and FCB Brasil (Interpublic Group agencies)
orgs.d: MullenLowe Brasil and FCB Brasil, advertising agencies then owned by the Interpublic Group, accepted responsibility for paying bribes to win advertising bids at Brazilian federal bodies: the state bank Caixa, the health ministry and the fuel distributor BR Distribuidora. In 2015 Judge Sergio Moro convicted former deputy André Vargas and Ricardo Hoffmann, a former MullenLowe director, over about R$1.1 million paid to companies controlled by Vargas and his brothers. An appeal court upheld the convictions in 2017. A joint leniency deal in April 2018 returned R$53.1 million to the bodies affected.
orgs.cite: IstoÉ Dinheiro, 16 Mar 2018; Tribuna do Paraná/Estadão, 16 Apr 2018; Exame, Sept 2015; Jornal do Comércio, 31 May 2017
orgs.reach_src: IstoÉ Dinheiro, 16 Mar 2018; Tribuna do Paraná/Estadão, 16 Apr 2018; Exame, Sept 2015; Jornal do Comércio, 31 May 2017

orgs.d: Braskem, Brazil's petrochemical company, obtained federal contracts and official rules with improper payments, according to the federal comptroller (CGU). It signed a leniency deal, a cooperation agreement that reduces penalties, with the CGU and attorney general's office on 31 May 2019, agreeing to pay R$2.87 billion by January 2025. The CGU said the sum covers damage, illicit enrichment and fines over fraudulent contracts and over normative acts, meaning official rules, produced from improper payments. Braskem gave evidence on more than 60 people and companies. The report does not name the officials or the rules.
orgs.cite: Estadão via Tribuna do Paraná, 3 June 2019
orgs.reach_src: Estadão via Tribuna do Paraná, 3 June 2019

orgs.d: Alstom, the French power and rail engineering group, used consultants to disguise bribes that reached a senior Indonesian member of parliament and the head of the state electricity company. The money helped win a $118 million contract for Alstom Power and the Japanese trader Marubeni. Alstom and three subsidiaries resolved a US case with the Justice Department in December 2014. Charges against a former senior executive, Lawrence Hoskins, were brought in July 2013, and in November 2019 a jury convicted him on 11 of 12 counts. Later rulings in his case are not covered in the record.
orgs.cite: Miller & Chevalier, FCPA Winter Review 2020

orgs.d: Teva, the Israeli drug maker, paid health officials to steer state purchasing and approvals towards its drugs, the US Justice Department says. Executives and staff at its Russian subsidiary paid a high-ranking Russian official to boost sales of Copaxone in health ministry auctions from 2010 to at least 2012. It also paid a senior Ukrainian health official about $200,000, and its Mexican subsidiary paid government doctors. On 22 December 2016 it agreed a $283 million criminal penalty and about $236 million to the Securities and Exchange Commission. The sources do not name the officials.
orgs.cite: US Justice Department, 22 Dec 2016; Phillips & Cohen
orgs.reach_src: US Justice Department, 22 Dec 2016; Phillips & Cohen

orgs.n: Mitsubishi Hitachi Power Systems (now Mitsubishi Power)
orgs.d: Executives of this Japanese power-equipment maker paid a Thai Transport Ministry official 11 million baht in February 2015 for favourable treatment when unloading cargo that had failed clearance conditions. The firm held a 30-billion-baht contract to supply a gas-fired power plant in Nakhon Si Thammarat. The case came out in Japan's first plea bargain, in which the company avoided indictment by cooperating. In 2020 the Tokyo High Court fined former executive Satoshi Uchida ¥2.5 million, finding he failed to stop the bribe, and he appealed. No Thai officials had been charged by 2019.
orgs.cite: Bangkok Post/Kyodo, 13 Sep 2019; Japan Times, 21 Jul 2020; MLex, 4 Aug 2020
orgs.reach_src: Bangkok Post/Kyodo, 13 Sep 2019; Japan Times, 21 Jul 2020; MLex, 4 Aug 2020

orgs.d: Rikvip, an online gambling operation in Vietnam, had two senior police chiefs covering for it inside the Ministry of Public Security. Its sites drew up to 42.9 million players and VND9.85 trillion in revenue in 28 months. The court found Phan Van Vinh, head of the General Police Department, and Nguyen Thanh Hoa, head of high-tech crime police, covered up its activity. Vinh had signed the decision setting up the ring leader's firm, CNC, a ministry shell company. They got nine and ten years in 2018. Ring leader Nguyen Van Duong said he gave both large sums, which they denied.
orgs.cite: Viet Nam News, 30 Nov 2018; Tuoi Tre News, 30 Nov 2018
orgs.reach_src: Viet Nam News, 30 Nov 2018; Tuoi Tre News, 30 Nov 2018

orgs.d: Union Development Group, which the US Treasury calls a Chinese state-owned company, allegedly used a local company and Cambodia's military to obtain and clear coastal land. Treasury says it got a 99-year lease in 2008 on the Dara Sakor project, almost 20 per cent of Cambodia's coastline, by forming a local company as leaseholder, with ownership later reverting to Chinese hands. It says the military used violence to help clear land and that Kun Kim, a senior general, benefited financially. Treasury imposed sanctions in 2020. Cambodia and China rejected the allegations.
orgs.cite: AP via KSL, 16 Sep 2020; US Treasury press release sm1121, 15 Sep 2020
orgs.reach_src: AP via KSL, 16 Sep 2020; US Treasury press release sm1121, 15 Sep 2020

orgs.d: Nuctech, a Chinese state-owned maker of security scanners, was accused in Namibia of inflating a roughly $55.3 million finance ministry deal to fund a 'commission' for a firm owned by a serving official. Prosecutors alleged at least $12.8 million went to Teko Trading, owned by Public Service Commission member Teckla Lameck and her partner Jerobeam Mokaxwa, and said Teko had no role in the deal. They and Nuctech's Africa representative, Yang Fan, were arrested in July 2009 and later found not guilty of fraud and corruption.
orgs.cite: AFP via Solar Daily, 21 July 2009; The Namibian; NBC News Namibia
orgs.reach_src: AFP via Solar Daily, 21 July 2009; The Namibian; NBC News Namibia

orgs.d: Panalpina, a Swiss freight company, and its oil-sector customers paid officials of the Nigeria Customs Service through brokers so that import rules were set aside, according to US regulators. From about 2002 to 2007, GlobalSantaFe paid for documents showing rigs had left Nigerian waters when they had never moved, Noble obtained import permits with false papers, and Tidewater reimbursed a broker about $1.6 million. Invoices called the bribes 'special handling' or 'local processing' fees. In November 2010 the firms settled with US authorities, the seven companies paying more than $236 million in all.
orgs.cite: US Securities and Exchange Commission, 4 Nov 2010; National Law Review, 2010
orgs.reach_src: US Securities and Exchange Commission, 4 Nov 2010; National Law Review, 2010

orgs.d: The Taliban is the Islamist movement that ruled Afghanistan from 1996 and again from 2021, and it got inside the republic it was fighting by enlisting serving soldiers and policemen rather than only attacking them from outside. Recruits already in uniform were used for so-called insider or green-on-blue killings: in three months of 2021 Taliban men inside the Afghan army and police shot 115 of their own colleagues. The same method gave the movement advance notice of operations and let whole checkpoints and units change sides as districts fell.
orgs.cite: Reporting on Taliban insider attacks on Afghan army and police units, 2021.

orgs.d: Ansar Allah, usually called the Houthi movement, is the Zaidi Shia armed movement that seized Sanaa in 2014 and now runs the institutions of northern Yemen. It takes over a state body by installing loyalists in its management and supervisory posts rather than abolishing it. The national carrier Yemenia Airways is the clearest case: Houthi-appointed people hold its Sanaa offices, decide its routes and staffing, and the authorities have kept about $100 million of the airline's revenue held in Sanaa accounts out of reach of the rival government in Aden.
orgs.cite: Reporting and UN panel material on Houthi control of Yemenia Airways and its funds.

orgs.d: The Rapid Support Forces grew out of Darfur's Janjaweed militias and were given legal status as a Sudanese paramilitary force in 2013, building a business empire in gold, livestock and construction alongside their brigades. Companies tied to the force bought their way into the financial system: in 2019 RSF-linked firms took a majority stake in Al Khaleej Bank, giving the paramilitary group ownership of a licensed Sudanese bank and the payment channels that go with it. The force later fought the regular army for control of the state itself.
orgs.cite: Reporting on RSF-linked companies' majority stake in Al Khaleej Bank, 2019.

orgs.d: The Agwelek are a Shilluk armed force from the Upper Nile region of South Sudan, raised and led by Johnson Olony, which has moved in and out of the national army as peace deals were made and broken. Rather than being disbanded, the force was absorbed with its commander: Olony was appointed one of the deputy chiefs of staff of South Sudan's army in 2025, which put a militia leader and his own fighters inside the command structure they had previously fought. Their weapons and chain of command stayed theirs.
orgs.cite: Reporting on Johnson Olony's appointment as a deputy army chief of staff, 2025.

orgs.n: Babylon Movement and Kataib Babiliyoun (PMF 50th Brigade)
orgs.d: The Babylon Movement is the political wing of Kataib Babiliyoun, the 50th Brigade of Iraq's Popular Mobilisation Forces, led by Rayan al-Kildani and aligned with Iran. It is nominally a Christian militia and party, and it uses that label to capture the seats and offices reserved for Iraq's Christian minority. With mostly Shia votes behind it, the movement took the quota seats set aside for Christians in parliament and positions on the Nineveh provincial council, so that representation meant for a community passed to an armed group it largely rejects.
orgs.cite: Reporting on Babylon Movement's capture of Iraq's Christian quota seats and Nineveh council posts.

orgs.d: Kataib Hezbollah is an Iran-aligned Iraqi militia that was folded into the state as brigades of the Popular Mobilisation Forces, so its fighters draw government salaries and carry official authority. It uses that standing to settle who holds public office. In 2025 its state-paid brigades stormed a Baghdad government office to keep their own appointee in place, a show of force by men formally under the prime minister's command against the administration they belong to. The group also holds commercial and security interests built on its position inside the apparatus.
orgs.cite: Reporting on Kataib Hezbollah brigades storming a Baghdad office over an appointment, 2025.

orgs.d: Jemaah Islamiyah was a clandestine South-East Asian militant network, responsible for the 2002 Bali bombings, which kept a legal face in schools, charities and religious bodies while its armed wing operated underground. That double life reached the top of Indonesia's religious establishment: a Jemaah Islamiyah leader sat on the fatwa commission of the Indonesian Ulema Council, the body whose rulings guide the state on religious questions. The network's leaders announced its dissolution in 2024, after years of arrests and the unpicking of its foundations and boarding schools.
orgs.cite: Reporting on a JI leader's seat on Indonesia's Ulema Council fatwa commission; 2024 dissolution statements.

orgs.d: TÜGVA, the Turkey Youth Foundation, is a youth organisation founded in 2013 whose board has included President Erdogan's son, and which runs student houses and courses across the country. Leaked internal files published in 2021 showed it working as a placement service for the state: the foundation kept lists of its own members and recommended them for posts in ministries, the judiciary, the police and state companies, with notes on which officials would help. Public jobs were being distributed through a private foundation's membership rolls.
orgs.cite: Leaked TÜGVA files reported in 2021 on placement of members in state posts.

orgs.d: The Proud Boys are a US far-right street movement founded in 2016, organised in local chapters and best known for the 6 January 2021 attack on the Capitol, for which several leaders were convicted of seditious conspiracy. The movement also draws on sympathisers inside police forces. A police lieutenant in Washington State was found to have passed inside information to a Proud Boys leader, including warnings about investigations, giving the group advance knowledge of what the authorities were preparing against it.
orgs.cite: Reporting and court material on a Washington police lieutenant feeding information to a Proud Boys leader.

orgs.d: The Order of Nine Angles is a British-founded occult neo-Nazi order, organised as scattered cells rather than a membership body, which openly urges followers to join armies and police forces to gain training and access for attacks. One American follower did exactly that: he enlisted in the US Army and passed details of his own unit's movements and defences to an outside contact so that it could be ambushed. The order's writings treat such service as a test of commitment, and its influence runs through several militant accelerationist groups.
orgs.cite: US prosecution of an O9A follower who joined the Army and passed his unit's plans.

orgs.d: A loose network of lawyers, businessmen and activists formed after the 2020 US presidential election to prove it had been stolen, and it got at voting equipment by persuading or recruiting the county officials who hold the keys. A Colorado clerk let an associate of Mike Lindell copy her county's election systems. Sidney Powell's team was admitted to a Georgia county office to image its machines. A Pennsylvania county allowed a Trump-allied firm to inspect its equipment, and three Michigan activists were charged over tabulators obtained from local clerks.
orgs.cite: Indictments and reporting from Colorado, Georgia, Pennsylvania and Michigan, 2021-2025.

orgs.d: The Awami League is Bangladesh's oldest major party and governed from 2009 until it was driven from office in 2024. In its later years the party worked through the officials who run elections rather than only through voters. Bangladesh's former chief election commissioner was arrested over the 2018 general election, the so-called midnight vote, in which ballot boxes were reported stuffed before polling began and the commission certified the result. The party's appointees also filled university and administrative posts, which is why the 2024 government removed them wholesale.
orgs.cite: Arrest of Bangladesh's former chief election commissioner over the 2018 election.

orgs.d: PDI-P is Indonesia's largest party and was in government from 2014 to 2024. Its reach into the machinery that counts votes came out in a bribery case: a party official paid a member of the General Elections Commission to move a parliamentary seat to a PDI-P candidate who had not won it. The commissioner was convicted, and the party's secretary general was later pursued over the same payments. Deciding who sits in parliament had been settled inside the commission rather than at the ballot box.
orgs.cite: Convictions in the Indonesian General Elections Commission bribery case.

orgs.n: Polish communist Security Service (Służba Bezpieczeństwa, SB)
orgs.d: The Służba Bezpieczeństwa was the secret police of communist Poland, and its foreign department worked hard on the Catholic Church, recruiting priests and lay staff as informants. That effort reached the Vatican itself: Polish files opened after 1989 showed the service ran an informant inside the Holy See, reporting on its offices and on the Polish pope's circle. Recruitment relied on travel permits, family pressure and payment, and the records were kept well enough that the identities surfaced decades later in church and state archives.
orgs.cite: Polish archive material on SB informants in the Vatican, published from 2005.

orgs.d: The BIA is Serbia's civilian intelligence service, created in 2002 out of the former State Security Service, and it works across the former Yugoslavia through politicians, journalists and businessmen in neighbouring states. In North Macedonia a BIA officer was recorded giving instructions to a serving member of parliament during the political crisis over the country's name, a case reported alongside parallel Russian activity. The service's advantage is language and family ties: handlers meet contacts as compatriots rather than as foreign agents.
orgs.cite: Reporting on a BIA officer instructing a North Macedonian MP, 2017.

orgs.n: Azerbaijani special services (State Security Service and military intelligence)
orgs.d: Azerbaijan's security and military intelligence services run agents inside the Armenian forces they have fought over Nagorno-Karabakh. They recruit at a distance and cheaply: officers were approached through fake social-media profiles offering money or compromising material, a method Armenian counter-intelligence described after several arrests. The results were military. An Armenian army commander was convicted of passing troop positions and movements to Azerbaijan during the 2020 war, information that bore directly on where attacks fell and on how many soldiers died.
orgs.cite: Armenian prosecutions of officers recruited by Azerbaijani services, 2021-2022.

orgs.n: Greek military junta (Regime of the Colonels)
orgs.d: The colonels who seized power in Greece in 1967 ruled through officers rather than parties, and they held Cyprus in the same way, by the Greek officers who commanded the island's National Guard and the mainland contingent. In July 1974 Dimitrios Ioannidis used those officers to overthrow President Makarios and install Nikos Sampson, a coup carried out by the island's own armed forces under Athens's direction. Turkey invaded within days, Cyprus was partitioned, and the junta fell in Athens weeks later.
orgs.cite: Accounts of the 1974 coup against Makarios by junta-controlled Cypriot National Guard officers.

orgs.d: The Tito and Dino cartel is a cocaine network run by the Bosnian-Dutch trafficker Edin Gacanin from Dubai, shipping to Europe through Latin American suppliers and ranked by police among the largest wholesale importers on the continent. Its protection was bought at home. Bosnian officials were alleged to have taken payments from the Gacanin organisation, and Bosnia's special police chief was detained over ties to the cartel, which put a man in charge of serious-crime policing within reach of the group he was supposed to pursue.
orgs.cite: Europol and Bosnian prosecution material on the Gacanin network and officials, 2024.

orgs.d: Los Lobos are the largest of the gangs that broke away from Los Choneros and now hold much of Ecuador's cocaine export trade, its prisons and some of its illegal gold mining. They work the justice system from the inside through court and prosecution employees. In Babahoyo a worker in the prosecutor's office was alleged to be acting for Los Lobos, with access to case files and to the timing of operations. Judges and prison staff elsewhere in the country have faced similar accusations.
orgs.cite: Ecuadorian prosecution reporting on a Babahoyo prosecutor's office employee linked to Los Lobos, 2025.

orgs.d: The Akasha family of Mombasa ran one of East Africa's biggest heroin networks, moving Afghan product through the Kenyan coast to Europe, and bought the institutions that might have stopped it. Baktash and Ibrahim Akasha were found to have paid Kenyan judges, prosecutors and police to keep cases from reaching trial, and earlier charges against the family collapsed in just that way. They were eventually taken out of Kenya altogether: extradited to the United States in 2017 and sentenced in New York.
orgs.cite: US prosecution and Kenyan reporting on Akasha payments to judges, prosecutors and police.

orgs.d: Semion Mogilevich is a Ukrainian-born organised crime figure who built his business around companies rather than street rackets, using banks, trading firms and front shareholders across Europe and Israel. His reach was alleged to extend to the gas trade between Russia and Ukraine: investigators and US cables said he stood behind RosUkrEnergo, the intermediary company that took a margin on every unit of gas crossing into Ukraine and whose contracts were settled by the two governments. He was on the FBI's most wanted list and never tried in the West.
orgs.cite: US and Ukrainian investigative material on Mogilevich's alleged control of RosUkrEnergo.

orgs.d: Truong Van Cam, known as Nam Cam, ran gambling dens, protection and loan-sharking in Ho Chi Minh City, and survived for years by paying the officials who were supposed to close him down. The 2003 trial, the largest corruption case Vietnam had held, convicted more than one hundred people with him, among them a city police chief and a senior prosecutor who had taken his money and warned him of operations. Nam Cam was executed in 2004 and the network broken up.
orgs.cite: Vietnamese court records and reporting from the 2003 Nam Cam trial.

orgs.d: Roberto Suárez Gómez was Bolivia's dominant cocaine supplier in the late 1970s, flying paste to the Medellín Cartel for refining, and he bought a government outright rather than merely bribing one. His money and his aircraft helped finance the 1980 Cocaine Coup that put General Luis García Meza in power, after which traffickers held interior ministry posts and the state's own security apparatus protected the trade. Suárez was arrested in 1988 and the junta's officials were later convicted of the coup.
orgs.cite: Accounts and Bolivian trials of the 1980 coup financed by Suárez.

orgs.n: Vasil Bozhkov's gambling and political network
orgs.d: Vasil Bozhkov built Bulgaria's largest betting business and surrounded it with football clubs, media and political funding. The regulator meant to police the industry was staffed by his people: Bulgarian prosecutors charged officials of the state gambling commission as members of a criminal group run by Bozhkov, accusing them of setting licences and inspections to suit his companies and squeeze competitors. Bozhkov left for Dubai in 2020 as the charges were brought, and later returned to contest them and to fund a party.
orgs.cite: Bulgarian prosecution case against gambling commission officials as members of Bozhkov's group, 2020.

orgs.n: Kamlesh Pattni's gold and diamond network
orgs.d: Kamlesh Pattni is the Kenyan businessman at the centre of the 1990s Goldenberg affair, in which fictitious gold exports drained the Kenyan treasury, and he rebuilt the same trade elsewhere in Africa. Britain and the United States sanctioned him in 2024 over Zimbabwe's gold business, finding that he paid officials to obtain export licences and preferential access and used diplomatic cover and state marketing channels to move the metal, taking a cut from a trade the state was supposed to control.
orgs.cite: UK and US sanctions designations of Kamlesh Pattni, 2024; Goldenberg inquiry records.

orgs.n: Haftar family network and its financiers
orgs.d: Khalifa Haftar's Libyan Arab Armed Forces hold eastern Libya, and the family around him, with his sons Saddam and Khaled and the financier Ahmed Gadalla, has taken the financial institutions there as well as the ground. Haftar-linked men took over the Bank of Commerce and Development in Benghazi; a $300 million state deposit was used to back loans to a Gadalla company; Wahda Bank issued $55 million in uncovered cheques under the same influence; and a Haftar-aligned chairman was reported to run the National Oil Corporation's eastern operations for the family.
orgs.cite: Reporting and audit material on Haftar-linked control of Libyan banks and oil institutions, 2019-2024.

orgs.n: Zdravko Mamić's football and bribery network
orgs.d: Zdravko Mamić ran Dinamo Zagreb and, through it, much of Croatian football, taking a share of players' transfer fees and spending part of it on the judges who heard his cases. He was accused of paying three Croatian judges for favourable rulings, and the president of Bosnia's state court was accused of taking a bribe from him, which put the senior judiciary of two countries inside the same payments. Mamić fled to Bosnia and Herzegovina, where he avoided extradition while his Croatian convictions stood.
orgs.cite: Croatian and Bosnian prosecution material on payments from Mamić to judges.

orgs.d: Marian Kočner was a Slovak property businessman who kept judges, prosecutors and officials on call and recorded his dealings with them. The encrypted Threema messages seized from him in 2018 exposed thirteen Slovak judges, several of whom were charged or removed, and showed him asking for rulings, delays and files in cases that concerned his companies. He was convicted of forging promissory notes and later of ordering the murder of the journalist Ján Kuciak, who had been investigating him, a conviction reached after an acquittal was overturned.
orgs.cite: Slovak prosecutions arising from the Threema messages seized from Kočner.

orgs.d: Norbert Bödör is a Slovak businessman from Nitra whose family security and services companies lived on state contracts, and whose influence was alleged to run through the police rather than around it. Investigators accused his group of effectively choosing Slovakia's police leadership, with senior officers appointed and protected on his say and investigations into his associates steered away. Several of those officers were charged after the 2020 change of government, and Bödör was prosecuted in connection with payments to police and tax officials.
orgs.cite: Slovak charges against senior police officers and Bödör, 2020 onwards.

orgs.d: Juan Antonio Roca was Marbella's municipal planning chief, and he turned the town hall into a shop for building permissions, collecting payments from property developers through a web of companies while holding no elected office. The Malaya investigation in 2006 found councillors, mayors and officials on the same payments, and the Spanish government dissolved the town council, the first such dissolution in modern Spain. Roca was convicted and jailed, and the assets seized included art, estates and racehorses bought with the proceeds.
orgs.cite: Spanish Malaya case judgments and the 2006 dissolution of Marbella council.

orgs.d: The JLN Group was Janet Lim-Napoles's cluster of trading companies and fake non-governmental organisations, built to receive Philippine lawmakers' discretionary development funds. Legislators signed their allocations over to her paper NGOs for projects that were never carried out, and the money came back to them as commissions, with officials of the implementing agencies paid to sign off the transfers. The scheme ran for years and about ten billion pesos went through it before whistleblowers and an audit exposed it in 2013; senators were charged and Napoles convicted.
orgs.cite: Philippine Commission on Audit report and plunder prosecutions, 2013 onwards.

orgs.d: Jack Abramoff ran a Washington lobbying practice that billed Native American casino tribes tens of millions and spent part of it on the officials whose decisions his clients needed. Congressman Bob Ney took trips, meals and skybox tickets and put statements into the record for Abramoff's clients; staff were hired out of congressional offices and placed back into them; and interior department officials were courted over tribal gaming rulings. Abramoff, Ney and several aides and officials were convicted between 2006 and 2008.
orgs.cite: US prosecutions of Abramoff, Representative Ney and associated officials, 2006-2008.

orgs.n: Salt Lake City 2002 Olympic bid committee
orgs.d: The committee that won the 2002 Winter Olympics for Salt Lake City worked on the International Olympic Committee members who cast the votes, treating them as the market for its campaign. It paid cash, medical treatment, shopping trips and university tuition for members' relatives, spending that surfaced in 1998 and led the IOC in Lausanne to expel or sanction more than a dozen of its own members. Two bid executives were prosecuted and acquitted; the rules on gifts and visits to candidate cities were rewritten afterwards.
orgs.cite: IOC inquiry findings of 1999 and US prosecution of the Salt Lake bid executives.

orgs.n: Sports-marketing companies in the FIFA case (Traffic, Torneos y Competencias, Full Play, Media World, Klefer)
orgs.d: These are the marketing firms that bought and resold the television and sponsorship rights to football in the Americas, and they secured those contracts by paying the officials who awarded them. The United States prosecution begun in 2015 showed Traffic, Torneos y Competencias, Full Play, Media World and Klefer paying confederation and federation presidents year after year. Those who admitted taking the money included CONCACAF's Jeffrey Webb and Alfredo Hawit, CONMEBOL's Juan Angel Napout, and the federation heads of Colombia, Costa Rica, Chile, Nicaragua, Brazil, Honduras and Venezuela.
orgs.cite: US Department of Justice FIFA indictment and guilty pleas, 2015 onwards.

orgs.d: The Club de la Construcción was an agreement among Peruvian and foreign construction companies to share out the transport ministry's road contracts and to pay for the privilege. Prosecutors say the firms set aside a percentage of each contract for ministry officials and for the politicians above them, and divided at least thirty public works between themselves at prices fixed in advance. The case grew out of the Odebrecht confessions and named ministers of successive governments; several company executives became cooperating witnesses.
orgs.cite: Peruvian prosecutors' Club de la Construcción case files and cooperation agreements.

orgs.d: Equalize was a Milan private intelligence company that sold dossiers to businesses, lawyers and politicians, and filled them from inside the Italian state. Prosecutors allege in 2024 that it paid serving police officers and financial police to pull records from national law-enforcement and tax databases, and that it used an unlawful copy of an interior ministry system, assembling files on thousands of people including politicians and bankers. Its directors included a former police officer; the company was shut down and its managers arrested.
orgs.cite: Milan prosecutors' Equalize investigation, 2024.

orgs.d: MG Baltic is one of Lithuania's largest business groups, holding retail, construction, drinks and, importantly, television and news outlets. A Lithuanian court found that its vice-president had bribed the leader of the Liberal Movement and made payments to political parties in exchange for votes and influence over legislation that touched the group's businesses, with its media used in parallel. The Liberal Movement itself was convicted as a legal person, the first such conviction of a Lithuanian party, and MG Baltic was fined.
orgs.cite: Lithuanian court judgment in the MG Baltic political corruption case.

orgs.d: Daimler is the German maker of Mercedes-Benz vehicles, and for years it won government fleet orders by giving officials the cars and cash that went with them. A US settlement in 2010 covered payments in twenty-two countries, made through agents, inflated invoices and so-called third-party accounts. In Turkmenistan the company gave a top official an armoured Mercedes as a birthday present while the government was buying its vehicles. Daimler paid $185 million to settle the US charges and agreed to an outside monitor.
orgs.cite: US Department of Justice and SEC settlements with Daimler AG, 2010.

orgs.d: Baker Hughes is an American oilfield services company whose contracts depend on decisions by state oil companies and ministries. In 2007 it admitted a US foreign bribery case over Kazakhstan: $4.1 million was paid to an agent in the knowledge that the money was meant for an official of the state oil company, to help secure work on the Karachaganak field. The company paid about $44 million in penalties, one of the first to combine a criminal plea with a securities settlement, and dismissed the executives involved.
orgs.cite: US Department of Justice and SEC settlements with Baker Hughes, 2007.

orgs.d: Alcoa is the American aluminium producer, and its supply agreements with state-owned smelters were kept in place by payments to the people who signed them. A US settlement in 2014 found that Alcoa's Australian subsidiary used a London middleman to channel money to Bahraini royals and officials of Alba, the state aluminium company, inflating the price of alumina supplied to it and taking the difference out through the intermediary. Alcoa paid $384 million to settle the criminal and securities cases.
orgs.cite: US Department of Justice and SEC settlements with Alcoa, 2014.
